Configure via .spec.containers.readinessProbe with httpGet/tcpSocket/exec and fields like initialDelaySeconds, periodSeconds, successThreshold, and failureThreshold. During a Deployment rollout, kube-controller waits for new Pods to become Ready before progressing; verify with kubectl rollout status deployment/my-deploy and kubectl get endpoints my-service or kubectl get pods -o wide to see READY column. Use kubectl describe pod to inspect probe events and kube-apiserver metrics (endpoint controller) to troubleshoot. This prevents traffic to initializing containers and reduces failed requests during deployment.

5413. [Deployment Strategies and Rollback] What happens when readiness probes are incorrectly configured?
Answer: If readiness probes are misconfigured to fail, the kubelet marks Pods NotReady and the Endpoints controller removes them from Service endpoints so kube-proxy stops routing traffic; Deployments can stall because new replicas never receive traffic and rolling updates or canary promotions may not progress (check with kubectl rollout status deployment/<name>). If probes always succeed incorrectly, unhealthy Pods will receive production traffic and cause errors. Verify with kubectl get pods -o wide, kubectl describe pod <pod>, kubectl get endpoints <service>, kubectl logs <pod>, and curl or kubectl exec to exercise the probe path. Fixes include correcting HTTP/TCPSocket/exec probe fields and adjusting initialDelaySeconds, periodSeconds, failureThreshold, and successThreshold.


Pipeline Security
-----------------
5414. [Pipeline Security] How do you implement least privilege in pipelines?
Answer: Create distinct identities for CI/CD (separate runner/service accounts), grant only needed actions via minimal IAM roles, and prefer short‑lived or dynamic secrets (OIDC tokens, Vault dynamic DB/Cloud credentials). Example patterns: configure GitHub Actions OIDC to assume an AWS role (trust policy), use AWS IAM role with least privileges and verify with aws sts get-caller-identity and aws iam simulate-principal-policy. In Kubernetes use RBAC roles/RoleBindings and verify with kubectl auth can-i --as=system:serviceaccount:ci:runner create pods. Use Vault dynamic secrets (vault read database/creds/readonly) and enforce policy-as-code (OPA/conftest or terraform plan + sentinel) to block over-permissive bindings. Periodically audit with cloud IAM simulation and automated policy checks.

5415. [Pipeline Security] How do pipelines authenticate to cloud environments?
Answer: Pipelines authenticate using short‑lived credentials mapped to cloud identities: on GKE/GCE they use the metadata server token endpoint (GET http://metadata/computeMetadata/v1/instance/service-accounts/default/token with header Metadata‑Flavor: Google) or Workload Identity (bind Kubernetes service account to a Google service account via gcloud iam service-accounts add-iam-policy-binding --role roles/iam.workloadIdentityUser --member "serviceAccount:PROJECT.svc.id.goog[namespace/ksa]"); Cloud Build runs under its build service account. For external CI you use Workload Identity Federation (create a workload identity pool/provider and exchange external OIDC/AWS tokens for Google access tokens via sts:token). Verify by calling gcloud auth print-access-token, curling the metadata token endpoint, or inspecting iam policy with gcloud iam service-accounts get-iam-policy.

5416. [Pipeline Security] Should pipelines use service-account keys?
Answer: No — pipelines should not use long-lived service-account keys. Use short-lived, provider-native identities: GCP Workload Identity (bind K8s ServiceAccount to a GCP SA with gcloud iam service-accounts add-iam-policy-binding ... --member="serviceAccount:PROJECT.svc.id.goog[NAMESPACE/KSA]"), AWS OIDC + sts:assume-role (aws sts assume-role --role-arn arn:aws:iam::ACCOUNT:role/RoleName), or Azure Managed Identity. Verify by ensuring no active long-lived keys (GCP: gcloud iam service-accounts keys list --iam-account=SA && delete with gcloud iam service-accounts keys delete KEY_ID; AWS: aws iam list-access-keys/ delete-access-key) and by confirming tokens are short-lived (check token expiry or use aws eks get-token / kubectl describe pod). Long-lived keys should be deleted and replaced with short-lived credential flows.

5417. [Pipeline Security] How do you avoid long-lived credentials?
Answer: Use short-lived, automatically rotated identities: issue temporary AWS credentials via aws sts assume-role --role-arn arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/RoleName --duration-seconds 3600 and verify with aws sts get-caller-identity; use GCP Workload Identity (use google-auth library to fetch short-lived tokens) and verify with gcloud auth print-identity-token; prefer Azure Managed Identity (IMDS endpoints / MSI) instead of client secrets and verify via curl to http://169.254.169.254/metadata/identity/oauth2/token. In Kubernetes, use the TokenRequest API (kubectl create token my-sa --duration=1h) or project service account tokens; manage secrets via HashiCorp Vault (vault token create -ttl=1h) and enforce TTL/renewal. Automate rotation in CI/CD, refuse embedded secrets in repos, and monitor with IAM/CloudTrail logs for stale-credential usage.

5418. [Pipeline Security] How can GitHub Actions authenticate to GCP without a service-account key?
Answer: To authenticate to GCP without a service account key, you can use the `gcloud auth` command with the `--impersonate-service-account` flag and provide the email address of the service account. Alternatively, you can use the `gcloud auth application-default` command, which uses the default credentials set in the environment variables.

For GitHub Actions, you can use the `gcloud auth` command as a step in your workflow file to authenticate to GCP without a service account key. For example:

```yaml
steps:
  - name: Authenticate with GCP
    uses: google/gcs-github-action@v0
    with:
      gcp-service-account-email: 'your-service-account-email@google.com'
```

Or, you can use the `gcloud auth application-default` command as a step:

```yaml
steps:
  - name: Authenticate with GCP
    run: |
      gcloud auth application-default
```

This allows GitHub Actions to authenticate to GCP without requiring a service account key.

5419. [Pipeline Security] How do you secure self-hosted runners?
Answer: Use dedicated, patched hosts or ephemeral autoscaled runners (cloud images) and run the runner as an unprivileged user. Register with the official runner tools using an ephemeral registration token: ./config.sh --url https://github.com/org/repo --token TOKEN --unattended --name my-runner --labels self-hosted. Install as a service via ./svc.sh install && ./svc.sh start (or systemctl). Prefer containerized runners or ephemeral VMs to avoid stateful secrets, and use OIDC for cloud credentials instead of long-lived PATs; restrict repository/org runner access and use runner groups. Harden OS (patches, firewall, IMDSv2 for AWS), enforce least privilege on runner workdir ownership, and verify via systemctl status actions.runner.*.service, GitHub UI runner “Online” state, and Audit Log entries.

5420. [Pipeline Security] What are the risks of using self-hosted runners?
Answer: Self-hosted runners increase attack surface: a compromised runner gives attackers host-level access, potential lateral movement, and ability to exfiltrate secrets (GITHUB_TOKEN, other repo secrets) that workflows expose. They require patching, kernel/agent updates, and resource isolation you must manage—unpatched OS or stale runner binaries enable persistence. Untrusted PRs can execute code on your infrastructure (use pull_request_target cautiously). Verify and operate via the GitHub REST API GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/actions/runners to list registered runners, check runner status in systemd (systemctl status actions.runner.<name>.service) or process list (ps aux | grep Runner.Listener), and rotate/remove runners with DELETE /repos/{owner}/{repo}/actions/runners/{runner_id} to mitigate risk.

5421. [Pipeline Security] How do you isolate runners for different projects?
Answer: Use dedicated runner instances (or Kubernetes namespaces) per project, register them with project-scoped tokens, and enforce tag/lock policies. Example GitLab: on the runner host run gitlab-runner register --url https://gitlab.example.com/ --registration-token <project-token> --executor docker --docker-image alpine:3.17 --tag-list "project-a" --run-untagged=false --locked=true and verify with gitlab-runner verify. For GitHub Actions use the repo token and labels: ./config.sh --url https://github.com/OWNER/REPO --token <token> --labels project-a, then confirm via GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/actions/runners. On Kubernetes use separate namespaces, set values.runners.kubernetes.namespace and nodeSelector in the GitLab Runner Helm chart, and enforce resource limits via pod spec to prevent cross-project interference.

5422. [Pipeline Security] How do you restrict production deployment permissions?
Answer: Use least-privilege RBAC and workflow-enforced gates: create separate production IAM roles (AWS/GCP/Azure) and deny direct pushes; require role-assumption (aws sts assume-role) from CI. Enforce protected branches and required reviews using GitHub branch protection via API (PUT /repos/:owner/:repo/branches/:branch/protection) and require signed commits. Add environment protection rules (GitHub Environments approvals or GitLab environment approvals) and a ManualApproval action in AWS CodePipeline. Apply Kubernetes RBAC for prod namespaces and verify with kubectl auth can-i --namespace prod create deployments. Audit and verify with CloudTrail (aws cloudtrail lookup-events), GitHub audit log, or terraform plan/apply logs to confirm only authorized principals deployed.

5423. [Pipeline Security] How do you protect production environments?
Answer: Segment networks (VPCs, subnets, security groups, NACLs) and enforce least privilege via IAM and Service Control Policies; verify with aws iam get-role and aws organizations describe-policy. Store secrets in Vault or AWS Secrets Manager and access via kms-encrypted endpoints; test with vault kv get secret/path or aws secretsmanager get-secret-value. Scan images and IaC in CI: trivy image --severity HIGH,CRITICAL repo/image:tag and checkov --quiet -d . Sign artifacts (cosign sign --key key.pem repo/image:tag) and use immutable, canary deployments in CI/CD. Enable audit logging and detection: aws cloudtrail create-trail --name prod-trail --s3-bucket-name my-audit-bucket and validate with aws cloudtrail lookup-events. Monitor runtime with Falco and GuardDuty and enforce Kubernetes RBAC with kubectl get clusterrolebindings.

5424. [Pipeline Security] How do you configure branch protection?
Answer: Use the repository’s branch protection rules (UI: Settings → Branches → Add rule, or GitHub REST API PATCH /repos/{owner}/{repo}/branches/{branch}/protection). Configure JSON fields such as required_status_checks (strict and list of context names), required_pull_request_reviews (dismiss_stale_reviews, require_code_owner_reviews, required_approving_review_count), restrictions (users/teams/apps who can push), enforce_admins, required_conversation_resolution, required_linear_history, allow_force_pushes/allow_deletions. Example curl: curl -X PATCH -H "Authorization: token $GITHUB_TOKEN" -H "Accept: application/vnd.github+json" https://api.github.com/repos/owner/repo/branches/main/protection -d '{ "required_status_checks": {"strict": true, "contexts":["ci/build"]}, "enforce_admins": true }'. Verify with GET /branches/main/protection and confirm merges are blocked in the Pull Request UI.

5425. [Pipeline Security] How do you configure required reviewers?
Answer: On GitHub: enable a branch protection rule (Repository > Settings > Branches) or via API PUT /repos/{owner}/{repo}/branches/{branch}/protection with JSON key "required_pull_request_reviews" (e.g. "required_approving_review_count": 2). Use a CODEOWNERS file to auto-request specific reviewers. Verify with GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/branches/{branch}/protection or open a pull request—GitHub shows “x required reviewers” and blocks merge until satisfied.

On GitLab: set “Merge request approvals” in Project > Settings > General > Merge request approvals or via API PUT /projects/:id/merge_request_approvals (e.g. "approvals_before_merge": 2, "approver_ids"). Verify with GET /projects/:id/merge_request_approvals and by confirming the MR shows required approvals.

5426. [Pipeline Security] How do you restrict who can approve deployments?
Answer: Restrict approvals by enforcing least-privilege RBAC in the source control and CI/CD system, requiring explicit approver groups for protected environments (e.g., GitHub Environments or GitLab Protected Environments) and disabling broad “maintainer” approvals. Require human approval gates tied to an identity provider (SSO + MFA) and group membership, and separate deploy service accounts from human accounts. Enforce via policy-as-code (e.g., OPA/Gatekeeper) to block noncompliant runs. Verify by checking audit logs and pipeline run metadata for approver identity, by listing environment protection settings in your platform UI, and by testing a deploy attempt from a nonapproved account to confirm it is denied.

5427. [Pipeline Security] How do you prevent direct deployment from a developer branch?
Answer: Make the developer branch non-deployable by enforcing branch protection + pipeline gating and RBAC. In GitHub: enable Branch protection rules (Require pull request reviews, Require status checks to pass, Restrict who can push) and make deploy jobs conditional (example in GitHub Actions: if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'). Require environments for production deployments and add required reviewers in Settings → Environments; workflows using environment: production will block until approval. Verify protection via the API: curl -H "Authorization: token $TOKEN" https://api.github.com/repos/ORG/REPO/branches/dev/protection returns JSON. In GitLab, mark branch as Protected (Settings → Repository → Protected branches) and restrict who can merge/push. These measures prevent direct push or CI-triggered deploys from a developer branch.

5428. [Pipeline Security] How do you protect pipeline configuration files?
Answer: Store pipeline config in Git with branch-protection and signed-commit requirements, keep secrets out of repo, and fetch secrets at runtime from a secrets manager (HashiCorp Vault, AWS KMS/Secrets Manager, GCP Secret Manager). Encrypt any checked-in config with Mozilla SOPS (sops --encrypt config.yaml > config.yaml.enc; verify with sops --decrypt config.yaml.enc) or use sealed-secrets for Kubernetes (kubeseal --cert pubcert.pem < secret.yaml > sealedsecret.yaml). Use OIDC for short-lived CI credentials (GitHub Actions OIDC -> aws sts assume-role-with-web-identity; verify in workflow via aws sts get-caller-identity). Enforce pre-merge scanning (git-secrets --scan . or truffleHog) and audit with CI logs and periodic secret-manager access logs.

5429. [Pipeline Security] How do you protect secrets stored in CI/CD tools?
Answer: Store secrets outside repo in a secrets manager (HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, Azure Key Vault) and grant CI ephemeral access via OIDC or short-lived creds. Example: vault kv put secret/app API_KEY=sensitive and vault kv get secret/app for retrieval; or aws secretsmanager get-secret-value --secret-id my/secret. In GitHub Actions use repository/org secrets (gh secret set NAME --body) and prefer OIDC to assume AWS roles (aws sts assume-role-with-web-identity --role-arn ... --role-session-name ... --web-identity-token $ACTIONS_ID_TOKEN). Encrypt any at-rest files with sops (sops --encrypt --kms arn:aws:kms:... file.yaml). Enforce least privilege, rotate keys, enable audit logs, mask outputs (CI systems mask secrets), and verify by listing secrets (gh secret list, vault audit enable and vault audit list).

5430. [Pipeline Security] How do you rotate pipeline credentials?
Answer: Store pipeline credentials in a secrets service (AWS Secrets Manager, HashiCorp Vault, GCP Secret Manager) and rotate by creating a new secret/version, updating the CI/CD secret reference, then revoking the old secret. Example AWS flow: aws iam create-access-key --user-name ci-deploy; aws secretsmanager put-secret-value --secret-id /ci/deploy --secret-string '{"AccessKeyId":"AKIA...","SecretAccessKey":"..."}'. Update pipeline secret (GitHub CLI: gh secret set AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID --body "$ID"; gh secret set AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY --body "$KEY") and trigger a pipeline run. Verify successful job using the new creds and confirm the old key is unused via CloudTrail and iam delete-access-key --user-name ci-deploy --access-key-id OLDID.

5431. [Pipeline Security] How do you audit pipeline activity?
Answer: Enable and centralize immutable audit logs for your CI/CD platform, streaming pipeline and control-plane events to a SIEM and object storage with versioning/retention. Examples: enable AWS CloudTrail and CloudWatch Logs for CodePipeline and use aws cloudtrail lookup-events --lookup-attributes AttributeKey=ResourceName,AttributeValue=<pipeline-name> and aws codepipeline get-pipeline-execution --pipeline-name <name> --pipeline-execution-id <id>. For GitLab, use the Audit Events API (GET /groups/:id/audit_events); for GitHub Enterprise use the Audit Log API (GET /orgs/:org/audit-log). Verify by querying logs for execution IDs, user/service-account principals, commit SHAs, and artifact digests, and confirm artifacts are signed and stored with object versioning enabled.

5432. [Pipeline Security] How do you prevent artifact tampering?
Answer: Use cryptographic signatures, immutability, provenance, and strict access control. Sign artifacts with sigstore/cosign: cosign sign --key cosign.key registry/repo:tag and verify with cosign verify --key cosign.pub registry/repo:tag; publish attestations (rekor) and store signed SBOMs. Pin deployments to digests (docker pull registry/repo@sha256:<digest>). Enforce immutable storage: enable S3 Object Lock with Governance/Compliance mode (aws s3api put-object-retention ...) or use registries that support immutability/policy. Restrict write/delete via least-privilege IAM and MFA for high-risk ops. Continuously verify integrity via automated CI checks (cosign verify, sha256sum) and alert on signature/provenance mismatches.

5433. [Pipeline Security] How do you verify artifact integrity?
Answer: Use cryptographic hashes and signatures, verify keys via a trusted channel, and check provenance records. For files: produce and compare checksums (sha256sum file; sha256sum -c checksums.txt). For detached GPG signatures: gpg --verify file.sig file and confirm the signer fingerprint matches a trusted key (fetch/verify via a keyserver or your PKI). For OCI/container images: use sigstore/cosign (cosign verify --key /path/to/pubkey.pem ghcr.io/org/image:tag) or cosign verify --certificate for Fulcio-signed bundles and inspect Rekor entries. For reproducible builds, rebuild and compare byte-for-byte (sha256sum) with the published artifact. Always store verification keys in hardware-backed KMS or an organizational trust store and log verification results for audit.

5434. [Pipeline Security] What is software-supply-chain security?
Answer: Software supply chain security protects the full path from source code to production artifact. It includes dependency scanning, signed commits, secure builds, SBOMs, provenance, image signing, vulnerability management, and controlled deployment.

Detailed interview explanation:
Software Supply Chain Security belongs to the software delivery lifecycle. In interviews, explain how it helps teams move from source code to production safely. The key themes are automation, repeatability, traceability, testing, security validation, deployment control, and rollback.

Production example:
A production pipeline may start when a pull request is opened. CI runs unit tests, integration tests, static analysis, dependency scanning, and image scanning. After approval, the pipeline builds an immutable artifact, pushes it to an artifact registry, and deploys it using Kubernetes, Helm, Argo CD, Flux, or another deployment system. For production releases, teams add approval gates, canary or blue-green rollout, SLO checks, and rollback automation.

Best practices to mention:
- Keep pipeline definitions in Git and review them like application code.
- Promote the same immutable artifact across environments.
- Use secret managers and short-lived credentials instead of hardcoded secrets.
- Add automated checks for tests, security, policy, and deployment health.
- Measure delivery using DORA metrics: deployment frequency, lead time, change failure rate, and MTTR.

Common interview follow-ups:
You may be asked how to handle flaky tests, slow pipelines, failed deployments, manual approvals, artifact promotion, branch strategy, GitOps drift, or rollback. A strong answer connects the concept to faster feedback, safer releases, and better auditability.

5435. [Pipeline Security] How do you generate and validate an SBOM?
Answer: Use Syft to generate and SBOM for an image or filesystem and emit a standard format, e.g.:
syft myimage:tag -o cyclonedx-json > sbom.json
Or for SPDX:
syft ./project -o spdx-json > sbom.spdx.json

Validate schema and semantics with the CycloneDX CLI and reproducibility by regenerating and comparing hashes:
cyclonedx-cli validate --input sbom.json
sha256sum sbom.json sbom.generated.json && cmp sbom.json sbom.generated.json

Sign and verify authenticity with Sigstore/cosign:
cosign sign-blob --key cosign.key sbom.json > sbom.sig
cosign verify-blob --key cosign.pub --signature sbom.sig sbom.json

Optionally scan the SBOM for vulnerabilities:
grype sbom:sbom.json
These steps validate format, integrity, signature, and vulnerability content.

5436. [Pipeline Security] What is provenance in a software build?
Answer: Provenance is a verifiable record of how, when, and by whom a software artifact was produced: source commit IDs, build inputs and versions, builder identity, build instructions, environment, and resulting artifact hashes. Modern provenance is expressed as signed attestations (in-toto/SLSA predicates, SPDX) and stored with the artifact (container image manifest/config, OCI artifact, or separate attestation). To operationally verify provenance, compare recorded commit and input hashes to source control, check artifact digest with docker inspect or sha256sum, and validate attestation signatures (for example cosign verify --key <publicKey> <image> or in-toto-verify against the public key and link/attestation). Provenance enables reproducible builds and policy-based admission controls.

5437. [Pipeline Security] How do you prevent untrusted pull requests from accessing secrets?
Answer: Run untrusted PRs without repository secrets, use least-privilege tokens, and require explicit human gating. Practical controls: disable "Allow fork pull request workflows" in GitHub repo settings, set default workflow permissions to minimal (e.g., permissions: contents: read) and grant id-token: write only when using OIDC. Store secrets in GitHub Secrets and bind them to protected environments that require reviewers/approval; secrets are not passed to workflows from forked repositories. Use actions/checkout@v4 for base ref in pull_request_target only when you avoid checking out untrusted head, and test by opening a forked PR that runs a job which echoes $MY_SECRET (it must be empty). Verify via Actions logs and audit events.

5438. [Pipeline Security] How do you scan Docker images before deployment?
Answer: Use automated vulnerability and policy scanners in CI to fail builds before deployment. Example tools/commands: Docker Scan (Snyk): docker scan myrepo/app:1.2.3; Trivy: trivy image --scanners vuln,secret,config --severity HIGH,CRITICAL --exit-code 1 myrepo/app:1.2.3; Grype: grype myrepo/app:1.2.3 --fail-on high. Generate and store SBOMs for auditing: trivy image --format cyclonedx --output sbom.xml myrepo/app:1.2.3. In pipelines, run scans as a blocking stage, parse exit codes or JSON output (trivy --format json) to enforce policy, and verify results by re-running the same scan locally to reproduce findings before promoting the image.

5439. [Pipeline Security] How do you prevent vulnerable images from reaching production?
Answer: Integrate multi-layer controls: fail CI on vulnerability scans (e.g., trivy image --severity CRITICAL,HIGH --exit-code 1 myrepo/app:sha) and generate an SBOM with Syft (syft packages -o spdx-json myrepo/app:sha). Require image signing with cosign (cosign sign --key k myrepo/app:sha) and enforce signatures in Kubernetes via an admission controller (e.g., OPA Gatekeeper or sigstore policy-controller) to reject unsigned or untrusted images. Enable registry scanning (Amazon ECR image scanning or GCR Container Analysis) and block promotions when scan results contain findings above threshold via pipeline gates. Verify by running cosign verify myrepo/app:sha and checking CI job status and registry scan findings before allowing deployment.


Jenkins
-------
5440. [Jenkins] Explain Jenkins architecture.
Answer: Jenkins Architecture
Jenkins is an open-source automation server used to automate build, test, and deployment processes in CI/CD pipelines.
Its architecture follows a Controller-Agent (Master-Agent) model.
Jenkins Architecture Diagram
                   Developers
                         |
                         v
                    GitHub/GitLab
                         |
                         v
                Jenkins Controller
               (Master Node)
         +----------------------+
         | Scheduler            |
         | Job Management       |
         | Plugins              |
         | UI & Configuration   |
         +----------------------+
              /          \
             /            \
            v              v
     Jenkins Agent 1   Jenkins Agent 2
      (Linux Build)     (Windows Build)
            |                  |
            v                  v
      Build/Test App      Build/Test App
________________


1. Jenkins Controller (Master)
The Controller is the central component responsible for:
               * Managing Jenkins configuration
               * Scheduling jobs
               * Managing agents
               * Installing plugins
               * Monitoring pipeline execution
               * Providing the Jenkins web UI
Responsibilities
               * Receives build triggers
               * Assigns jobs to agents
               * Maintains build history
               * Stores pipeline definitions
               * Coordinates distributed builds
________________


2. Jenkins Agents (Workers)
Agents are machines that execute the actual jobs assigned by the Controller.
They can be:
               * Physical servers
               * Virtual machines
               * Kubernetes Pods
               * Docker Containers
Responsibilities
               * Build code
               * Run tests
               * Execute deployment scripts
               * Generate artifacts
Example:
Agent 1 → Java Build
Agent 2 → Python Build
Agent 3 → Docker Build
________________


3. Communication Between Controller and Agents
Jenkins Controller communicates with agents through:
               * SSH
               * JNLP (Java Network Launch Protocol)
               * WebSocket
Common setup:
Controller
     |
     | SSH
     |
Agent
________________


4. Jenkins Pipeline
A Pipeline is a series of automated stages.
Example:
Checkout Code
      ↓
Build
      ↓
Unit Test
      ↓
Security Scan
      ↓
Docker Build
      ↓
Push Image
      ↓
Deploy
Pipeline code is stored in a file called:
Jenkinsfile
________________


5. Jenkins Plugins
Jenkins is highly extensible through plugins.
Popular plugins:
               * Git Plugin
               * Docker Plugin
               * Kubernetes Plugin
               * SonarQube Scanner for Jenkins
               * Slack Notification Plugin

Why Use Multiple Agents?
Benefits:
               * Parallel execution
               * Faster builds
               * Better resource utilization
               * Platform-specific builds

Interview Answer (2 Minutes)
Jenkins follows a Controller-Agent architecture. The Jenkins Controller manages job scheduling, pipeline execution, plugins, user authentication, and the web interface. Agents are worker nodes that execute the actual build, test, and deployment tasks. When a developer commits code, Jenkins receives a trigger, schedules the job, and assigns it to an available agent. The agent performs the required tasks and reports the results back to the Controller. This distributed architecture enables scalability, parallel execution, and efficient resource utilization. In enterprise environments, Jenkins is often integrated with GitHub, Docker, Kubernetes, SonarQube, and artifact repositories to build complete CI/CD pipelines.

5441. [Jenkins] What is the role of the Jenkins controller?
Answer: The Jenkins controller is the central orchestration and management process that hosts the web UI and REST API, stores job and system configuration in JENKINS_HOME (e.g., config.xml, jobs/), manages plugins, security, credentials, the build queue, and schedules work to connected agents (SSH, JNLP, Kubernetes plugin). It allocates executors, persists pipeline state, and coordinates artifacts and logs. Run as java -jar jenkins.war or as a packaged service; verify it is responsive with curl -s http://JENKINS_URL/api/json, inspect agents and executors via http://JENKINS_URL/computer/api/json, and view queue via http://JENKINS_URL/queue/api/json to confirm controller activity.

5442. [Jenkins] What is a Jenkins agent?
Answer: A Jenkins agent is a separate JVM process (historically called a “slave”) that the Jenkins controller delegates build and pipeline execution to. Agents run on remote machines, containers, or ephemeral Kubernetes pods and are registered under Manage Jenkins → Manage Nodes with configurable labels, executors, and launch methods (SSH, JNLP/agent.jar, WebSocket, Windows service, Kubernetes plugin). Communication uses the Remoting protocol via agent.jar (or WebSocket transport) and agents execute workspace-bound steps, tools, and environment on behalf of the controller. To verify an agent, check its online status and logs in Manage Nodes, confirm labels match the pipeline’s agent directive, and run a job pinned to that node to observe workspace creation, console output, and exit status.

5443. [Jenkins] What is the difference between a permanent and ephemeral agent?
Answer: A permanent (static) agent is a long-lived node you provision and register in Jenkins (Manage Nodes or via SSH/agent.jar) that keeps workspace, installed tools, and persistent configuration; verify with the Jenkins REST API (curl -u user:token 'http://JENKINS/computer/api/json') or the UI under Manage Nodes. An ephemeral agent is created on-demand (for example the Kubernetes plugin’s podTemplate or a Docker container) for a single build and destroyed afterward, providing clean, immutable build environments; verify with kubectl (kubectl get pods -o wide, kubectl describe pod <name>, kubectl logs <name>) or by observing nodes appear/disappear in the Jenkins computer API during a job. Permanent agents retain state; ephemeral do not.

5444. [Jenkins] What is a Jenkins job?
Answer: A Jenkins job is a stored build configuration that defines how and when Jenkins runs a task (build, test, deploy). Jobs include Freestyle, Pipeline (Declarative/Scripted via Jenkinsfile), Multibranch Pipeline and Folder types; their configuration is persisted as XML under JENKINS_HOME/jobs/<jobname>/config.xml and build records under JENKINS_HOME/jobs/<jobname>/builds. Jobs run on the controller or on agents matched by node labels, can be triggered by SCM polling, cron (build periodically), GitHub/GitLab webhooks (e.g. POST to /github-webhook/), or manual/API triggers. Verify or operate jobs via CLI or HTTP API, for example: java -jar jenkins-cli.jar -s http://jenkins/ list-jobs or curl -u user:apiToken -X POST http://jenkins/job/name/build?token=TOKEN.

5445. [Jenkins] What is the difference between a declarative and scripted pipeline?
Answer: Declarative pipelines use the top-level "pipeline { ... }" syntax with structured blocks (agent, stages, steps, environment, post, when, options, triggers) and enforce a model that enables predictable stage visualization in Blue Ocean and automatic features like automatic agent allocation and Declarative Linter validation (Manage Jenkins → Pipeline Syntax → Declarative Linter or POST /pipeline-model-converter/validate). Scripted pipelines are plain Groovy CPS scripts using "node { ... }", arbitrary control flow, and full programmatic flexibility via loops, conditionals, and try/catch. Both run under Jenkins’ Groovy CPS and can call @Library shared libraries, but scripted offers more imperative control while declarative provides safer, opinionated structure and built-in lifecycle hooks for easier maintenance and visualization.

5446. [Jenkins] Which pipeline type have you worked with?
Answer: [CONTEXT] I worked across Jenkins Declarative and Scripted pipelines, GitLab CI (gitlab-ci.yml), GitHub Actions workflows, Tekton tasks/pipelines, and GitOps deployments with Argo CD/Flux. [ACTION] In Jenkins I used Declarative Jenkinsfiles (pipeline { agent any; stages { stage('Build') { steps { sh 'mvn -B package' }}}}), in GitLab I authored jobs with script: and artifacts:, in GitHub Actions I used workflow files with jobs and uses:, and I invoked argocd CLI (argocd app sync <app>) to reconcile clusters. [RESULT] Verification included Jenkins Blue Ocean pipeline views, gitlab pipeline job logs and artifacts, GitHub Actions run logs, and Argo CD showing Synced/Healthy for deployed apps.

5447. [Jenkins] Explain the stages in your Jenkins pipeline.
Answer: Stages: Checkout — sh 'git checkout ${GIT_BRANCH}' and stash/unstash sources; Build — sh 'mvn -B package' or 'npm ci && npm run build', archiveArtifacts artifacts: 'target/*.jar'; Unit Test — sh 'mvn test' and publish results with junit '**/target/surefire-reports/*.xml'; Static Analysis — sh 'sonar-scanner -Dsonar.projectKey=proj'; Package/Containerize — sh "docker build -t myrepo/myapp:${GIT_COMMIT} ." and docker push; Integration/Acceptance — run integration tests and publish results; Security Scan — run Snyk/Trivy and fail pipeline on high severity; Deploy — helm upgrade --install myrelease ./chart --set image.tag=${GIT_COMMIT} and verify with kubectl rollout status deployment/myapp -n prod; Post-deploy Smoke — curl --fail http://service/health and notify via slackSend.

5448. [Jenkins] What is the agent block?
Answer: In Jenkins Declarative Pipeline, the agent block declares where the pipeline or a specific stage runs (executor/node or container). Examples: pipeline { agent any } uses any available executor; agent none disables a global agent so stages must declare their own agents; agent { label 'linux' } binds to a node with that label; agent { docker { image 'node:14' args '-v /tmp:/tmp' } } runs steps inside a Docker container. You can also use agent per-stage: stage('build') { agent { label 'builder' } steps { ... } }. Verify behavior in the build console (it prints node/container allocation) or in Jenkins UI’s Build Executor Status and Blue Ocean run details.

5449. [Jenkins] What is the environment block?
Answer: In a Declarative Jenkins Pipeline, the environment block defines environment variables that are injected into the pipeline or a specific stage. Syntax examples: global: environment { PATH = "/custom/bin:$PATH" BRANCH = "master" } or stage-scoped: stage('Build') { environment { SVC = "api" } steps { sh 'echo "$SVC"' } }. You can bind credentials with credentials(): environment { MY_SECRET = credentials('cred-id') } and access variables in Groovy as env.MY_SECRET or in shell as $MY_SECRET. You cannot include steps inside the block. Verify by running a step such as sh 'env' or sh 'echo "$MY_SECRET"' to confirm the variables are present.

5450. [Jenkins] What is the parameters block?
Answer: In Jenkins Declarative Pipeline the parameters block is a top-level directive that declares build parameters (string, booleanParam, choice, password, etc.) which render on the job’s build form and create entries in the params map at runtime. Example:

pipeline {
  agent any
  parameters {
    string(name: 'BRANCH', defaultValue: 'main', description: 'Git branch')
    booleanParam(name: 'RUN_INTEGRATION', defaultValue: false, description: 'Run integration tests')
  }
  stages { ... }
}

At runtime you access values as params.BRANCH or params.RUN_INTEGRATION. For scripted pipelines use properties([parameters(...)]). You can trigger a parameterized job remotely via JENKINS_URL/job/JOB_NAME/buildWithParameters with --data-urlencode "BRANCH=develop" and verify by echoing params in a stage.

5451. [Jenkins] What is the post block?
Answer: In Jenkins Declarative Pipeline, the post block is a top-level directive that runs defined steps after the pipeline (or a stage) completes, conditioned by result keywords such as always, success, failure, unstable, changed, fixed, regression, aborted and cleanup. Example: post { failure { mail to: 'team@example.com', subject: "Build failed" } always { archiveArtifacts artifacts: 'logs/**' } }. Post blocks execute after stages finish (even on errors) and inherit the pipeline agent/context unless you use a script step. Verify behavior by inspecting the build Console Output for post-step logs or querying the build REST API at /job/<name>/<build>/api/json to confirm result and archived artifacts.

5452. [Jenkins] What is the when condition?
Answer: In Jenkins Declarative Pipeline, the when directive is a stage-level conditional that controls whether a stage runs. Syntax examples: when { branch 'main' }, when { environment name: 'DEPLOY', value: 'true' }, when { anyOf { branch 'main'; tag '*' } }, when { expression { return env.BRANCH_NAME == 'main' } }, and boolean combinators not/allOf/anyOf. Use beforeAgent true to evaluate the when condition before allocating an agent. If the condition is false the stage is marked SKIPPED and its steps are not executed; verify in Blue Ocean or the classic console where the stage shows SKIPPED and no agent is allocated, or inspect stage status via the Pipeline REST API.

5453. [Jenkins] What is the difference between stages and steps?
Answer: A stage is a logical phase in a Jenkins Pipeline used for visualization, grouping, conditional execution, parallelism and agent allocation; it appears in the Stage View/Blue Ocean UI and accepts directives like agent, when, post and parallel. A step is an atomic executable action (a Step API implementation) such as sh, checkout, archiveArtifacts or junit; steps run on a pipeline executor within an agent and are placed inside a steps block in Declarative Pipeline. Example: stage('Test') { agent { label 'linux' } steps { sh 'mvn -B test' junit 'target/surefire-reports/*.xml' } } Verify behavior by viewing stage status in Blue Ocean or checking executor activity on the node.

5454. [Jenkins] How do you run stages in parallel?
Answer: In Declarative Pipeline, use a stage with a parallel block:

pipeline {
  agent any
  stages {
    stage('Parallel work') {
      parallel {
        stage('Unit') { steps { sh 'make test' } }
        stage('Integration') { steps { sh 'make integration' } }
      }
    }
  }
}

In Scripted Pipeline use the parallel step with a map (and optional failFast):

parallel(
  unit: { node { sh 'make test' } },
  integration: { node { sh 'make integration' } },
  failFast: true
)

Each parallel branch runs on its own executor/agent; verify concurrent execution in the build console (overlapping timestamps) and the Jenkins "Build Executor Status" or Blue Ocean UI showing multiple active executors.

5455. [Jenkins] How do you handle credentials in Jenkins?
Answer: Store secrets in the Jenkins Credentials Store (Manage Jenkins → Credentials) and use the Credentials Binding and Credentials plugins in pipelines. In Declarative: environment { GIT_CREDS = credentials('git-creds-id') } or in Scripted/steps: withCredentials([usernamePassword(credentialsId: 'git-creds-id', usernameVariable: 'USER', passwordVariable: 'PASS')]) { sh 'git clone https://$USER:$PASS@repo' }. For SSH: sshagent(credentials: ['ssh-key-id']) { sh 'ssh user@host' }. Prefer external secret backends (HashiCorp Vault plugin, Kubernetes Secrets) and enable Jenkins’ secret encryption (hudson.util.Secret). Verify by running a build and confirming sensitive values are masked in the console log and that credentials appear under the correct domain in the Credentials UI.

5456. [Jenkins] What is the Jenkins Credentials Store?
Answer: The Jenkins Credentials Store is the centralized storage provided by the Credentials Plugin for managing secrets (Username/password, SSH private keys, Secret text, Certificates) scoped by domain and folder/global contexts. Credentials are persisted under JENKINS_HOME (credentials.xml and folder-specific stores) and their secret values are encrypted on disk using Jenkins’ secrets files (secrets/master.key and secrets/hudson.util.Secret). Access is via the UI (Manage Jenkins → Credentials), the Credentials API (com.cloudbees.plugins.credentials.*), pipeline steps (withCredentials, credentials), or the Credentials CLI/subcommands if installed. To verify, view entries in the UI or inspect JENKINS_HOME/credentials.xml and confirm presence of encrypted secret blocks and corresponding secrets/* key files.

5457. [Jenkins] How do you inject credentials into a pipeline?
Answer: In Jenkins Pipeline use the Credentials Binding Plugin: withCredentials([usernamePassword(credentialsId: 'creds-id', usernameVariable: 'USER', passwordVariable: 'PASS')]) { sh 'printf "%s\n" "$USER" && # DO NOT print $PASS' } — credentials are stored in Jenkins > Credentials and secrets are masked in console output. In GitHub Actions set repository Secrets and reference as ${{ secrets.MY_TOKEN }} (e.g., uses: actions/checkout@v4 with: token: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}). In GitLab CI set CI/CD Variables (masked/protected) and read $MY_VAR in jobs. In Kubernetes create a Secret (kubectl create secret generic my-secret --from-literal=token=... ) and mount it as env or volume; verify with kubectl describe secret my-secret.

5458. [Jenkins] How do you prevent Jenkins from printing credentials?
Answer: Use the Credentials Binding plugin and never print secrets directly. In a Pipeline use withCredentials to bind a secret and the plugin will mask it in console output, for example:

withCredentials([string(credentialsId: 'my-secret-id', variable: 'SECRET')]) {
  sh '''
    # do not echo $SECRET in logs for debugging; if printed it will be masked
    ./use-secret.sh "$SECRET"
  '''
}

For username/password use usernamePassword(credentialsId: 'id', usernameVariable: 'USER', passwordVariable: 'PASS'). Verify by running the job and checking Jenkins → job → Build → Console Output: bound values appear masked (****) and the Credentials Binding plugin logs masking activity rather than the raw secret.

5459. [Jenkins] What are shared libraries?
Answer: Shared Libraries in Jenkins are reusable pipeline code packaged in an SCM repository with a prescribed layout (vars/, src/, resources/). They are configured under Manage Jenkins → Configure System → Global Pipeline Libraries (specify name, SCM, credentials, Default Version). Use them in pipelines via @Library('name@version') _ or library identifier syntax, then call vars functions or classes (e.g., @Library('shared@master') _; mySharedStep('arg')). Implement classes under src/com/example/ and global steps as vars/foo.groovy (callable as foo()). Verify by running a Jenkinsfile that imports the library and observing step execution in build logs; unit-test library logic with JenkinsPipelineUnit and manage versions via git tag/git push.

5460. [Jenkins] Why do you use Jenkins shared libraries?
Answer: I use Jenkins Shared Libraries to centralize reusable pipeline logic (vars/, src/, resources/) and enforce DRY, consistent release/credential handling, and testable classes across teams. Load with @Library('my-lib@1.2') _ in a Jenkinsfile or configure as a Global Pipeline Library in Manage Jenkins (SCM URL, credentials). Implement global steps as vars/foo.groovy and classes under src/org/foo/*.groovy; call foo() or new org.foo.Bar().run(). Pin versions via branches/tags (e.g., @Library('lib@release-2026.01')). Verify by running the multibranch job and observing the library checkout in the build log ("Checking out from SCM") and under the workspace @libs/<lib>@<version>, and by asserting expected step output in the Pipeline console.

5461. [Jenkins] How do you create reusable Jenkins pipeline code?
Answer: Create a Git-backed Shared Pipeline Library and call it from Jenkinsfiles. Structure the repo with vars/<name>.groovy for simple steps and src/<org>/... for reusable classes. In Jenkins: Manage Jenkins → Configure System → Global Pipeline Libraries, add the library name and Git repository URL and default version (branch/tag). In a Jenkinsfile use the annotation and call functions, e.g.:
@Library('my-shared-lib@master') _
myStep('args')
Or in Declarative pipeline use libraries: [ 'my-shared-lib@master' ] and call vars. Verify by running a job and inspecting the console log for library load messages (e.g. "[Pipeline] library" and your step output), and update the library repo to propagate changes without editing individual Jenkinsfiles.

5462. [Jenkins] How do you trigger Jenkins from Git?
Answer: Configure a webhook in the Git host to POST commits to Jenkins (preferred) or enable Poll SCM in the job. For GitHub: add a webhook URL https://jenkins.example.com/github-webhook/ (Content-Type: application/json) and set a secret; enable the GitHub or GitHub Branch Source plugin in Jenkins and configure the same secret in job/global credentials. For GitLab/Bitbucket use the corresponding /gitlab/ or /bitbucket-hook/ endpoints or install Generic Webhook Trigger and use /generic-webhook-trigger/invoke?token=TOKEN. Verify by pushing a commit and checking the Jenkins UI or query the job REST API, e.g. curl -u user:apiToken https://jenkins.example.com/job/MYJOB/lastBuild/api/json to confirm the build started.

5463. [Jenkins] What is a webhook?
Answer: A webhook is an HTTP callback: a remote service sends an HTTP POST (commonly JSON) to a configured URL when an event occurs (e.g., GitHub push, GitLab pipeline event). Implementations should verify authenticity (GitHub uses X-Hub-Signature-256 HMAC SHA-256 of the payload with a shared secret), require TLS, and return a 2xx status to acknowledge receipt; non-2xx responses trigger provider retries (GitHub uses exponential backoff). For testing, simulate a delivery with curl: curl -v -H "Content-Type: application/json" -H "X-Hub-Signature-256: sha256=<sig>" -d @payload.json https://ci.example.com/webhook and confirm your app computes and matches the HMAC, logs the event, and processes idempotently.

5464. [Jenkins] What is polling SCM?
Answer: Polling SCM is a Jenkins build trigger that periodically runs the job’s SCM plugin to fetch remote refs (e.g., git fetch) and compare remote HEAD(s) to the job’s last built revision using the cron-like schedule entered in the job’s “Poll SCM” field. If differences are found the job is queued; otherwise nothing runs. It differs from webhooks which push events. Verify by observing “Poll SCM” schedule in job configuration, checking the job’s Build History and console or Manage Jenkins → System Log for polling entries, or run git fetch && git rev-parse origin/branch && git rev-parse HEAD to see whether remote and local SHAs differ. Polling wastes resources and adds latency compared to webhooks.

5465. [Jenkins] Why are webhooks preferred over polling?
Answer: Webhooks are preferred because they use a push model: the source (e.g., GitHub) POSTs an event to a subscriber URL immediately, producing lower latency and far fewer requests than periodic polling. Practically, GitHub sends JSON to your endpoint and includes X-Hub-Signature-256 for HMAC verification; you can validate with openssl dgst -sha256 -hmac. Webhooks reduce API rate usage and resource overhead versus Poll SCM cron schedules (e.g., H/5 * * * *). They also support retries and visibility (GitHub “Recent Deliveries” shows status and retry attempts). To verify integration, watch access logs or tcpdump, observe a successful 2xx response, and confirm Jenkins builds are triggered by the webhook.

5466. [Jenkins] How do you trigger one Jenkins job from another?
Answer: In a Freestyle job use the “Build other projects” (or Parameterized Trigger) post-build action; in Pipeline use the build step, e.g. scripted: build job: 'downstream-job', parameters: [string(name: 'ENV', value: 'prod')], wait: true, propagate: true. Alternatively call the REST API: obtain a crumb (curl -u user:APITOKEN JENKINS_URL/crumbIssuer/api/json), then POST to /job/Downstream/buildWithParameters with credentials and crumb, for example: curl -X POST JENKINS_URL/job/Downstream/buildWithParameters --user user:APITOKEN -H "Jenkins-Crumb:CRUMB" --data-urlencode "PARAM=value". Verify by observing the downstream build in the Queue or the downstream job’s build history and console output.

5467. [Jenkins] How do you pass parameters between Jenkins jobs?
Answer: For Freestyle jobs use the Parameterized Trigger Plugin: add "Trigger/call builds on other projects" (or "Trigger parameterized build on other projects"), choose "Predefined parameters", "Current build parameters" or "Parameters from properties file". In Pipeline use the build step with explicit parameters, e.g. build job: 'downstream', parameters: [string(name: 'FOO', value: 'bar'), booleanParam(name: 'FLAG', value: true)], plus propagate: false if needed. Downstream Jenkinsfile/Job must declare matching parameters (parameters { string(name: 'FOO') } or use params.FOO in Pipeline). Verify by viewing the downstream build’s "Parameters" section in the UI or by printing params.FOO in the downstream console log.

5468. [Jenkins] How do you archive artifacts?
Answer: In Jenkins Pipeline use the archiveArtifacts step, e.g. archiveArtifacts artifacts: 'target/*.jar', fingerprint: true, allowEmptyArchive: false. For Freestyle enable "Archive the artifacts" in Post-build Actions and supply a glob. Control retention with a Build Discarder: properties([buildDiscarder(logRotator(numToKeepStr: '10', artifactNumToKeepStr: '5'))]). For off-server long‑term storage upload artifacts to object storage, e.g. aws s3 cp target/ s3://my-bucket/path/ --recursive, or use the S3 plugin. Verify archives via the build page "Artifacts" link, by inspecting $JENKINS_HOME/jobs/<job>/builds/<build>/archive, or by listing S3 (aws s3 ls s3://my-bucket/path/).

5469. [Jenkins] How do you retain build logs?
Answer: Keep console output in Jenkins and push archival copies externally. For Jenkins pipelines add a build discard policy and archive artifacts: properties([buildDiscarder(logRotator(numToKeepStr: '50', daysToKeepStr: '90'))]) and archiveArtifacts artifacts: 'logs/**', allowEmptyArchive: true. To export console text programmatically use the REST API or CLI: curl -sSL "https://jenkins.example.com/job/NAME/123/consoleText" -u user:token > build-123-console.txt && aws s3 cp build-123-console.txt s3://ci-logs/NAME/123-console.txt. Verify retention by inspecting job config.xml for <logRotator> entries and confirming archived artifacts on the build page or presence of files in S3. This ensures Jenkins retains recent builds while external storage preserves long-term logs.

5470. [Jenkins] How do you manage build history?
Answer: Use per-job build retention and artifact retention plus global policies. In Pipeline jobs add properties([buildDiscarder(logRotator(numToKeepStr:'10', daysToKeepStr:'30', artifactNumToKeepStr:'5'))]) or, for Job DSL, logRotator(10, 30, 5). Archive only required artifacts with archiveArtifacts 'dist/**/*.zip' and avoid archiving large temp files. For ad-hoc cleanup use workspace cleanup and node-level GC, and S3/Blob lifecycle rules for remote storage. Verify retention via the REST API: curl -s -u user:token "http://jenkins/job/NAME/api/json?tree=builds[number,id]" and confirm artifact counts at /lastSuccessfulBuild/api/json. Monitor disk usage with the Disk Usage Plugin and confirm reclaimed space by checking Jenkins home free space.

5471. [Jenkins] How do you clean old Jenkins workspaces?
Answer: Use one or more of these supported approaches:

- Pipeline: call deleteDir() at start/end of a Declarative/Scripted Pipeline to remove the workspace directory, e.g. stage('Clean'){ steps { deleteDir() } } and/or run sh 'git clean -fdx' to remove untracked files.
- Workspace Cleanup Plugin: enable “Delete workspace before build starts” or add the plugin’s post-build step to remove files.
- OS cron or maintenance job: e.g. sudo find /var/jenkins_home/workspace -maxdepth 1 -mtime +30 -type d -exec rm -rf {} + to remove workspaces older than 30 days.
- Verification: inspect sizes with du -sh /var/jenkins_home/workspace/* or check job workspace presence in the job’s workspace browser in the Jenkins UI.

5472. [Jenkins] How do you troubleshoot a Jenkins agent that is offline?
Answer: Check the Jenkins UI (Manage Jenkins → Nodes/agent list) for the agent status and recent log link, then inspect logs: tail -f /var/log/jenkins/agent.log or use the agent’s “Log” from the node page. For SSH agents, run ssh -vvv user@agent and verify java is present (java -version) and the ssh launch command in the node configuration. For JNLP/agent.jar agents, fetch and run the same agent.jar with the controller URL: java -jar agent.jar -jnlpUrl https://jenkins.example.com/computer/AGENT_NAME/slave-agent.jnlp and watch for “Connected” in the output; ensure versions of remoting/agent.jar match the controller. Check controller connectivity (curl -k https://jenkins.example.com/computer/AGENT_NAME/api/json) and firewall rules (tcp/50000 or configured agent port) and confirm systemd service (systemctl status jenkins-agent) or Kubernetes pod logs when using the Kubernetes plugin.

5473. [Jenkins] How do you troubleshoot a stuck Jenkins build?
Answer: Check the build console and Jenkins logs: curl -u user:APITOKEN http://jenkins:8080/job/JOBNAME/lastBuild/consoleText and tail -f /var/log/jenkins/jenkins.log. Inspect queue and executors: curl -u user:APITOKEN http://jenkins:8080/queue/api/json and http://jenkins:8080/computer/api/json?pretty=true. If an agent is hung, ssh to the agent and inspect processes (ps aux | grep java) and docker containers (docker ps); restart the agent or kill the stuck process. For pipelines waiting on input, approve or abort from Blue Ocean or POST to the input API: curl -X POST -u user:APITOKEN http://jenkins:8080/job/JOBNAME/BUILDNUMBER/input/ID/proceed. To abort a build: curl -X POST -u user:APITOKEN http://jenkins:8080/job/JOBNAME/lastBuild/stop, then verify state via the build API.

5474. [Jenkins] How do you scale Jenkins agents?
Answer: Scale Jenkins agents by using cloud-based clouds/plugins with autoscaling: e.g., Kubernetes plugin (podTemplate) or EC2 plugin. Configure a cloud in Manage Jenkins -> Configure System with podTemplates referencing jenkins/inbound-agent and the JNLP args ${computer.jnlpmac} ${computer.name}, or EC2 instance templates/AMI and instance cap. Set reasonable "Executors per agent" and retention/idle minutes so Jenkins provisions new agents when the queue has pending builds for a label. Run agents with java -jar agent.jar for static agents. Verify scaling by observing provisioning: kubectl get pods -n jenkins (Kubernetes) or jenkins-cli -s http://jenkins:8080 list-nodes, and inspect cloud provisioning logs in Manage Jenkins -> System Log.

5475. [Jenkins] How do you run Jenkins agents on Kubernetes?
Answer: Install and configure the Jenkins Kubernetes plugin (Kubernetes Cloud). In Jenkins configure a Kubernetes cloud pointing to the cluster (use in-cluster ServiceAccount or kubeconfig credential), add a Pod Template with a jnlp container using the official image (jenkins/inbound-agent) and any build containers, set a label for jobs, workspaceVolume/hostPath if needed, and optional initContainers/volumes. Trigger a pipeline/ freestyle job that specifies the agent label; Jenkins will create an ephemeral Pod for each agent. Verify with kubectl get pods -n <ns> and inspect logs: kubectl logs <pod-name> -c jnlp; check Jenkins > Nodes for the pod agent. Ensure RBAC grants the ServiceAccount permissions to create pods.

5476. [Jenkins] How do you back up Jenkins?
Answer: Stop or quiesce Jenkins, then back up the entire JENKINS_HOME (by default /var/lib/jenkins) including config.xml, jobs/, plugins/, users/, credentials.xml and secrets/ (preserve ownership/permissions). Example sequence: java -jar jenkins-cli.jar -s http://jenkins:8080/ quiet-down; sudo tar -C /var/lib -czpf /backup/jenkins-home-$(date +%F).tar.gz jenkins; sudo chown root:root /backup/...; java -jar jenkins-cli.jar -s http://jenkins:8080/ cancel-quiet-down. Alternatively use rsync -a --delete /var/lib/jenkins/ /backup/jenkins-home/ for incremental copies. For automated/exportable config, use Jenkins Configuration as Code and backup plugin options (thinBackup). Verify by restoring to a test instance, starting Jenkins and running java -jar jenkins-cli.jar -s http://test:8080/ list-jobs to confirm jobs are present.

5477. [Jenkins] How do you restore Jenkins after failure?
Answer: Stop Jenkins, restore a clean JENKINS_HOME from your backup, ensure permissions, then start and verify. Example (systemd): systemctl stop jenkins; tar xzf /backups/jenkins_home.tgz -C /var/lib/jenkins; chown -R jenkins:jenkins /var/lib/jenkins; systemctl start jenkins. For Docker: docker stop jenkins; docker run --rm -v /backups/jenkins_home:/restore busybox tar xzf /restore/jenkins_home.tgz -C /var/jenkins_home; docker start jenkins. After start, check logs (journalctl -u jenkins -f or docker logs -f jenkins) for errors, verify web UI and API: curl -fsS http://localhost:8080/login and java -jar jenkins-cli.jar -s http://localhost:8080/ who-am-i. Reinstall plugins if missing using install-plugins.sh or the Update Center, then validate jobs and credentials.

5478. [Jenkins] How do you upgrade Jenkins safely?
Answer: Stop changes, back up JENKINS_HOME and config: tar czf /backup/jenkins_home-$(date +%F).tar.gz /var/lib/jenkins and export plugin list: java -jar jenkins-cli.jar -s http://localhost:8080/ -auth user:APITOKEN list-plugins > plugins.txt. Test on a staging Jenkins by running with a copy of JENKINS_HOME or by pulling the new Docker image (docker pull jenkins/jenkins:lts) and starting a container with -v /staging/jenkins_home:/var/jenkins_home. Upgrade Jenkins package (apt: apt-get update && apt-get install jenkins) or replace Docker image, then run java -jar jenkins-cli.jar -s http://localhost:8080/ -auth user:APITOKEN safe-restart. Verify health: curl -sI http://localhost:8080/ | grep X-Jenkins and confirm agent connectivity and job builds (jenkins log and /computer/api/json).

5479. [Jenkins] How do you manage Jenkins plugins?
Answer: Use the Plugin Manager (Manage Jenkins → Manage Plugins) for ad‑hoc installs/updates and the Update Center for version metadata. Automate installs in images/CI with jenkins-plugin-cli (from official Docker image): e.g. jenkins-plugin-cli --plugins workflow-aggregator:2.6 credentials-binding:1.27. For running servers use Jenkins CLI: java -jar jenkins-cli.jar -s http://jenkins:8080/ -auth user:APITOKEN install-plugin git matrix-auth && java -jar jenkins-cli.jar -s http://jenkins:8080/ -auth user:APITOKEN safe-restart. Declare plugins in Configuration-as-Code YAML (JCasC) or place .groovy bootstrap scripts in $JENKINS_HOME/init.groovy.d for immutable installs. Verify with java -jar jenkins-cli.jar -s URL -auth user:token list-plugins or GET /pluginManager/api/json?depth=1 and check $JENKINS_HOME/plugins/*.jpi files.

5480. [Jenkins] What risks are associated with Jenkins plugins?
Answer: Jenkins plugins risk supply‑chain and privilege escalation vulnerabilities (plugins run inside the Jenkins master JVM and can execute arbitrary code), unmaintained or incompatible versions causing upgrade breakage, dependency conflicts, memory/thread leaks degrading performance, and accidental disclosure through misconfigured plugin features. Operationally verify installed plugins with the CLI (jenkins-cli.jar -s http://JENKINS list-plugins) or jenkins-plugin-cli --list, check HPI checksums (sha256sum plugin.hpi) against update-center metadata, and test upgrades in a staging instance before production. Mitigations include strict RBAC, running agents isolated/ephemeral, pinning plugin versions, and monitoring JVM heap/threads and audit logs for anomalous behavior.

5481. [Jenkins] How do you integrate Jenkins with SonarQube?
Answer: Install and configure the "SonarQube Scanner" and "SonarQube" plugins in Jenkins, add SonarQube server URL and a Sonar token (created in SonarQube: My Account → Security) under Manage Jenkins → Configure System. In declarative pipeline, run analysis with Maven/Gradle or sonar-scanner and use the plugin helpers:

- Maven: sh "mvn -B sonar:sonar -Dsonar.host.url=${SONAR_HOST_URL} -Dsonar.login=${SONAR_TOKEN}"
- CLI with tool: withSonarQubeEnv('SonarQubeServer') { sh "${tool 'sonar-scanner'}/bin/sonar-scanner -Dsonar.projectKey=proj -Dsonar.login=${SONAR_TOKEN}" }

Then call waitForQualityGate() to block the build until SonarQube computes the Quality Gate; it returns a map (status 'OK'/'ERROR') and will fail the pipeline if gate fails. Verify by viewing analysis in SonarQube UI and pipeline logs showing "ANALYSIS SUCCESSFUL".

5482. [Jenkins] How do you integrate Jenkins with Docker?
Answer: Run Jenkins with Docker access (bind-mount the socket or use TCP/DIND). Example: docker run -d --name jenkins -p 8080:8080 -v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock -v jenkins_home:/var/jenkins_home jenkins/jenkins:lts. Install the "Docker" and "Docker Pipeline" plugins, add Docker credentials in Jenkins credentials store, and configure a Docker cloud/agent template under Manage Jenkins → Configure System (use unix:///var/run/docker.sock or tcp://host:2375). In Declarative Pipeline use agent { docker { image 'maven:3.6-jdk11' } } or use scripted Docker API: docker.image('myapp').inside { sh 'mvn -v' }. For registry pushes use docker.withRegistry('https://registry.hub.docker.com', 'creds-id') { docker.build('org/app:tag').push() }. Verify by running a build and checking docker ps / docker images on the host.

5483. [Jenkins] How do you integrate Jenkins with Kubernetes?
Answer: Install and configure the official Kubernetes Plugin in Jenkins, then provide cluster access via a kubeconfig file or in-cluster service account. Create a Kubernetes service account and bind it with RBAC: kubectl create namespace jenkins && kubectl create serviceaccount jenkins-sa -n jenkins && kubectl create clusterrolebinding jenkins-sa-binding --clusterrole=edit --serviceaccount=jenkins:jenkins-sa. In Jenkins Manage Jenkins → Configure Clouds → Add a Kubernetes cloud, point to the API server and credentials, configure podTemplate/containers or use a YAML template. Use a Pipeline with agent { kubernetes { yamlFile 'pod.yaml' } } or agent { kubernetes { label 'mypod' } } to launch build pods. Verify by running a pipeline and observing pods: kubectl get pods -n jenkins and kubectl describe pod <pod-name> to inspect init containers, logs, and volume mounts.

5484. [Jenkins] How do you deploy a Helm chart through Jenkins?
Answer: Create a Jenkins pipeline that provides kubeconfig to the agent (Credentials "file" or Kubernetes plugin) and run Helm v3 commands on the agent. Example Declarative snippet:

pipeline {
  agent any
  stages {
    stage('Deploy') {
      steps {
        withCredentials([file(credentialsId: 'kubeconfig', variable: 'KUBECONFIG')]) {
          sh 'kubectl config use-context my-cluster'
          sh 'helm repo add myrepo https://charts.example.com && helm repo update'
          sh 'helm upgrade --install my-release myrepo/my-chart --namespace my-ns --create-namespace --values values.yaml'
          sh 'helm status my-release -n my-ns'
          sh 'kubectl rollout status deployment/my-deployment -n my-ns'
        }
      }
    }
  }
}

Verify with helm list -n my-ns and kubectl get pods -n my-ns to confirm rollout.

5485. [Jenkins] How do you implement approval before production deployment?
Answer: Use a gated change + manual sync pattern: require code promotion via a protected-branch PR (GitHub branch protection: required reviews and required status checks) and a paused CI job that needs human approval. In Jenkins Pipeline use the input step: input message: "Approve deploy to prod?"; when paused the console shows "Waiting for input". You can approve via the Jenkins UI or programmatically with the input submit endpoint (POST /job/<jobName>/<buildNumber>/input/<inputId>/submit with Jenkins-Crumb). For GitOps (Argo CD) keep spec.syncPolicy.automated unset (manual sync) and run argocd app sync myapp to deploy. Verify by checking Jenkins console for approval state and argocd app get myapp shows STATUS sync: Synced and HEALTH: Healthy after approval.


GitHub Actions
--------------
5486. [GitHub Actions] What is a GitHub Actions workflow?
Answer: A GitHub Actions workflow is a YAML file stored in .github/workflows that defines automated CI/CD processes. It declares triggers in an on: block (push, pull_request, schedule, workflow_dispatch, workflow_run, repository_dispatch, etc.), one or more jobs, and for each job a runs-on runner, steps, and either uses: actions/* or run: shell commands. Jobs can be parallel or sequenced via needs:, can use strategy: matrix for permutations, and access secrets and environment variables via secrets.NAME and env. Workflow runs appear in the repository’s Actions tab with per-step logs, exit codes determine success/failure, artifacts can be uploaded/downloaded with actions/upload-artifact and actions/download-artifact, and reusable workflows can be called with uses:.

5487. [GitHub Actions] Where are workflow files stored?
Answer: Workflow files live in the repository under .github/workflows as YAML files (e.g., .github/workflows/ci.yml). You can verify locally with git ls-files '.github/workflows/*' or ls .github/workflows, and via the REST API GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/contents/.github/workflows to list files. Workflows are evaluated from the commit that triggers the event (for push, pull_request, etc.); scheduled and workflow_dispatch events use the workflow definition on the default branch. Reusable workflows can be referenced cross-repository with uses: owner/repo/.github/workflows/name.yml@ref. Workflow filenames must end in .yml or .yaml and be valid GitHub Actions workflow syntax for them to appear in the Actions UI.

5488. [GitHub Actions] What is the purpose of the .github/workflows directory?
Answer: .github/workflows stores GitHub Actions workflow definition files (*.yml or *.yaml). Each file describes triggers (on: push, pull_request, schedule, workflow_dispatch), jobs, steps, actions (uses:) or shell commands (run:), and permissions/secrets. Workflows in that directory on the repository’s default branch are discovered and executed by GitHub Actions; multiple files allow separate pipelines. Verify by listing files (ls .github/workflows or git ls-files .github/workflows) and by checking the Actions tab in the repository or querying the API: curl -H "Authorization: token <TOKEN>" https://api.github.com/repos/{owner}/{repo}/actions/runs. Workflow filenames must be valid YAML and placed under .github/workflows to be active.

5489. [GitHub Actions] What is an event trigger?
Answer: An event trigger is the condition that causes a GitHub Actions workflow to run, declared under the workflow’s top-level on: key (for example on: push, pull_request, schedule, workflow_dispatch, repository_dispatch, workflow_call, or workflow_run). Triggers support filters such as branches, tags, and paths (e.g., on: push: branches: [main] paths: ["src/**"]). schedule uses cron syntax. workflow_dispatch supports user-provided inputs. Events arrive as GitHub webhook payloads and create workflow runs shown in the Actions UI. You can verify runs programmatically via the REST API, e.g. GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/actions/workflows/{workflow_id}/runs or curl -H "Authorization: token $GITHUB_TOKEN" https://api.github.com/repos/OWNER/REPO/actions/runs.

5490. [GitHub Actions] What is workflow_dispatch?
Answer: workflow_dispatch is a GitHub Actions event that enables manually triggered workflow runs. In a workflow YAML you declare on: workflow_dispatch and may define inputs with name, description, required, default and type (string, boolean, choice). Manual runs are started from the repository Actions UI (“Run workflow” button) or programmatically via the REST API: POST /repos/{owner}/{repo}/actions/workflows/{workflow_id}/dispatches with JSON {"ref":"branch-or-tag","inputs":{...}}. You must supply a ref (branch or tag). Verify execution by viewing the run in Actions or via GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/actions/runs. workflows triggered by workflow_dispatch run with the same authorization rules as other Actions executions.

5491. [GitHub Actions] Why does gh workflow run fail when workflow_dispatch is missing?
Answer: gh workflow run uses GitHub’s "workflow_dispatch" API: it POSTs to /repos/{owner}/{repo}/actions/workflows/{workflow_id}/dispatches, which only enqueues workflows that declare on: workflow_dispatch (or workflow_call invoked via other means). If your workflow YAML lacks on: workflow_dispatch, the API rejects the request and gh prints an error (the action cannot be manually triggered). Verify by inspecting the workflow file for the trigger (grep -n "workflow_dispatch" .github/workflows/*.yml) or by viewing triggers with gh workflow view WORKFLOW_NAME (it lists the "On:" section). Fix by adding an explicit on: workflow_dispatch (optionally with inputs) and then run gh workflow run WORKFLOW_NAME --ref main successfully.

5492. [GitHub Actions] How do you add a manual trigger to a workflow?
Answer: Add the workflow_dispatch event to the workflow YAML and push it to .github/workflows/*.yml. Example:

name: "Manual CI"
on:
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      environment:
        description: "Target environment"
        required: true
        default: "staging"

Commit and push the file; GitHub automatically exposes a "Run workflow" button in the repository Actions tab and on individual workflow pages. To trigger from CLI, use: gh workflow run "<workflow file name>" --ref main --field environment=staging. Verify the run appears in Actions or with gh run list --workflow "<workflow file name>" and inspect logs with gh run view <run-id> --log for operational details.

5493. [GitHub Actions] What is push trigger?
Answer: The push trigger in GitHub Actions is the on: push event that starts workflows when commits are pushed to refs (branches or tags) in the repository. You configure filters in the workflow YAML: branches, branches-ignore, tags, tags-ignore, paths, and paths-ignore. The runner receives environment variables like GITHUB_REF (ref that was pushed) and GITHUB_SHA (commit SHA), and the event payload includes ref, before, after, and commits. To verify a push-triggered run, push a commit, then confirm a workflow run appears under the repository’s Actions tab and inspect the run’s event payload or GITHUB_REF/GITHUB_SHA in the job logs. Push differs from pull_request; it triggers on pushes to the target repo’s refs.

5494. [GitHub Actions] What is pull_request trigger?
Answer: The pull_request trigger in GitHub Actions starts workflows when pull request lifecycle events occur against a repository (opened, reopened, synchronize, labeled, etc.). Configure it in workflow YAML: e.g.
on:
  pull_request:
    types: [opened, synchronize]
    branches: [main]
The event payload is available at github.event.pull_request (fields like head.sha, head.ref, base.ref); github.head_ref and github.base_ref are also set. actions/checkout@v4 can check out the PR commit (use ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }} or allow the default checkout of the merge ref). Note: secrets are not available to workflows triggered by forks unless explicitly allowed via repository settings. Verification: view the run in the Actions tab and inspect the event payload.

5495. [GitHub Actions] What is schedule trigger?
Answer: A schedule trigger is an automated workflow trigger that runs a GitHub Actions workflow at times defined by a cron expression. In a workflow YAML you declare it as:
on:
  schedule:
    - cron: '0 0 * * *'
GitHub evaluates the five-field POSIX cron expression in UTC (minute hour day month weekday) and enqueues the workflow on the repository’s default branch using the workflow file present there. Scheduled runs won’t be triggered in forked repositories and require Actions to be enabled. Verify execution via the Actions tab run history or the REST API GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/actions/runs (or gh api) to list recent scheduled workflow runs.

5496. [GitHub Actions] What is workflow_call?
Answer: on: workflow_call is a GitHub Actions event that defines a reusable workflow which other workflows can invoke. You declare it in the callee YAML (e.g., "on: workflow_call") and optionally define inputs, secrets, and outputs under the workflow_call key. Callers invoke it from a job:
jobs:
  call:
    uses: owner/repo/.github/workflows/reusable.yml@v1
    with:
      input1: value
    secrets:
      SECRET: ${{ secrets.NAME }}
The reusable run executes as its own workflow run (with its own run id). Verify by viewing Actions → run details (event = workflow_call) and inspecting the called workflow’s logs and outputs; secrets are redacted in logs.

5497. [GitHub Actions] What is the difference between a workflow and a job?
Answer: A workflow is the top-level YAML file in .github/workflows that declares triggers (on:), concurrency, defaults, permissions, environment variables, and the jobs: map. A job is a single unit of execution inside that workflow; jobs run on a runner specified by runs-on, contain steps (uses: or run:), can define strategy: matrix, container or services, set needs for dependencies, and emit outputs. Operationally, workflows orchestrate CI/CD and trigger runs; jobs are the parallel or sequential execution units within a run. To verify, view a run in the Actions UI to see workflow-level metadata and per-job logs, or call the API GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/actions/runs/{run_id}/jobs to list job details.

5498. [GitHub Actions] What is the difference between a job and a step?
Answer: A job is a collection of sequential steps that executes on a single runner (specified with runs-on) and can run in parallel with other jobs unless constrained by needs. A step is a single action invocation (uses) or shell command (run) executed in order inside its job, sharing the same workspace and filesystem and able to set outputs or environment variables for later steps. To set a step output write to GITHUB_OUTPUT: echo "result=ok" >> $GITHUB_OUTPUT and reference it as ${{ steps.step_id.outputs.result }}. To expose a job output map a step output in jobs.job_id.outputs and read it from downstream jobs with ${{ needs.job_id.outputs.some }}.

5499. [GitHub Actions] What is the difference between GitHub-hosted and self-hosted runners?
Answer: GitHub-hosted runners are ephemeral VMs managed by GitHub: they boot a clean image per job, include a curated set of preinstalled tools, scale automatically, and are subject to GitHub Actions usage limits and billing. Self-hosted runners are machines you provision and maintain (on‑premises or cloud), registered to a repo/org with a registration token and the runner application; they can access internal networks, custom hardware (GPUs), and arbitrary software, but you must handle updates, security, and scaling. Verify runner type in repo/org Settings → Actions → Runners or via the REST API (GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/actions/runners). Register a self-hosted runner with ./config.sh --url <repo-url> --token <token> and check service status with ./svc.sh status.

5500. [GitHub Actions] How do you select a runner using runs-on?
Answer: Use the runs-on key in job YAML to pick a runner by label. For GitHub-hosted runners specify a single label such as ubuntu-latest, windows-latest, or macos-latest: runs-on: ubuntu-latest. For self-hosted runners supply a string or array of labels; all labels in an array must match the runner (e.g., runs-on: [self-hosted, linux, x64, gpu]). Verify available self-hosted runner labels in Settings → Actions → Runners or via the REST API GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/actions/runners and examine each runner.labels. Confirm which runner executed a job in the Actions UI or job log where the runner name and labels are shown at the start of the job.

5501. [GitHub Actions] How do you use a marketplace action?
Answer: Find the action in GitHub Marketplace, read its README and required inputs/permissions, then reference it in your workflow YAML with a pinned ref. Example step:
- uses: actions/checkout@v3
  with:
    token: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
Or pin to a commit: uses: owner/repo@<commit-sha>. Supply inputs via with:, secrets via ${{ secrets.NAME }}, and set permissions or environment in the workflow or job. Verify by running the workflow, inspecting the Actions run log and step output, and reviewing the action’s source at github.com/owner/repo to confirm behavior and any required permissions.

5502. [GitHub Actions] What are reusable workflows?
Answer: Reusable workflows in GitHub Actions are workflow files declared with on: workflow_call that other workflows can invoke via a uses: reference (e.g., uses: owner/repo/.github/workflows/reusable.yml@v1). They accept defined inputs and secrets, expose outputs via job outputs, and run as a separate workflow with its own jobs and logs. To call one: create a job in the caller workflow that uses the reusable workflow and pass inputs/secrets, e.g. jobs.call: uses: org/repo/.github/workflows/reusable.yml@main with: my-input: value. Verify by viewing the caller run in the Actions UI—its Jobs list shows the called reusable workflow and you can inspect step logs and outputs (accessible as jobs.call.outputs.<name>) to confirm correct execution.

5503. [GitHub Actions] What are composite actions?
Answer: Composite actions are GitHub Actions defined with an action.yml that uses "runs: using: composite" to compose multiple workflow steps into a single reusable action. A composite action can declare inputs and outputs, set environment variables, and run multiple "run:" steps or call other actions via "uses:". They execute on the workflow runner (not inside a container provided by the action) and therefore cannot use "runs: using: docker" behavior or define JavaScript-style post handlers. Invoke them with uses: owner/repo/path@ref and read outputs as steps.<step-id>.outputs.<output-name>. Verify by viewing the workflow run logs (each composed step appears as a Run line) or by echoing an output to $GITHUB_OUTPUT in the calling workflow.

5504. [GitHub Actions] What is a matrix strategy?
