Protect production paths with a circuit breaker (pybreaker.CircuitBreaker) and fall back to cached or degraded responses from Redis (GET/SET) or serve stale data. Offload non‑critical work to a queue (Celery/RabbitMQ) for retry, and return clear 5xx involvement to callers. Emit metrics and logs (Prometheus counters, OpenTelemetry spans) and alert on error-rate and latency thresholds; verify behavior by curling with timeout (curl --max-time 5) and checking /metrics scrapes.

6707. [High Availability and Resilience] What is chaos engineering?
Answer: Chaos engineering is the discipline of running controlled experiments that inject failures into production-like systems to validate hypotheses about system resilience and reduce unknown risks. Practically, you define a steady-state (SLOs, request latency, error rate), form a hypothesis, limit blast radius, then inject faults using tools like kubectl delete pod, docker kill <container>, tc qdisc netem to add latency, AWS SSM (aws ssm send-command) to stop instances, or platforms such as Gremlin, Chaos Mesh or LitmusChaos. Verify by observing monitoring and alerting (Prometheus metrics, Grafana dashboards, CloudWatch logs), automated rollbacks or remediation, and postmortems. Experiments must be incremental, reversible, and tied to measurable impact on SLOs.

6708. [High Availability and Resilience] What is fault injection?
Answer: Fault injection is the deliberate introduction of errors or adverse conditions into a system to validate its resilience, monitoring, and recovery. Common techniques include killing processes (kubectl delete pod <name>), CPU/memory exhaustion (stress-ng), network faults (tc qdisc add dev eth0 root netem delay 200ms loss 5%), packet drops (iptables -A OUTPUT -p tcp --dport 80 -j DROP), injecting AWS failures with AWS Fault Injection Simulator (aws fis start-experiment), or targeted chaos via Gremlin/Chaos Toolkit. Verify effects by checking health endpoints (curl /health), observing orchestration reaction (kubectl get pods; kubectl describe pod), metric/alert changes in Prometheus/Grafana, and that automated recovery (autoscaling, leader re-election) completes within SLOs.

6709. [High Availability and Resilience] Have you performed a game day?
Answer: [CONTEXT] I organized a game day for a microservices platform running on EKS with ASGs, Prometheus/Grafana, and PagerDuty. [ACTION] I executed controlled failures: aws autoscaling terminate-instance-in-auto-scaling-group --instance-id i-0123456789abcdef0 --no-decrement-desired-capacity, kubectl cordon <node> && kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data, and killed a deployment with kubectl rollout restart deployment/myservice to test rolling restart behavior. I validated recovery with kubectl get pods -o wide, curl -f http://myservice.internal/health for smoke tests, and Prometheus API queries: curl -g 'http://prometheus:9090/api/v1/query?query=up{job="myservice"}'. [RESULT] The runbook and monitoring triggered PagerDuty incidents and autoscaling replaced capacity within expected SLO windows.


Disaster Recovery and Backup
----------------------------
6710. [Disaster Recovery and Backup] What is business continuity?
Answer: Business continuity is the set of policies, procedures, and technical controls that ensure critical business functions continue during and after disruptive events. It includes identifying critical processes, defining RTO (Recovery Time Objective) and RPO (Recovery Point Objective), redundancy/replication, backup and restore procedures, incident runbooks, and regular tabletop and live failover tests. Verification is operational: run backup integrity checks (restic check, borg check, or sha256sum) and periodic restores (restic restore or pg_restore) and execute failover drills (promote read replica with aws rds promote-read-replica --db-instance-identifier <id> and validate traffic cutover). Business continuity is validated by meeting RTO/RPO in documented tests.

6711. [Disaster Recovery and Backup] What is the difference between high availability and disaster recovery?
Answer: High availability (HA) minimizes planned and unplanned downtime within a production environment by removing single points of failure: redundant instances, active-active load balancers, clustering (e.g., Pacemaker/Corosync), replicated storage (RAID, multipath), and synchronous replication to achieve very low RTO/RPO. Verify HA with automated health checks, simulated node kills and observing load‑balancer failover and metric continuity. Disaster recovery (DR) handles catastrophic, site‑level loss: geo‑replication, asynchronous backups/snapshots, cold/warm/hot secondary sites and documented runbooks. Verify DR with periodic full restore tests (e.g., restore from S3 via aws s3 cp and pg_restore), DNS failover tests (Route 53 health checks/failover) and measured RTO/RPO against recovery objectives.

6712. [Disaster Recovery and Backup] What is RTO?
Answer: RTO (Recovery Time Objective) is the maximum acceptable elapsed time between a disruption and restoration of a service or application to meet business requirements. It’s a target used to design DR processes and SLAs and is distinct from RPO (data loss tolerance). Operationally you measure RTO from the incident timestamp to the time synthetic healthchecks succeed: e.g., record start=$(date +%s.%N) when failover begins, poll the app endpoint with curl until HTTP 200, then end=$(date +%s.%N) and compute elapsed=$(echo "$end - $start" | bc). Use this measured value to validate runbooks and adjust architecture (replication, warm standby, automation).

6713. [Disaster Recovery and Backup] What is RPO?
Answer: Recovery Point Objective (RPO) is the maximum acceptable age of data after a disruption—i.e., how much data loss (measured in time) is tolerable. It drives backup/replication frequency: a 1-hour RPO requires backups or continuous replication at least hourly. You verify RPO by checking the age of the latest recoverable point: for example, run aws backup list-recovery-points-by-backup-vault --backup-vault-name my-vault and inspect the CreationDate, or for Restic run restic snapshots --json and examine the newest snapshot time. RPO is distinct from RTO (Recovery Time Objective), which defines how long restoration may take.

6714. [Disaster Recovery and Backup] How do RTO and RPO influence architecture?
Answer: RTO (time-to-recover) drives automation, orchestration and prebuilt images: use AMIs and infrastructure-as-code (Terraform) plus scripts to restore VMs/containers quickly (aws ec2 create-image; aws ec2 run-instances) and measure with time aws rds restore-db-instance-from-db-snapshot. RPO (acceptable data loss) sets replication and backup cadence: synchronous replication or primary+hot-standby for near-zero RPO (PostgreSQL streaming replication; verify with SELECT pg_current_wal_lsn() / pg_last_wal_replay_lsn()), or periodic snapshots/backups for larger RPO (aws rds create-db-snapshot, pg_basebackup). Operationally, lower RTO requires DNS TTLs and Route53 failover settings tuned (ChangeResourceRecordSets) and routine recovery drills where you time restores and validate via pg_isready or dig +short to confirm recovery windows.

6715. [Disaster Recovery and Backup] What is a backup strategy?
Answer: A backup strategy is a documented plan specifying what data is backed up, how (full/incremental/differential), where (on-site, off-site, cloud), cadence, retention, encryption, and measurable RTO/RPO targets. It follows principles like 3-2-1 (three copies, two media, one off-site) and uses concrete tools (e.g., restic backup ./data && restic check, or aws s3 cp /backup s3://bucket/ --recursive and aws s3api list-objects). It mandates verification: periodic test restores (restic restore or aws s3 cp s3://bucket/file ./ && sha256sum file) and snapshot consistency (aws ec2 create-snapshot --volume-id vol-xxxx). It includes monitoring and runbooks for failover, retention enforcement, and secure key management.

6716. [Disaster Recovery and Backup] What is full backup?
Answer: A full backup involves capturing all data and configurations of a system at a given point in time. To ensure its integrity, I verify changes by checking logs, metrics, configuration files, access permissions, and post-change health signals. For example, on GCP, I would use the `gsutil` command to take a snapshot of a storage bucket: `gsutil -m rsync gs://[BUCKET_NAME] gs://[BACKUP_BUCKET_NAME]/[TIMESTAMP]`. This process is crucial for disaster recovery and business continuity, as it allows us to quickly restore data in case of an outage or data loss.

6717. [Disaster Recovery and Backup] What is incremental backup?
Answer: An incremental backup saves only data changed since a prior backup (typically the last full or last incremental) to minimize storage and transfer. Implementation examples: GNU tar supports incremental sets via tar --listed-incremental=snapshot.file -cf incr-YYYYMMDD.tar /data (snapshot.file records inode/mtime state); rsync can produce space-efficient “incrementals” using hard-linking with rsync -a --link-dest=/backups/full /data /backups/incr-YYYYMMDD; modern tools (Borg, restic, Veeam) store deltas and metadata and provide commands like borg create /repo::incr-YYYYMMDD /data and borg check to verify repo integrity. Restores require the last full plus all subsequent incrementals in order; verify by mounting or listing archives (borg mount, restic restore) and checksum or tool-provided check operations.

6718. [Disaster Recovery and Backup] What is differential backup?
Answer: A differential backup copies all data changed since the last full backup, producing progressively larger backup sets until the next full backup. Unlike incremental backups, which capture only changes since the previous incremental, a differential requires only the most recent full plus the most recent differential to perform a complete restore. Operationally, verify by restoring the last full backup and the latest differential to a test system and comparing file checksums or timestamps (e.g., sha256sum) against production, or by mounting the backup image and validating application consistency (database log replay or vendor tools). Differential backups trade increased storage and runtime against faster, simpler restores.

6719. [Disaster Recovery and Backup] How do you verify backups?
Answer: Verify backups by automating integrity checks, metadata checks, and full restores. Examples: compute checksums locally and after transfer (sha256sum file && aws s3 cp file s3://bucket/ && aws s3api head-object --bucket bucket --key file && aws s3 cp s3://bucket/file - | sha256sum). For repository tools use built-ins: borg check --verify-data repo, restic check && restic snapshots && restic restore latest --target /tmp/test-restore. For databases perform logical restore or apply WAL: pg_restore -d testdb dump.sql and run schema & smoke queries, or restore Percona XtraBackup and mysql --execute "SELECT COUNT(*) FROM important_table;". Automate pass/fail on exit codes and schedule periodic full restores to staging.

6720. [Disaster Recovery and Backup] Why is an untested backup not reliable?
Answer: An untested backup is unreliable because you don’t know whether data is complete, consistent, or restorable: media can be corrupted, backups can omit files or ACLs, encryption keys may be unavailable, application-state (e.g., DB transactions) can be inconsistent, or restore tooling/configuration may fail. Verify backups by executing regular test restores into an isolated environment (e.g., aws rds restore-db-instance-to-point-in-time for RDS, or restore VM from snapshot and boot), run checksum comparisons (sha256sum or borg check/restic check), confirm application health (pg_restore then pg_isready, MySQL replicas), validate encryption keys in KMS, and measure RTO/RPO during drills to ensure restores complete within SLA.

6721. [Disaster Recovery and Backup] How frequently should restore tests be performed?
Answer: Restore-test frequency should be risk-aligned: run automated restore verification daily for highest‑critical data (e.g., transaction DBs), weekly for important systems, and a full, end‑to‑end disaster recovery drill (application failover, DNS, load‑balancers, RTO/RPO verification) at least quarterly; include an annual compliance audit. Operationally: perform automated object restores (example: aws rds restore-db-instance-to-point-in-time --source-db-instance-identifier ...), run restic check and restic restore for file stores, then validate with application smoke tests (psql -h <host> -U <user> -c '\l' or mysql -e 'SHOW DATABASES;') and file integrity checks (sha256sum). Record RTO/RPO outcomes and ticket any deviations.

6722. [Disaster Recovery and Backup] What is cross-region backup?
Answer: Cross-region backup is storing backup copies in a geographically separate cloud region to protect against regional failures, disasters, or regulatory requirements. It typically uses provider mechanisms like AWS S3 Cross-Region Replication (CRR) or AWS Backup cross-region copy, Azure Backup/Recovery Services vault geo-replication, or GCP snapshot copy. Implementations enforce encryption in transit (TLS) and at rest (KMS/CMEK); example commands to operate and verify include aws s3api get-bucket-replication --bucket my-bucket and aws s3api list-objects-v2 --bucket my-destination-bucket, or aws ec2 copy-snapshot --source-region us-east-1 --source-snapshot-id snap-12345 followed by aws ec2 describe-snapshots --snapshot-ids snap-67890 to confirm. Test restores, monitor replication status and costs (egress, storage, operations) to validate RTO/RPO.

6723. [Disaster Recovery and Backup] What is immutable backup?
Answer: Immutable backup is backup data stored so it cannot be altered or deleted for a defined retention period (WORM semantics), preventing ransomware or human tampering. Examples: S3 Object Lock (governance or compliance modes; verify with aws s3api get-object-lock-configuration --bucket my-bucket), Azure Blob immutable storage/immutability policies (inspect with az storage container immutability-policy show --account-name myacct --container-name mycontainer), or immutable repositories in backup products (e.g., Veeam immutable Linux repository). Operational verification includes attempting deletion during retention and observing access denied, and auditing object-lock/immutability-policy metadata and retention timestamps. Immutable backups ensure integrity and retention enforcement.

6724. [Disaster Recovery and Backup] What is air-gapped backup?
Answer: An air-gapped backup is a copy of data physically or logically isolated from production networks so attackers cannot reach it. Typical implementations: removable media/tape stored offline, vaulting, or cloud object immutability plus network controls. On-premises: eject and store LTO tapes in a secure vault; verify with md5sum or sha256sum and periodic test restores. Cloud: enable S3 Object Lock (bucket must have ObjectLockEnabled), use --object-lock-mode COMPLIANCE via aws s3api put-object, verify with aws s3api get-object-lock-configuration, and restrict IAM/network paths. Operational controls include chain-of-custody, encrypted media, documented retention, scheduled restore drills, and checksum/hash verification to ensure integrity.

6725. [Disaster Recovery and Backup] How do you back up Kubernetes resources?
Answer: To back up Kubernetes resources, I assess the production mechanism, configuration involved, and operational risk it controls. For example, I use `kubectl get events` to track changes and verify their impact on [SERVICE]. I also monitor readiness probes, Service selectors, Ingress routing, NetworkPolicy, DNS, and node capacity using metrics like CPU utilization and disk space. Key failure modes include data loss due to incomplete backups or misconfigured storage. To mitigate this, we implement a 3-2-1 backup strategy: three copies of data on two different types of storage with one copy offsite. Rollback steps involve using `kubectl rollout undo` and verifying application functionality through load testing.

6726. [Disaster Recovery and Backup] How do you back up persistent volumes?
Answer: To back up persistent volumes, I assess the production mechanism and configuration involved, considering the operational risk it controls. In Disaster Recovery and Backup, I identify what changes are made, who or what is affected, and how it's verified. For validation, I check logs, metrics, configuration, access permissions, and post-change health signals before closing the issue. Specifically, for GCP Persistent Disks, I use `gsutil` to create a snapshot: `gsutil snapshot gs://[BUCKET_NAME]/[DISK_NAME]`. This ensures data integrity and facilitates rollback or recovery in case of failures.

6727. [Disaster Recovery and Backup] How do you back up etcd?
Answer: In our production environment, we back up etcd using a combination of automated scripts and manual verification. We use the `etcdctl` command to snapshot the database periodically, storing it in a secure location such as Google Cloud Storage. The configuration involves setting up a cron job to run the backup script daily, with a retention policy to keep 30 days' worth of backups. To verify the integrity of the backups, we check the etcd cluster's health metrics and logs after each snapshot. If there are any issues, we can roll back to a previous version using the `etcdctl` command with the `--from-key` option.

6728. [Disaster Recovery and Backup] How do you restore a Kubernetes cluster?
Answer: Restore etcd first (control plane state), e.g. stop API server, run: ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl snapshot restore snapshot.db --data-dir=/var/lib/etcd --name node1 --initial-cluster node1=https://127.0.0.1:2380 --initial-cluster-token etcd-cluster-1 --initial-cluster-state new (include your TLS flags --cacert/--cert/--key if used). Start kube-apiserver/kubelet and confirm etcd with etcdctl --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 endpoint status and API with kubectl get --raw=/healthz. Restore workloads and PVs using your backup tool (Velero: velero restore create --from-backup <backup>; velero restore describe <name>) or cloud-provider volume snapshots and rebind PVCs. Verify cluster health with kubectl get nodes,pods -A, kubectl get pv,pvc and exercise critical apps and Services/Ingress to confirm full recovery.

6729. [Disaster Recovery and Backup] How have you used Kasten K10?
Answer: [CONTEXT] I operated Kasten K10 v5.x to protect multiple Kubernetes clusters (EKS/GKE) and stateful workloads (Postgres, Cassandra) using on-prem and S3-compatible object storage.
[ACTION] I installed via Helm: helm repo add kasten https://charts.kasten.io/ && helm repo update && helm install k10 kasten/k10 --namespace kasten-io --create-namespace. I created Profiles and Policies in the K10 UI and used kubectl to inspect CRs: kubectl get backups -n kasten-io and kubectl get restores -n kasten-io. For UI access I used kubectl port-forward service/gateway -n kasten-io 8080:8000 and validated jobs with kubectl get pods -n kasten-io. I tested restores by performing a namespace-level backup and a restore to a sandbox namespace.
[RESULT] Backups completed successfully, restores verified by kubectl get pods and application-level smoke tests.

6730. [Disaster Recovery and Backup] How have you used Veeam?
Answer: I used Veeam Backup & Replication to protect VMware and Hyper‑V fleets, Veeam Agents for Windows/Linux for physical and cloud VMs, and storage‑integrated backups (NetApp snapshots and SAN hardware snapshots). I automated and triggered jobs via PowerShell (Add-PSSnapin VeeamPSSnapIn; Get-VBRJob; Start-VBRJob -Name "Daily-Full" -RunAsync) and via Enterprise Manager REST (POST /api/jobs/{jobId}/run) for orchestration. For recoverability I used Instant VM Recovery, replica failover, and SureBackup application‑group boots to validate guest‑OS and SQL/IIS connectivity. I verified success with Get-VBRBackupSession | Select Name, CreationTime, Result and by mounting restore points (Get-VBRRestorePoint) to perform file-level and DB restores.

6731. [Disaster Recovery and Backup] What is a disaster-recovery drill?
Answer: A disaster-recovery drill is a planned, repeatable exercise that simulates a real outage to verify people, runbooks, backups, and failover mechanisms meet RTO/RPO targets. Typical steps: trigger failover (e.g., promote replica or run aws rds restore-db-instance-to-point-in-time, or execute aws route53 change-resource-record-sets to switch DNS), restore an AMI/snapshot (aws ec2 create-snapshot then aws ec2 register-image/launch), or restore Kubernetes from etcd/velero backups (velero restore create). Verify by running smoke tests and health checks (curl -f /health, kubectl get pods --watch), validate data integrity with checksums or queries, and measure time-to-recovery against runbook timers and monitoring alerts to document gaps and corrective actions.

6732. [Disaster Recovery and Backup] How do you document a DR procedure?
Answer: Create a single authoritative runbook in Git (markdown) with: scope, RTO/RPO, dependencies, step-by-step recovery commands, required credentials location (vault), contact/escalation matrix, acceptance tests, rollback, and verification. Store scripts and IaC (Terraform/CloudFormation) alongside the runbook and enforce changes via PRs and CI that runs linting and smoke-test scripts. Include concrete commands to run during recovery and verification, e.g. aws ec2 start-instances --instance-ids i-0123456789abcdef0; aws ec2 describe-instance-status --instance-ids i-0123456789abcdef0; kubectl apply -f namespace.yaml && kubectl rollout status deployment/myapp -n myns; restic restore latest --target /restore && restic snapshots. Schedule quarterly tabletop exercises and periodic automated DR drills that run the verification commands and record outcomes.

6733. [Disaster Recovery and Backup] How do you fail over to a secondary region?
Answer: Promote or restore data in the secondary region, switch networking, update DNS/load balancing, verify services and monitoring. Example AWS sequence: promote a replica with aws rds promote-read-replica --db-instance-identifier my-replica; restore AMIs/EBS from snapshots (create-image / aws ec2 run-instances) and register EC2 instances in the secondary target group; attach Elastic IPs or update ALB target groups; update DNS via Route 53 using aws route53 change-resource-record-sets --hosted-zone-id Z —change-batch file://changes.json (use low TTL beforehand). Verify: aws rds describe-db-instances to confirm MASTER, curl/health-check endpoints through ALB/DNS, check logs and CloudWatch metrics for request rates/errors, and validate data consistency with application-level reads/writes before declaring failover complete.

6734. [Disaster Recovery and Backup] How do you fail back to the primary region?
Answer: Validate the primary region is healthy, sync data, and perform a controlled cutover: promote any standby/replica in the primary region (e.g., for RDS MySQL/Postgres run aws rds promote-read-replica --db-instance-identifier <id>), restore point-in-time backups if needed (RDS Console or aws rds restore-db-instance-to-point-in-time), and register primary instances with load balancers (aws elbv2 register-targets --target-group-arn <arn> --targets Id=<instance-id>). Update DNS to point traffic back (Route 53: aws route53 change-resource-record-sets --hosted-zone-id Z123 --change-batch file://changes.json) and lower failover region weight/disable failover health checks. Verify with health checks, CloudWatch metrics, application smoke tests (curl HTTP 200), and confirm replication/resync (S3 replication status, DMS task state).

6735. [Disaster Recovery and Backup] What is pilot-light architecture?
Answer: Pilot-light is a DR pattern where a minimal, always-on subset of production services (the "pilot") runs in the recovery region with continuously replicated data; full capacity is launched on demand. Typically you run small instances or services plus data replication (for example, an RDS read replica created with aws rds create-db-instance-read-replica or continuous EBS snapshots and AMIs created with aws ec2 create-image). During failover you scale using IaC: aws cloudformation deploy or terraform apply to create full stacks, aws autoscaling set-desired-capacity to raise instance count, and aws rds restore-db-instance-from-snapshot if needed. Verify by running health checks (Route 53 health checks) and functional tests against the restored endpoints.

6736. [Disaster Recovery and Backup] What is warm-standby architecture?
Answer: Warm-standby architecture keeps a scaled-down, running copy of production services and data that can be scaled up or promoted during failover to meet target RTO/RPO. Data is continuously replicated (synchronous or asynchronous) using mechanisms such as database replication (e.g., PostgreSQL streaming replication with base backup + wal shipping) or block-level replication (rsync, DRBD, or cloud provider replication). Verify readiness by monitoring replication lag (Postgres: SELECT now() - pg_last_xact_replay_timestamp() AS replication_lag;), health checks (curl -f http://host:port/health), and automated failover drill: promote standby (pg_ctl promote) or switch DNS/ELB with low TTL/Route 53 failover and confirm application connectivity. Operationally, ensure configuration, backups, and regular drills.

6737. [Disaster Recovery and Backup] What is multi-site active-active DR?
Answer: Multi-site active-active DR is an architecture where two or more geographically separated sites concurrently serve live traffic and replicate state so any site can fail without service interruption. It requires synchronous or bounded-asynchronous replication, global traffic distribution (DNS TTL/BGP/Route 53/Global Accelerator), conflict resolution (application-level idempotency or CRDTs), and quorum/consensus to avoid split-brain. Operational checks include verifying replication health (MySQL: SHOW SLAVE STATUS\G and Seconds_Behind_Master; PostgreSQL: SELECT pg_last_wal_receive_lsn(), pg_last_wal_replay_lsn(); Consul: consul members), exercising failover by draining a site and validating <dig/host/curl> responses and metrics, and running periodic recovery drills to confirm RPO/RTO targets are met.

6738. [Disaster Recovery and Backup] How do you choose the right DR strategy?
Answer: Choose a DR strategy by mapping business impact to RTO and RPO, classifying systems (critical, important, nonessential), and selecting technologies that meet those targets within cost and compliance constraints. For example, use synchronous replication or active-active for sub-minute RPO (e.g., database cluster HA), async replication or periodic EBS snapshots (aws ec2 create-snapshot) and RDS point-in-time restores (aws rds restore-db-instance-to-point-in-time) for hourly RPOs, and cold backups to S3 Glacier for archival. Define failover automation (Terraform/CloudFormation or Route 53 failover with health checks and low TTL), runbook steps, and scheduled DR drills that perform restores and validate functionality (restore from snapshot, run integration smoke tests, verify DB consistency). Continuous verification and cost-risk tradeoffs dictate the final choice.


Kubernetes Production Troubleshooting
-------------------------------------
6739. [Kubernetes Production Troubleshooting] A pod is in CrashLoopBackOff. How do you troubleshoot it?
Answer: kubectl describe pod <pod> to see events and containerStatuses (restartCount, state, lastState.terminated.exitCode/message). Fetch container logs including previous run: kubectl logs <pod> -c <container> --previous. Inspect YAML for command/args, env, image, probes, volumes: kubectl get pod <pod> -o yaml. Check probe failures (liveness/readiness) and probe configuration and thresholds. If logs are empty, kubectl exec into a running sidecar or node and inspect filesystem; use kubectl cp to extract files. Check node and kubelet logs (journalctl -u kubelet) for OOM/kubelet issues, and kubectl get events --sort-by=.metadata.creationTimestamp for cluster-level events. Fix root cause (crash, bad image, probe, permissions, OOM) and redeploy, then verify with kubectl logs and kubectl get pod.

6740. [Kubernetes Production Troubleshooting] What commands do you use for CrashLoopBackOff?
Answer: kubectl get pods --all-namespaces | grep CrashLoopBackOff; kubectl describe pod <pod> -n <ns> to read events and container state; kubectl logs <pod> -n <ns> [-c <container>] and kubectl logs <pod> -n <ns> -c <container> -p to fetch previous failed run logs; kubectl get pod <pod> -n <ns> -o wide and kubectl get node <node> -o wide to check scheduling; kubectl get pod <pod> -n <ns> -o jsonpath='{.status.containerStatuses[*].restartCount}' to see restart count; journalctl -u kubelet -n 200 on the node for kubelet/container runtime errors; kubectl exec -it <pod> -n <ns> -- sh (if container is running briefly) to inspect filesystem; fix image/command/config and kubectl rollout restart deployment/<name> or kubectl delete pod <pod> -n <ns> to force recreate, then reverify logs and describe.

6741. [Kubernetes Production Troubleshooting] How do you inspect the previous container logs?
Answer: Run kubectl logs with the --previous (or -p) flag for the restarted container: kubectl logs <pod-name> -c <container-name> --previous. If you don’t know the pod, list pods: kubectl get pods -n <ns>. To verify why it restarted, inspect the pod status: kubectl describe pod <pod-name> -n <ns> and check the “Last State/State” terminated block (exitCode, reason, message) and the restartCount. If the pod was evicted or the node lost logs, retrieve runtime logs on the node (for dockershim: docker logs <container-id>, or for CRI-O/containerd use crictl inspect/crictl pods and node-level journalctl -u kubelet) to correlate with kubectl --previous output.

6742. [Kubernetes Production Troubleshooting] What can cause a container to restart repeatedly?
Answer: Common causes include application process exit (non‑zero exit code), failing or misconfigured livenessProbe/readinessProbe, OOMKilled due to container memory limit/cgroup eviction, imagePullBackOff or bad image, CrashLoopBackOff from repeated crashes, node resource pressure or kubelet eviction, and host/kernel issues (OOM killer, cgroup failures). Verify with kubectl describe pod <pod> and kubectl logs <pod> and kubectl logs -p <pod> for previous container logs, check events via kubectl get events --sort-by=.metadata.creationTimestamp, inspect node resource and pods with kubectl top node and kubectl top pod, view kubelet/system logs with journalctl -u kubelet and dmesg for OOM messages, and confirm probe configs in the Pod spec.

6743. [Kubernetes Production Troubleshooting] How can incorrect probes cause CrashLoopBackOff?
Answer: If liveness probes are too strict (short timeoutSeconds, low failureThreshold, aggressive periodSeconds) Kubernetes will kill a container that is still initializing or temporarily slow, causing repeated restarts and CrashLoopBackOff. Readiness probes don’t cause restarts but misconfigurations can route traffic to unhealthy pods; startupProbe can be used to avoid liveness kills during long startup. Diagnose with kubectl describe pod <pod> (look for “Liveness probe failed” and “Back-off restarting failed container”) and kubectl logs -p <pod> or kubectl exec to run the probe command manually (curl or tcping). Fix by tuning initialDelaySeconds, timeoutSeconds, failureThreshold or adding a startupProbe, then kubectl rollout restart deployment/<name> and verify pod becomes Ready.

6744. [Kubernetes Production Troubleshooting] A pod is Pending. What do you check?
Answer: kubectl describe pod <pod> and kubectl get events --sort-by='.metadata.creationTimestamp' to see FailedScheduling reasons. If FailedScheduling, check node capacity/allocatable vs pod requests (kubectl describe node <node>, kubectl top nodes if metrics-server installed). Verify taints/tolerations and nodeSelector/nodeAffinity mismatches (kubectl describe node; inspect pod.spec.affinity/spec.tolerations). Check ResourceQuota/LimitRange blocking creation (kubectl get resourcequota, kubectl describe quota). If PVC-backed, ensure PVC is Bound and PV/provisioner succeeded (kubectl get pvc, kubectl describe pvc, kubectl get pv, kubectl get storageclass). If scheduler issues suspected, inspect kube-scheduler logs in kube-system. Use these commands to confirm cause before remediating.

6745. [Kubernetes Production Troubleshooting] How do you identify insufficient CPU or memory?
Answer: Use kubectl and metrics to compare usage vs capacity/requests/limits. Commands: kubectl top nodes and kubectl top pods --all-namespaces (requires metrics-server) to see realtime CPU/memory. kubectl describe node <node> to check Allocatable, Capacity and Conditions (MemoryPressure/Pressure). kubectl get events --all-namespaces and kubectl describe pod <pod> to see OOMKilled or eviction events. Inspect cgroup metrics (node): cat /sys/fs/cgroup/memory/kubepods.slice/... or check /proc/<pid>/oom_score. In Prometheus, query rate(container_cpu_usage_seconds_total[5m]) and node_memory_MemAvailable_bytes, and check container_cpu_cfs_throttled_periods_total to verify CPU throttling. These checks confirm insufficient CPU/memory.

6746. [Kubernetes Production Troubleshooting] How do taints prevent pod scheduling?
Answer: A taint on a Node is a key=value:effect applied via kubectl taint nodes <node> key=value:NoSchedule|PreferNoSchedule|NoExecute; it tells the kube-scheduler not to place pods that do not have a matching toleration. A pod declares a toleration in its spec (tolerations: - key: "key" operator: "Equal" value: "value" effect: "NoSchedule"), and the scheduler only binds pods to nodes when the pod’s tolerations tolerate all node taints that would otherwise prevent scheduling. PreferNoSchedule is best-effort, NoSchedule blocks scheduling, and NoExecute also evicts existing non‑tolerating pods (eviction enforced by kubelet). Verify with kubectl describe node (taints shown), kubectl get pods to see scheduling failures/events, and kubectl taint/untaint to test behavior.

6747. [Kubernetes Production Troubleshooting] How can affinity rules cause a pod to remain Pending?
Answer: Hard affinity is evaluated as a hard scheduling constraint; nodeAffinity with type requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution or podAffinity/podAntiAffinity with topologyKey and operator In/NotIn can make no node eligible and leave a Pod Pending. Common causes: labels referenced by nodeSelector/nodeAffinity don’t exist on any node, podAntiAffinity excludes all reachable topology domains, or conflicting constraints with taints/tolerations and resource availability. Verify with kubectl describe pod <name> (Events show messages like “pod has unbound immediate PersistentVolumeClaims” or “did not match node selector/affinity”), kubectl get nodes --show-labels, kubectl get pods -o wide, and scheduler logs (kube-system/kube-scheduler). Fix by relaxing requiredDuringScheduling rules to preferredDuringScheduling, correcting labels, or modifying the affinity expression.

6748. [Kubernetes Production Troubleshooting] How can an unbound PVC block pod scheduling?
Answer: An unbound PVC can block scheduling because the scheduler refuses to place a Pod that references a PersistentVolumeClaim which is not bound to a PersistentVolume, emitting events like "pod has unbound PersistentVolumeClaims" or "pod has unbound immediate PersistentVolumeClaims". Common causes: no matching PV, dynamic provisioner failing, or StorageClass volumeBindingMode/Toplogy constraints (e.g., WaitForFirstConsumer delays provisioning until scheduling). Verify with:
- kubectl get pvc -o wide && kubectl describe pvc <pvc>
- kubectl get pv && kubectl describe pv <pv>
- kubectl get sc <sc> -o yaml (check provisioner and volumeBindingMode)
- kubectl describe pod <pod> and kubectl get events -n <ns>.
Fix by creating a matching PV, repairing the provisioner, or correcting the StorageClass so the PVC binds.

6749. [Kubernetes Production Troubleshooting] A pod is in ImagePullBackOff. What do you check?
Answer: Run kubectl describe pod <pod> to read the Events and the precise pull error (ErrImagePull vs ImagePullBackOff). Verify the image name/tag and imagePullPolicy in the Pod spec (kubectl get pod <pod> -o yaml). Check imagePullSecrets and the serviceAccount secrets (kubectl get secret, kubectl get sa). On a node, attempt a manual pull with docker pull or crictl pull <image> to reproduce auth, TLS, network, or rate-limit errors; inspect kubelet logs (journalctl -u kubelet) and container runtime logs for pull failures. Confirm registry reachability (curl/openssl to registry), DNS/proxy/firewall, and Docker Hub rate-limit responses (HTTP 429). Fix credentials, image name, or network and re-check pod events.

6750. [Kubernetes Production Troubleshooting] How do you verify the image name and tag?
Answer: Run kubectl against the workload spec and the runtime, then verify the registry. For the declared image: kubectl get deployment/nginx -o=jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.containers[*].image}' or kubectl get pod my-pod -o=jsonpath='{.spec.containers[*].image}' (or kubectl describe pod my-pod and read the Image: line). For the actually running artifact and digest: kubectl get pod my-pod -o=jsonpath='{.status.containerStatuses[*].imageID}'. On the node check the runtime: crictl ps -a; crictl inspect <containerID> will show the image reference, or docker ps/docker inspect <containerID> on Docker. To confirm the tag exists upstream use skopeo inspect docker://registry.example.com/repo:tag or docker pull registry.example.com/repo:tag.

6751. [Kubernetes Production Troubleshooting] How do you troubleshoot registry authentication?
Answer: Check pod events and image pull errors: kubectl describe pod <pod> and kubectl get events --field-selector involvedObject.name=<pod>. Confirm ImagePullBackOff or ErrImagePull and note reason. Verify credentials against the registry with docker login <registry> or curl -u user:pass https://<registry>/v2/ (unauthenticated GET /v2/ returns 401). Create or refresh a Kubernetes secret: kubectl create secret docker-registry regcred --docker-server=<registry> --docker-username=<user> --docker-password='<pass>' --docker-email=<email>. Ensure the secret is referenced by the Pod spec or ServiceAccount (kubectl patch serviceaccount default -p '{"imagePullSecrets":[{"name":"regcred"}]}'). Check kubelet and registry logs (journalctl -u kubelet, registry container logs) for TLS/errors and validate TLS with openssl s_client -connect <registry>:443.

6752. [Kubernetes Production Troubleshooting] A pod is running but not receiving traffic. What do you inspect?
Answer: Check pod readiness and events (kubectl describe pod <pod> and kubectl get pod <pod> -o wide), inspect container logs (kubectl logs) and readinessProbe config in pod spec. Verify Service selects the pod (kubectl get svc <svc> -o yaml; kubectl get endpoints <svc> and kubectl get endpointslices) and that endpoint IP/port match containerPort/targetPort. From a node or another pod, curl the Service ClusterIP and pod IP (kubectl exec -it <client-pod> -- curl -svS <clusterIP>:<port> and curl <podIP>:<port>) to test connectivity. Check NetworkPolicy (kubectl get networkpolicy) and CNI/kube-proxy health and rules (system logs, iptables-save or ipvsadm on nodes) to confirm traffic path.

6753. [Kubernetes Production Troubleshooting] How do you validate service selectors?
Answer: Run kubectl describe svc <svc> and kubectl get svc <svc> -o yaml (or jsonpath='{.spec.selector}') to inspect the service selector. Confirm pods exist that match those labels with kubectl get pods -l key=value -n <ns> and compare count to endpoints: kubectl get endpoints <svc> -n <ns> and kubectl get endpointslices -n <ns> -l kubernetes.io/service-name=<svc>. If endpoints/endpointslices are empty, the selector doesn’t match pod labels or pods aren’t Ready. Verify targetPort name/type matches container ports in pod spec and test traffic with kubectl exec -n <ns> <pod> -- curl -sS http://<ClusterIP>:<port> or by port-forwarding.

6754. [Kubernetes Production Troubleshooting] How do you validate endpoint objects?
Answer: Run kubectl get endpoints <svc> -n <ns> and kubectl get endpointslices -n <ns> to list objects, then kubectl describe endpoints/<svc> -n <ns> and kubectl get endpoints/<svc> -n <ns> -o yaml (or endpointslices -o yaml) to inspect subsets/addresses, ports, targetRef and conditions.ready fields. Verify endpoints correspond to Ready pod IPs (kubectl get pods -o wide -n <ns>) and that service.spec.clusterIP matches endpoints’ ports. Confirm kube-proxy programmed rules: on a node run iptables-save | grep <svcClusterIP> or ipvsadm -L -n to see backend endpoints. Test connectivity with curl or nc to the ClusterIP/NodePort and directly to pod IPs, and check kube-controller-manager logs (kubectl logs -n kube-system <kcm-pod>) for endpoint controller errors.

6755. [Kubernetes Production Troubleshooting] How can readiness probes remove a pod from service endpoints?
Answer: A failing readinessProbe causes the kubelet to set PodCondition Ready=false, which the kube-apiserver reflects in the Pod Status. The Endpoints controller (in kube-controller-manager) watches Pod readiness and removes Pods that are not Ready from the Service’s Endpoints object; kube-proxy and load‑balancers then stop sending traffic to that Pod. Use httpGet/tcpSocket/exec probes with periodSeconds/failureThreshold to control sensitivity. Verify by describing the Pod (kubectl describe pod <pod>), inspecting the Ready condition (kubectl get pod <pod> -o jsonpath='{.status.conditions[?(@.type=="Ready")].status}'), and watching the Service endpoints (kubectl get endpoints <svc> -o yaml) to see the Pod removed.

6756. [Kubernetes Production Troubleshooting] How do you troubleshoot Kubernetes DNS?
Answer: Check CoreDNS pods and config: kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns (or deployment/coredns) and kubectl logs -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns. Inspect ConfigMap: kubectl get configmap coredns -n kube-system -o yaml. From a pod, run: kubectl run -i --rm --restart=Never busybox --image=busybox --ns default -- sh -c "nslookup kubernetes.default.svc.cluster.local || dig @10.96.0.10 kubernetes.default.svc.cluster.local +short". Verify kube-dns Service/endpoints: kubectl get svc kube-dns -n kube-system && kubectl get endpoints kube-dns -n kube-system. Check node resolv.conf and kubelet DNS settings (--cluster-dns). If config is bad, edit ConfigMap and reload or rollout restart deployment/coredns -n kube-system; verify queries succeed from pods.

6757. [Kubernetes Production Troubleshooting] How do you troubleshoot pod-to-pod connectivity?
Answer: From the source pod, verify DNS/IP and liveness: kubectl exec -it <src> -- sh; ip -4 addr; ip route; ping -c3 <dst-pod-IP> or curl -sS http://<dst-pod-IP>:<port> (or nc -vz <dst-pod-IP> <port>). If it fails, gather cluster state: kubectl get pods -o wide --all-namespaces, kubectl get nodes, kubectl get svc, kubectl get networkpolicy --all-namespaces. Check kube-proxy and CNI: kubectl logs -n kube-system daemonset/<cni-daemonset> and kubectl logs -n kube-system ds/kube-proxy. On the node, inspect iptables/ipvs and routes (iptables-save, ipvsadm -L, ip route) and run tcpdump on the node interface: sudo tcpdump -nn -i <iface> host <dst-IP> and port <port> to confirm packet flow. Adjust or disable NetworkPolicy/CNI rules and re-test until connectivity verifies.

6758. [Kubernetes Production Troubleshooting] How do you troubleshoot pod-to-service connectivity?
Answer: Check DNS and service objects: kubectl get svc -n NAMESPACE and kubectl get endpoints -n NAMESPACE to ensure the ClusterIP and endpoints exist. From a pod in the same namespace run kubectl exec -it POD -- sh and verify DNS and TCP: nslookup myservice, curl -sv http://myservice:PORT or wget -qO- http://myservice:PORT. If DNS resolves but TCP fails, check pod networking and node rules: kubectl get pods -o wide to see node placement, confirm CNI pods (kubectl get pods -n kube-system) are Running, and inspect kube-proxy (kubectl logs -n kube-system kube-proxy-XXX) or on the node run iptables-save or ipvsadm -L -n to verify service rules. Fix by restoring endpoints, CNI, or kube-proxy and re-verify with curl returning expected response.

6759. [Kubernetes Production Troubleshooting] How do you troubleshoot ingress connectivity?
Answer: Check DNS and LB: dig or nslookup the hostname, verify LoadBalancer external IP with kubectl get svc -n ingress-nginx. Inspect Ingress and controller: kubectl describe ingress <name> and kubectl get deploy, pods -n ingress-nginx. Review controller logs: kubectl logs -n ingress-nginx deployment/ingress-nginx-controller. Verify backend endpoints and services: kubectl get endpoints <svc> and kubectl exec -it <pod> -- curl -sv http://localhost:<port>. Test HTTP path resolution from outside with curl --resolve "host:80:EXTERNAL_IP" http://host/path and from a node. Check TLS certs: kubectl get certificate, secrets and describe for cert-manager. Investigate NetworkPolicy, iptables/kube-proxy, and node firewall rules; tcpdump on node can confirm packets reach pods.

6760. [Kubernetes Production Troubleshooting] How do network policies affect connectivity?
Answer: NetworkPolicies (networking.k8s.io/v1) control pod-to-pod and pod-to-external connectivity by selecting pods with label selectors and allowing specific ingress/egress traffic; they do not open ports. By default Kubernetes allows cluster pod traffic, but when any NetworkPolicy selects a pod it becomes isolated for the directions specified (e.g., a policy with only ingress rules blocks all ingress until allowed). Policies are additive; multiple policies combine their allow rules. Enforcement depends on the CNI (Calico, Cilium, Canal, etc.). Verify behavior with kubectl get networkpolicy -n <ns>, kubectl describe networkpolicy NAME -n <ns>, and functional tests like kubectl exec -n <ns> client-pod -- curl -sS http://target-pod:port to confirm allowed/blocked traffic.

6761. [Kubernetes Production Troubleshooting] A node is NotReady. What do you check?
Answer: kubectl get node <node> -o yaml and kubectl describe node <node> to inspect Conditions, LastHeartbeatTime/LastTransitionTime, and events. Check kubelet service and logs on the node: sudo systemctl status kubelet && sudo journalctl -u kubelet --no-pager -n 200 for CRI errors, certificate expiry, kubeconfig auth errors, or eviction signals (MemoryPressure/DiskPressure). Verify container runtime: sudo crictl ps or sudo docker ps / sudo systemctl status containerd. Confirm API connectivity from the node: curl -k --header "Authorization: Bearer $(cat /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token)" https://<apiserver>:6443/healthz or check kubelet --kubeconfig. Inspect CNI and kube-proxy pods on that node and node leases in kube-system for heartbeat age.

6762. [Kubernetes Production Troubleshooting] How do you inspect kubelet status?
Answer: Run node- and host-level checks: systemctl is-active kubelet && systemctl status kubelet --no-pager to see unit state and recent exit codes. Inspect logs with sudo journalctl -u kubelet -o cat -n 200 (or -f) to find startup flags, Kubelet errors, or auth failures. Verify kubelet process and flags with ps aux | grep kubelet or sudo systemctl cat kubelet.service. Use the kubelet health endpoint: curl --fail http://127.0.0.1:10248/healthz (read-only) — it should return “ok”; the HTTPS API on 10250 requires proper certs. From the control plane, check node condition: kubectl get nodes && kubectl describe node <node> to see KubeletReady, last heartbeat, and eviction conditions.

6763. [Kubernetes Production Troubleshooting] How do you troubleshoot disk pressure?
Answer: kubectl describe node <node> to inspect Conditions (DiskPressure), Capacity/Allocatable ephemeral-storage and Eviction stats; kubectl top node (metrics-server) for overall usage. On the node, run df -h and du -sh /var/lib/containerd /var/lib/docker /var/lib/kubelet to find large directories, and docker system df or crictl images/list + crictl ps for containers. Query kubelet summary API for per-pod/container storage: curl --unix-socket /var/run/kubelet.sock http://localhost/stats/summary. Inspect kubelet eviction config in /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml (evictionHard, evictionSoft, imageGCHighThresholdPercent). Remediate by deleting large/evicted pods, pruning images (docker system prune or crictl rmi), cleaning logs, or increasing disk; verify DiskPressure clears with kubectl describe node and kubectl get nodes Ready status.

6764. [Kubernetes Production Troubleshooting] How do you troubleshoot memory pressure?
Answer: Check node state and metrics: kubectl describe node <node> (look for Conditions: MemoryPressure True) and kubectl top node <node> and kubectl top pods --all-namespaces to identify heavy consumers. Inspect kubelet eviction settings: view /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml or ps aux | grep kubelet for --eviction-hard/soft (memory.available, nodefs.available). Review kubelet and system logs: journalctl -u kubelet, dmesg | grep -i oom to find OOM killer events. Confirm Pod QoS and requests/limits (kubectl get pod -o yaml) and reduce memory or add limits; prefer Guaranteed/Burstable over BestEffort. If needed cordon and drain the node: kubectl cordon <node>; kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data, then scale or reprovision nodes. Verify recovery via kubectl top and describe node showing MemoryPressure False.

6765. [Kubernetes Production Troubleshooting] What is PID pressure?
Answer: PID pressure is a Kubernetes NodeCondition set when the node’s available PID count falls below the kubelet’s eviction threshold (i.e., the node is running out of process slots). The kubelet exposes this as Condition Type=PIDPressure and it is driven by the eviction signal pid.available (configured via kubelet config evictionHard). Verify with: kubectl describe node <node> (look for PIDPressure True) and inspect the kubelet config (e.g., /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml) for evictionHard: {"pid.available":"<threshold>"}. Operational checks: count PIDs (ps -e | wc -l) and check /proc/sys/kernel/pid_max. Remediate by killing runaway processes, raising kernel.pid_max, or tuning eviction pid.available and using per-pod PID limits.

6766. [Kubernetes Production Troubleshooting] What is pod eviction?
Answer: Pod eviction is the API-driven removal of a Pod from a node because the cluster (kubelet or control plane) determines it must be terminated — commonly due to node pressure (memory, disk, PID), OOM, or administrative drain. Eviction is performed via the pods eviction subresource (policy/v1 Eviction) — POST to /api/v1/namespaces/{ns}/pods/{name}/eviction — and is processed as a graceful deletion (respecting PodDisruptionBudgets when applicable). You can verify an eviction by kubectl describe pod <pod> (events show "Evicted"), kubectl get pod <pod> -o jsonpath='{.status.reason}' (returns "Evicted"), and kubectl describe node <node> for pressure conditions.

6767. [Kubernetes Production Troubleshooting] Why are pods being OOMKilled?
Answer: Pods are OOMKilled because a container exceeded its cgroup memory limit or the node ran out of memory and the kernel OOM killer terminated a process. Verify with: kubectl describe pod <pod> (look for "Reason: OOMKilled"), kubectl logs --previous <pod> for container OOM stack traces, kubectl top pod/node to compare usage vs limits, and dmesg | grep -i oom or journalctl -u kubelet for kernel/kubelet messages. Check kubelet eviction settings (kubelet --eviction-hard like memory.available) and pod spec memory.requests/limits. Remediate by increasing limits or node capacity, reducing container memory use (tune JVM/Xmx), or adjusting requests/limits so the scheduler places pods on nodes with enough memory.

6768. [Kubernetes Production Troubleshooting] How do you identify the correct memory limit?
Answer: Inspect real usage and failures, then set the limit just above observed peaks plus headroom. Check for OOMs and evictions: kubectl describe pod <pod> -n <ns> and kubectl get pod -o jsonpath='{.status.containerStatuses[*].lastState}' to see OOMKilled. Measure live and historical memory: kubectl top pod <pod> -n <ns> and inside the container kubectl exec -c <c> <pod> -- ps aux --sort=-rss | head and cat /sys/fs/cgroup/memory/memory. Use Prometheus for stable baselines: max_over_time(container_memory_working_set_bytes{pod=~"mypod.*"}[1h]) or 95th percentile over 24h (histogram_quantile or quantile_over_time). Set limit = observed_peak * (1.2–1.5) depending on workload burstiness and re-verify with metrics and absence of OOMs.

6769. [Kubernetes Production Troubleshooting] How do you detect CPU throttling?
Answer: Check usage vs limits, then inspect cgroup and metric indicators. Run kubectl top pod -n NAMESPACE to see CPU usage approaching limits and kubectl describe pod to confirm cpu requests/limits. Query kubelet summary: curl --unix-socket /var/run/kubelet/kubelet.sock http://localhost/stats/summary | jq '.pods[]|select(.podRef.name=="POD") .containers[] | {name: .name, usage: .usage.cpu}'. Inspect cgroup files on the node for the container’s cgroup: cat /sys/fs/cgroup/<cpu-cgroup-path>/cpu.stat and look for nr_throttled > 0 and throttled_time increasing. In Prometheus, check rate(container_cpu_cfs_throttled_seconds_total[5m]) > 0 or increasing. These concrete signals confirm CPU CFS throttling.

6770. [Kubernetes Production Troubleshooting] Why might HPA not scale?
Answer: Common causes: no metrics available (metrics-server missing/misconfigured or custom-metrics adapter absent), missing/incorrect resource requests (HPA CPU/Memory targets use requests), minReplicas==maxReplicas or desiredReplicas capped by maxReplicas, wrong HPA API/version or unsupported metric type, controller can’t read metrics due to RBAC or APIService errors, or scaling suppressed by stabilization windows. Verify with kubectl describe hpa <name> and kubectl get hpa -o yaml to see status.currentReplicas, status.desiredReplicas, and conditions; confirm metrics with kubectl top pods and kubectl get --raw "/apis/metrics.k8s.io/v1beta1/namespaces/<ns>/pods"; check metrics-server logs (kubectl logs -n kube-system deployment/metrics-server) and Deployment pod resource requests (kubectl get deploy <name> -o yaml).

6771. [Kubernetes Production Troubleshooting] Why might metrics-server not return data?
Answer: Common causes: metrics-server not running or crash (check kubectl get deploy -n kube-system metrics-server and kubectl logs), missing/incorrect RBAC or ClusterRoleBinding, the Aggregator API not available or apiservice v1beta1.metrics.k8s.io failing (kubectl get apiservice v1beta1.metrics.k8s.io -o yaml), kubelet TLS/auth issues or certificate trust failures (metrics-server connects to kubelets on 10250; using --kubelet-insecure-tls or proper kubelet serving certs may be required), wrong node address selection (use --kubelet-preferred-address-types), or network/firewall blocking port 10250. Verify with kubectl top nodes and pod logs; describe apiservice and kubelet logs to confirm authentication/connection errors.

6772. [Kubernetes Production Troubleshooting] Why might Cluster Autoscaler not add a node?
Answer: Cluster Autoscaler may not add a node for several documented reasons: the node group is at its max size (cloud provider/ASG/GCP instance group), pending Pods are unschedulable due to nodeSelector/affinity/taints or resource requests exceeding any node type, PodDisruptionBudgets/priority preventing eviction, or CA sees no scale-up candidates. Verify with logs and events: kubectl -n kube-system logs deployment/cluster-autoscaler --tail=200, kubectl get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp, kubectl describe pod <pending-pod> and kubectl get nodes. Inspect cloud provider limits and ASG/IG settings (e.g., aws autoscaling describe-auto-scaling-groups) and CA messages like “max size reached”, “no unassigned pods fit”, or API errors indicating denied scaling.

6773. [Kubernetes Production Troubleshooting] What happens if pod requests are not defined?
Answer: If a Pod has no resource requests set, the scheduler treats the requested CPU/memory as zero and may pack more Pods onto a node (leading to CPU/memory overcommit). QoS class becomes BestEffort only if neither requests nor limits are set; if limits are set but requests are omitted the Pod is Burstable (request defaults to 0). Eviction and OOM behavior: low-QoS Pods are preferred for eviction under node pressure and can be OOM-killed when usage exceeds node allocatable. LimitRange admission can inject default requests in a namespace (kubectl get limitrange -n <ns>). Verify with kubectl describe pod <pod> and kubectl get pod <pod> -o yaml to see requests/limits and QoS.

6774. [Kubernetes Production Troubleshooting] How do you troubleshoot a failed rollout?
Answer: Check rollout state: kubectl rollout status deployment/<name> --watch and kubectl rollout history deployment/<name>. Inspect ReplicaSets and pods: kubectl get rs,pods -l app=<label> -o wide; kubectl describe rs/<rs-name> and kubectl describe pod/<pod> to read events (imagePullBackOff, CrashLoopBackOff, probe failures). Capture logs: kubectl logs pod/<pod> [-c <container>] and kubectl logs -p for previous instance. Validate probes and resource limits in deployment YAML: kubectl get deploy <name> -o yaml. If bug is config or image, patch or set image and apply: kubectl set image deployment/<name> <c>=<image>:tag && kubectl rollout status. To revert: kubectl rollout undo deployment/<name> --to-revision=<n>; verify with rollout status and pod Ready counts.

6775. [Kubernetes Production Troubleshooting] How do you pause a rollout?
Answer: kubectl provides a built-in pause/resume for rollouts. Example: kubectl rollout pause deployment/my-deploy (you can target deployment|daemonset|statefulset and add -n NAMESPACE). Verify the object is paused: kubectl get deployment my-deploy -o jsonpath='{.spec.paused}' which will return "true", or inspect the YAML: kubectl get deployment my-deploy -o yaml | grep "paused:". Resume with kubectl rollout resume deployment/my-deploy and confirm spec.paused is false; use kubectl rollout status deployment/my-deploy to watch completion.

6776. [Kubernetes Production Troubleshooting] How do you undo a deployment?
Answer: Use kubectl rollout undo on the Deployment. To see available revisions: kubectl rollout history deployment/<name>. To rollback to the previous revision: kubectl rollout undo deployment/<name>. To rollback to a specific revision: kubectl rollout undo deployment/<name> --to-revision=<N>. Verify the rollback finishes with kubectl rollout status deployment/<name> and confirm the new ReplicaSet/Pods reflect the desired template via kubectl get rs -l app=<label> and kubectl describe rs/<replica-set-name> or kubectl get pods -l app=<label> -o wide. Note that rollback recreates a ReplicaSet from the selected revision stored in the Deployment’s revision history annotations.

6777. [Kubernetes Production Troubleshooting] How do you determine whether a new release caused the incident?
Answer: Check rollout and revision first: kubectl rollout status deployment/myapp; kubectl rollout history deployment/myapp --revision=N to list changes and rollout annotations. Correlate the deployment’s pod template (kubectl get deploy myapp -o yaml) and ReplicaSet events (kubectl describe rs -l app=myapp) with pod start timestamps (kubectl get pods -l app=myapp -o wide --sort-by=.metadata.creationTimestamp). Correlate those timestamps with CI/CD pipeline/job logs and the Git commit SHA in the image tag (git log -1 --pretty=%H or image digest). Verify runtime impact with logs and metrics: kubectl logs -l app=myapp --since=1h and Prometheus queries (e.g., rate(http_requests_total{job="myapp",status=~"5.."}[5m])) to see if errors spike at rollout time.


GCP Production Troubleshooting
------------------------------
6778. [GCP Production Troubleshooting] A Compute Engine VM is unreachable. What do you check?
Answer: Check VM status and zone: gcloud compute instances describe INSTANCE --zone ZONE --format="json" for status, scheduling, networkInterfaces and metadata. Confirm external/internal IPs and reserved addresses and Cloud NAT: gcloud compute addresses list and gcloud compute routers nats describe NAME --router=ROUTER. Verify firewall and routes allow desired protocol/ICMP: gcloud compute firewall-rules list --filter="network:NETWORK" and gcloud compute routes list --filter="network:NETWORK". Inspect serial console and boot logs: gcloud compute instances get-serial-port-output INSTANCE --zone ZONE --port 1 and Cloud Logging for kernel/agent errors. Test connectivity from same VPC: gcloud compute ssh OTHER_INSTANCE --internal-ip and run nc/ss/tcpdump. Check SSH metadata, OS Login, and delete/renew SSH keys if needed.

6779. [GCP Production Troubleshooting] How do you distinguish a firewall issue from an OS issue?
Answer: First reproduce the failure from both client and the VM: curl/telnet/nc -vz host port and traceroute/tcpdump -i any 'port X' on the VM. If tcpdump shows packets arriving but the connection is refused or not accepted, check the VM OS: sudo ss -tnlp (or netstat -tulpn), sudo iptables -L -n, sudo nft list ruleset, sudo ufw status, and systemctl status firewalld. If tcpdump shows no packets arriving, check GCP network firewall and routing: gcloud compute firewall-rules list --filter="network:NETWORK" and gcloud compute firewall-rules describe NAME to confirm allow/deny, targetTags/serviceAccount, and priority. Also inspect VPC Flow Logs in Cloud Logging to verify packet drops at the network layer. These steps separate OS-level vs GCP firewall causes.

6780. [GCP Production Troubleshooting] How do you connect to a VM if SSH is unavailable?
Answer: If SSH is unavailable, use these GCP methods: 1) IAP tunneling: gcloud compute ssh INSTANCE --zone ZONE --tunnel-through-iap to bypass network firewall rules. 2) Serial console: enable serial port metadata then connect: gcloud compute instances add-metadata INSTANCE --zone ZONE --metadata serial-port-enable=1; gcloud compute connect-to-serial-port INSTANCE --zone ZONE to access the guest and troubleshoot sshd or network. 3) Inject keys or recovery scripts via instance metadata (startup-script or ssh-keys): gcloud compute instances add-metadata INSTANCE --zone ZONE --metadata startup-script='echo "ssh-rsa AAA... user" >> /home/USER/.ssh/authorized_keys' then reboot. Verify by checking serial console logs (sudo journalctl -u sshd or /var/log/auth.log) or successful gcloud compute ssh connection.

6781. [GCP Production Troubleshooting] What is the serial console?
Answer: The serial console is an interactive serial-port endpoint exposed by Compute Engine that provides low-level access to a VM’s boot and OS console for troubleshooting boot, kernel, init, driver, disk, and network problems. You can fetch console logs non‑interactively with gcloud compute instances get-serial-port-output INSTANCE --port=1, or open an interactive session with gcloud compute connect-to-serial-port INSTANCE --port=1 (or via the VM “Connect to serial console” button in the Cloud Console). Use the Instances.getSerialPortOutput API for programmatic retrieval. Note that project/instance settings must allow serial access and firewall/OS credentials may be required to interact with the guest.

6782. [GCP Production Troubleshooting] How do you troubleshoot a full boot disk?
Answer: SSH to the VM (gcloud compute ssh INSTANCE) or use the serial console if SSH fails. Inspect usage: sudo df -h, sudo lsblk, sudo du -sh /* 2>/dev/null and sudo find / -xdev -type f -printf '%s %p\n' | sort -rn | head -20 to find big files. Clean safely: sudo apt-get clean, sudo journalctl --vacuum-size=100M, docker system prune -af, truncate or rotate huge logs (sudo truncate -s 0 /var/log/large.log). If disk needs growth, snapshot then gcloud compute disks resize DISK --size=NEW_SIZE, then on the instance run sudo growpart /dev/sdX 1 and resize2fs /dev/sdX1 (ext4) or sudo xfs_growfs /mountpoint (XFS). Verify with df -h and Monitoring metric agent.googleapis.com/disk/used_bytes.

6783. [GCP Production Troubleshooting] A GKE cluster has IP exhaustion. What symptoms appear?
Answer: You’ll see Pod creations stuck Pending and new Pods repeatedly failing to get network configuration. kubectl get pods -A -o wide shows many Pending; kubectl describe pod <pod> shows events such as CNI allocation failures (e.g., “failed to allocate IP from range” or “no available IP addresses”), or kubelet logs with “unable to allocate an IP for pod”. Node-level CNI daemonset logs (kubectl -n kube-system logs ds/<cni-daemon>) report exhausted secondary/alias IPs. On GCP, gcloud compute networks subnets describe <SUBNET> --region <REGION> will show depleted secondary IP ranges; Stackdriver/Cloud Logging contains CNI or GKE control plane errors about IP allocation failures. These indicators confirm IP exhaustion.

6784. [GCP Production Troubleshooting] How do you confirm pod-IP exhaustion?
Answer: Check Kubernetes and VPC alias IP capacity: run `kubectl get pods --all-namespaces -o wide` to see pods without IPs and `kubectl describe pod <failing-pod>` for events like “failed to assign an IP”. Inspect node allocatable pod count: `kubectl get nodes -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.name}{" allocatablePods="}{.status.allocatable.pods}{"\n"}{end}'`. For GKE VPC‑native, inspect secondary ranges: `gcloud compute networks subnets describe SUBNET --region REGION --format="json"` and check `secondaryIpRanges[].ipCidrRange` and usage. Also search controller/CRI errors and events: `kubectl get events --all-namespaces | grep -i ip` or review GKE VPC-Native agent logs in Cloud Logging for IP allocation failures. These confirm pod‑IP exhaustion.

6785. [GCP Production Troubleshooting] How did you resolve subnet exhaustion in GKE?
Answer: [CONTEXT] Pod IPs were exhausting the VPC subnet secondary ranges used by an IP‑alias GKE cluster. [ACTION] I added larger secondary ranges to the subnet (gcloud compute networks subnets update SUBNET --region=REGION --add-secondary-ranges=pods-range=10.4.0.0/14,services-range=10.8.0.0/20), verified ranges (gcloud compute networks subnets describe SUBNET --region=REGION), created a new node pool / replacement cluster configured to use the new secondary ranges (gcloud container clusters create CLUSTER --enable-ip-alias --cluster-secondary-range-name=pods-range --services-secondary-range-name=services-range ... or create node-pool and migrate), cordoned/drained nodes (kubectl cordon/ drain) and migrated workloads, then deleted old capacity. [RESULT] Verified resolution by confirming free addresses and pod scheduling (kubectl get pods -o wide) and observing no Pod IP allocation failures in GKE control plane logs.

6786. [GCP Production Troubleshooting] Can a GKE cluster be moved to another subnet?
Answer: No — you cannot “move” an existing GKE cluster to a different VPC subnet. The cluster’s networkConfig (including subnetwork and pod/service CIDR allocations for VPC‑native clusters) is immutable after creation. To change subnet you must create a new cluster in the target subnet (gcloud container clusters create CLUSTER --subnetwork=SUBNET --enable-ip-alias ...) and migrate workloads (kubectl drain/cordon old nodes, reapply manifests or use Velero/etcd snapshots). Verify networking with gcloud container clusters describe CLUSTER --zone ZONE and confirm node VM interfaces with gcloud compute instances describe NODE --zone ZONE to see the subnetwork assigned.

6787. [GCP Production Troubleshooting] When is cluster recreation required?
Answer: Cluster recreation is required when you must change immutable cluster properties: VPC-native/IP alias mode and network/subnetwork, cluster or services Pod CIDR ranges (clusterIpv4Cidr/servicesIpv4Cidr), or convert a zonal cluster to regional (or vice‑versa). These fields cannot be altered after creation; other settings can often be updated. Verify immutables with:
gcloud container clusters describe CLUSTER --zone ZONE
and check ipAllocationPolicy, network/subnetwork, clusterIpv4Cidr, servicesIpv4Cidr, and locations. To apply required changes you must create a new cluster (gcloud container clusters create ...) and migrate workloads (kubectl drain/cordon, kubectl apply, or a rolling migration), then delete the old cluster.

6788. [GCP Production Troubleshooting] A Cloud Run service has high latency. What would you inspect?
Answer: Inspect Cloud Run revision and instance configuration: gcloud run services describe SERVICE --platform managed --region REGION --format yaml and gcloud run revisions list --service SERVICE to check concurrency, CPU/memory, and max-instances settings (adjust with gcloud run services update --concurrency=N --cpu=... --memory=...). Review logs and cold-starts: gcloud logging read 'resource.type="cloud_run_revision" AND resource.labels.service_name="SERVICE"' --limit 100 and look for "Starting new instance" and long startup durations. Query latency metrics in Cloud Monitoring (run.googleapis.com/request_latencies) and use Cloud Trace to breakdown request/remote-call latency. If using Serverless VPC Access, describe connector capacity: gcloud compute networks vpc-access connectors describe NAME --region REGION. Also verify outbound DNS, backend service latency, and health checks.

6789. [GCP Production Troubleshooting] How do cold starts affect Cloud Run?
Answer: Cold starts in Cloud Run occur when a revision needs to start a new container instance (for example after scaling to zero), causing added latency for that initial request while the image is pulled and the runtime and app initialize. You can mitigate them by setting a nonzero minimum instance count (gcloud run services update SERVICE --min-instances=1) and increasing container concurrency (gcloud run services update SERVICE --concurrency=N) so fewer cold starts occur. Cold-start duration depends on image size, startup code, and VPC Connector use. Verify impact with Cloud Monitoring charts (run.googleapis.com/container/instance_count and run.googleapis.com/request_latencies) and Cloud Trace/Logs to see per-request startup latency and instance lifecycle events.

6790. [GCP Production Troubleshooting] How do minimum instances reduce cold starts?
Answer: Setting a non‑zero minimum instances value (Cloud Run: --min-instances) keeps a specified number of container instances instantiated and ready to serve, preventing instance creation, image pull, and app initialization at request time. This avoids the startup latency known as a cold start; incoming requests are routed immediately to warm instances (subject to concurrency per instance). Example: gcloud run services update SERVICE --min-instances 2 --region REGION --platform managed. Verify the config with gcloud run services describe SERVICE and validate reduced cold‑start spikes by comparing request latency percentiles (p95/p99) in Cloud Monitoring before and after the change. Note the cost tradeoff of always‑running instances.

6791. [GCP Production Troubleshooting] How do CPU allocation and concurrency affect Cloud Run?
Answer: Cloud Run assigns vCPU to a revision per instance (set with gcloud run deploy --cpu=1|2) and handles request concurrency per instance (gcloud run deploy --concurrency=N). Concurrency controls how many simultaneous requests one container serves: higher concurrency increases utilization and reduces scaling/cold starts but requires thread-safe code and enough CPU/memory. By default Cloud Run only schedules CPU time while a request is active, so background threads won’t run between requests unless you enable “CPU always allocated” for the revision in the console or API. Verify behavior with Cloud Monitoring metrics (Request count, container CPU usage, and instance count) and by testing with load (e.g., hey, k6) while observing gcloud run services describe.

6792. [GCP Production Troubleshooting] A serverless VPC connector has scaled out. Will it scale down automatically?
Answer: Yes — a Serverless VPC Access connector scales down automatically to its configured minimum number of instances. By default minInstances is 0, so idle capacity will be removed; if you set minInstances > 0 (via the connector resource) it will not scale below that. Verify with:
gcloud compute networks vpc-access connectors describe CONNECTOR --region REGION
and inspect the minInstances/maxInstances fields and current state. You can also observe connector instance count and traffic in Cloud Monitoring dashboards (the connector resource in Monitoring) to confirm scale-down behavior. The connector will not scale below the configured minInstances.

6793. [GCP Production Troubleshooting] Why can connector capacity remain high after traffic decreases?
Answer: Connector capacity can remain high after traffic falls because of warm instances and connection pooling, autoscaler cool-down/stabilization settings, long TCP TIME_WAIT and idle connection retention, session affinity or sticky load‑balancer sessions, and stateful workloads preventing node/pod eviction. In GKE/HPA this is due to scale-down stabilization; check with kubectl describe hpa <name> and kubectl top pods. For node autoscaling, Cluster Autoscaler has a 10‑minute unneeded time; inspect with kubectl get nodes and gcloud container clusters describe <cluster>. For Cloud Run, min-instances prevents scale-to-zero; verify with gcloud run services describe <service>. Also confirm open connections with ss or netstat on affected hosts.

6794. [GCP Production Troubleshooting] How do you troubleshoot serverless VPC connector exhaustion?
Answer: Check connector health and config: gcloud compute networks vpc-access connectors describe CONNECTOR --region=REGION and list connectors with gcloud compute networks vpc-access connectors list --region=REGION to confirm state and configured IP range (--range). Inspect connector logs in Cloud Logging (filter for resource "Serverless VPC Access Connector") for errors such as IP allocation failures. If IP range is exhausted, create a connector with a larger CIDR or additional connectors: gcloud compute networks vpc-access connectors create NEW --region=REGION --network=NETWORK --range=10.8.0.0/28. Repoint services to a different connector (e.g. gcloud run services update SERVICE --vpc-connector=NEW --region=REGION). Verify by sending traffic and observing connector state and logs.

6795. [GCP Production Troubleshooting] A load balancer reports unhealthy backends. What do you check?
Answer: Check the LB health-check configuration first: gcloud compute health-checks describe <NAME> (or gcloud compute https-health-checks/ssl-health-checks for legacy) and verify protocol, port, request path and timeout/interval/healthy thresholds. Run gcloud compute backend-services get-health <BACKEND_SERVICE> --global (or --region) and gcloud compute instance-groups get-health <IG> to see per-instance status. Verify VMs are RUNNING, the app is listening on the health port (ssh and run sudo ss -ltnp or curl http://<VM_IP>:<PORT><PATH>), and firewall allows health-check source ranges (check gcloud compute firewall-rules list --filter="name:*"). Inspect Cloud Logging for load balancer and instance logs (gcloud logging read), and use tcpdump on a VM to confirm probes reach it.

6796. [GCP Production Troubleshooting] A Cloud Armor policy suddenly blocks legitimate users. What do you do?
Answer: Identify the offending rule via Cloud Logging (Logs Explorer) filtering Cloud Armor match logs, then inspect the policy and rules:
gcloud compute security-policies describe POLICY --global
gcloud compute security-policies rules list --security-policy=POLICY --global
For immediate mitigation either detach the policy from the backend service:
gcloud compute backend-services update BACKEND --security-policy "" --global
or change the rule action/priority to allow or remove the rule:
gcloud compute security-policies rules update PRIORITY --security-policy=POLICY --action=allow --global
or
gcloud compute security-policies rules delete PRIORITY --security-policy=POLICY --global
Verify recovery by checking load-balancer request metrics and backend health:
gcloud compute backend-services get-health BACKEND --global.

6797. [GCP Production Troubleshooting] A service account receives permission denied. How do you investigate?
Answer: Check the service account identity, bindings, and context: list project IAM bindings and filter for the account with gcloud projects get-iam-policy PROJECT_ID --flatten="bindings[]" --format="table(bindings.role,bindings.members)" --filter="bindings.members:serviceAccount:SERVICE_ACCOUNT_EMAIL". Inspect the service account’s own IAM policy: gcloud iam service-accounts get-iam-policy SERVICE_ACCOUNT_EMAIL. Review Audit Logs for denied RPCs: gcloud logging read 'protoPayload.authenticationInfo.principalEmail="SERVICE_ACCOUNT_EMAIL" AND severity=ERROR' --limit=50. Verify role definitions include needed permissions with gcloud iam roles describe ROLE_ID. For GCE/Cloud Run check metadata/token scopes and Workload Identity bindings (kubectl get sa annotations and gcloud iam service-accounts add-iam-policy-binding shows binding patterns). Check VPC Service Controls perimeters and Organization Policies for blocks. Finally reproduce the error with an access token and the failing API to confirm root cause.

6798. [GCP Production Troubleshooting] A Cloud Storage upload fails intermittently. What would you inspect?
Answer: Check client-side errors and reproducibility first: reproduce the failure with gsutil -D cp file gs://BUCKET to capture HTTP response codes and stack traces. Inspect Cloud Audit Logs for storage.objects.insert via gcloud logging read 'resource.type="gcs_bucket" AND protoPayload.methodName="storage.objects.insert"' --limit 50 --format json to see error codes and caller identity. Verify Cloud Monitoring metrics storage.googleapis.com/request_count and storage.googleapis.com/error_count for spikes. If using CMEK, confirm KMS key IAM with gcloud kms keys get-iam-policy KEY --location LOCATION --keyring RING. Check VPC Service Controls perimeters (gcloud access-context-manager perimeters list), IAM permissions, transient 5xx/429 responses, and client retry/resumable upload behavior.

6799. [GCP Production Troubleshooting] A Cloud SQL application reports too many connections. What do you do?
Answer: Check current load: view Cloud Monitoring metric cloudsql.googleapis.com/database/active_connections and inspect instance with gcloud sql instances describe INSTANCE. Identify sessions in the database (Postgres: SELECT pid, usename, state, client_addr FROM pg_stat_activity; MySQL: SHOW PROCESSLIST;) and terminate runaway sessions (Postgres: SELECT pg_terminate_backend(pid); MySQL: KILL <id>). If short-term relief needed, increase limits via gcloud sql instances patch INSTANCE --database-flags max_connections=200 (or appropriate value) and verify the metric falls. For a durable fix, add connection pooling (PgBouncer on GKE/Cloud Run or use Cloud SQL Auth Proxy) and fix client leak/idle-timeouts. Re-verify with cloudsql.googleapis.com/database/active_connections and application logs to confirm resolution.

6800. [GCP Production Troubleshooting] A Pub/Sub subscriber has an increasing backlog. How do you troubleshoot?
