Verify owning controller: kubectl get deployment,daemonset -n kube-system and kubectl rollout status. Check node health: kubectl get nodes; sudo journalctl -u kubelet on the node for kubelet errors. For EKS-managed add-ons, also run aws eks describe-addon --cluster-name <name> --addon-name <addon> to check addon status.


EKS Security and Networking
---------------------------
7686. [EKS Security and Networking] How do you secure workloads on EKS?
Answer: Use defense-in-depth: IRSA (associate OIDC provider and create IAM role for service account) with eksctl utils associate-iam-oidc-provider --cluster CLUSTER --approve and eksctl create iamserviceaccount --cluster CLUSTER --name SA --namespace NS --attach-policy-arn arn:aws:iam::...; verify with kubectl describe sa NS/SA and running aws sts get-caller-identity inside the pod. Enforce network segmentation with Kubernetes NetworkPolicy (or Calico) and Security Groups for Pods via the AWS VPC CNI; verify with kubectl get networkpolicy and in-pod connectivity tests (curl). Use Pod Security Admission (label namespaces pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted), image scanning in ECR (aws ecr start-image-scan / aws ecr describe-image-scan-findings), and encrypt Secrets with AWS KMS; monitor with Amazon GuardDuty, KINDS, and regular kube-bench scans.

7687. [EKS Security and Networking] What is IAM Roles for Service Accounts?
Answer: IAM Roles for Service Accounts (IRSA) lets pods assume AWS IAM roles by associating an IAM role to a Kubernetes ServiceAccount via an OIDC identity provider. You enable the cluster OIDC provider (eksctl utils associate-iam-oidc-provider or aws iam create-open-id-connect-provider), create an IAM role whose trust policy uses sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity with the OIDC provider and subject "system:serviceaccount:<namespace>:<name>", then annotate the ServiceAccount (eks.amazonaws.com/role-arn: arn:aws:iam::<acct>:role/<role>). The kubelet issues bound service account tokens (TokenRequest API), the AWS SDK calls STS AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity using that token, and you can verify by running aws sts get-caller-identity from inside the pod.

7688. [EKS Security and Networking] How does IRSA work?
Answer: IRSA maps a Kubernetes service account to an AWS IAM role via the cluster OIDC provider. You register the cluster’s OIDC issuer in IAM, create an IAM role whose trust policy allows the OIDC federated principal and constrains the "sub" (e.g., "system:serviceaccount:ns:sa") and "aud" = "sts.amazonaws.com", then annotate the Kubernetes ServiceAccount with eks.amazonaws.com/role-arn. Kubelet uses the TokenRequest API to mint a projected service-account JWT into the pod; AWS SDKs call STS AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity with that JWT. STS validates the JWT against the OIDC provider and the role trust policy, returning temporary credentials. Verify by execing into the pod and running "aws sts get-caller-identity" to confirm the assumed role.

7689. [EKS Security and Networking] What is the relationship between OIDC and IRSA?
Answer: IRSA (IAM Roles for Service Accounts) uses the cluster’s OIDC provider to let pods assume IAM roles without node credentials. You must register the EKS OIDC provider (arn:aws:iam::<acct>:oidc-provider/<issuer>) in IAM, create an IAM role whose trust policy allows sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity with that federated principal and a condition matching the Kubernetes service account (sub or StringEquals on oidc:sub). Annotate the ServiceAccount with eks.amazonaws.com/role-arn=<role-arn>. Kubernetes projects a TokenRequest-based OIDC token into the pod; AWS validates it and issues temporary credentials. Verify by kubectl describe sa -n <ns> <sa> (shows annotation) and kubectl exec -it <pod> -- aws sts get-caller-identity to confirm the assumed role.

7690. [EKS Security and Networking] How do you create an IAM role for a Kubernetes service account?
Answer: Enable the cluster OIDC provider, create an IAM role with a web identity trust policy that permits sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity for the cluster OIDC provider and the specific service account subject, attach policies, and annotate the K8s ServiceAccount with the role ARN. Example sequence:

1. eksctl utils associate-iam-oidc-provider --cluster my-cluster --approve
2. aws iam create-role --role-name eks-sa-role --assume-role-policy-document file://trust.json
   (trust.json uses "Effect":"Allow","Principal":{"Federated":"arn:aws:iam::123456789012:oidc-provider/oidc.eks.region.amazonaws.com/id/<id>"} and Condition StringEquals "<issuer>:sub":"system:serviceaccount:namespace:name" and "<issuer>:aud":"sts.amazonaws.com")
3. aws iam attach-role-policy --role-name eks-sa-role --policy-arn arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/ReadOnlyAccess
4. kubectl annotate serviceaccount -n namespace name eks.amazonaws.com/role-arn=arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/eks-sa-role

Verify with kubectl get sa -n namespace -o yaml and run a pod using that SA and inside run aws sts get-caller-identity to confirm the assumed role.

7691. [EKS Security and Networking] What problems does IRSA solve?
Answer: IRSA (IAM Roles for Service Accounts) solves pod-level least-privilege, credential sprawl, and long-lived node IAM credential problems by binding an IAM role to a Kubernetes ServiceAccount via the cluster OIDC provider. Operators run eksctl utils associate-iam-oidc-provider --cluster <name> --approve, create an IAM role whose trust policy permits sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity for the OIDC issuer with condition StringEquals: oidc.eks.<region>.amazonaws.com/id/<id>:sub = system:serviceaccount:<ns>:<sa>, and annotate the SA: kubectl annotate sa <sa> -n <ns> eks.amazonaws.com/role-arn=arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/RoleName. Pods receive short-lived STS credentials via the projected token (/var/run/secrets/eks.amazonaws.com/serviceaccount/token) and you can verify with aws sts get-caller-identity inside the pod.

7692. [EKS Security and Networking] How is EKS Pod Identity different from IRSA?
Answer: IRSA (IAM Roles for Service Accounts) is the AWS-native mechanism that uses the cluster's OIDC provider and projected ServiceAccount tokens plus STS AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity to give a pod an IAM role without node IAM credentials. Older "pod identity" patterns (kube2iam/kiam or node-agent based solutions often called pod-identity) inject credentials via a node-side daemon, iptables or metadata proxy and require node IAM permissions. Verify IRSA by checking a pod's projected token at /var/run/secrets/eks.amazonaws.com/serviceaccount/token and running aws sts get-caller-identity inside the pod to see the assumed role ARN; with node-agent solutions the EC2 instance role appears as the identity. IRSA eliminates extra daemons and host-level interception.

7693. [EKS Security and Networking] How do network policies work in EKS?
Answer: Kubernetes NetworkPolicy is an API object that expresses ingress/egress allow rules for pods; EKS enforces them only if the installed CNI implements NetworkPolicy (AWS VPC CNI does not; use Calico, Cilium, Kube‑router, etc.). Policies use podSelector and optional namespaceSelector/ipBlock to match endpoints and declare ingress/egress rules (ports, protocols, from/to). If no NetworkPolicy selects a pod, traffic is allowed; once any policy selects a pod, only allowed flows in policies are permitted. Apply with kubectl apply -f policy.yaml and list with kubectl get networkpolicy -n <ns>. Verify enforcement by kubectl exec into test pods and curl/tcping target pods, or inspect CNI-managed iptables/ipsets or eBPF maps on the node.

7694. [EKS Security and Networking] Does the default VPC CNI enforce network policies?
Answer: No. The Amazon VPC CNI (amazon-vpc-cni-k8s, the default on EKS) does not implement Kubernetes NetworkPolicy semantics, so applying NetworkPolicy objects alone will not block pod traffic. To enforce NetworkPolicy you must install a network-plugin that implements them (for example Calico or Cilium). Verify by creating two pods, applying a deny-all NetworkPolicy (kubectl apply -f deny-all.yaml) and testing connectivity (kubectl exec pod-a -- curl -sS http://pod-b:80); with the default VPC CNI the curl still succeeds, demonstrating the policy is not enforced.

7695. [EKS Security and Networking] Which tools can enforce network policies in EKS?
Answer: Common EKS-compatible network-policy enforcement options are Project Calico, Cilium, Antrea, Weave Net, kube-router, and AWS VPC CNI’s Security Groups for Pods feature. Each enforcer implements Kubernetes NetworkPolicy (Calico/Cilium/Antrea add richer CRDs: GlobalNetworkPolicy, CiliumNetworkPolicy, AntreaNetworkPolicy). Verify enforcement concretely: Calico — calicoctl get networkpolicy or kubectl get globalnetworkpolicy; Cilium — cilium status and kubectl get ciliumnetworkpolicies; Antrea — kubectl get antreanetworkpolicies; Weave/kube-router — kubectl get networkpolicies plus checking pod-to-pod connectivity (curl, netcat) for blocked flows. For Security Groups for Pods, confirm pod SG attachments via aws ec2 describe-network-interfaces and inspect pod annotations/ENI associations.

7696. [EKS Security and Networking] What are security groups for pods?
Answer: Security groups for pods is an AWS EKS capability (provided by the AWS VPC CNI and VPC Resource Controller) that lets you associate one or more EC2 security groups with individual Kubernetes pods so AWS network rules are enforced at the pod’s IP/ENI level instead of only at the node. This enables fine‑grained ingress/egress controls, isolation, and use of security group policies per workload. To verify, inspect the pod’s ENI and attached security groups in the EC2 console or via AWS CLI (aws ec2 describe-network-interfaces) and confirm traffic is allowed/denied per the security group rules while using kubectl describe pod to map pod IP to the ENI.

7697. [EKS Security and Networking] When should security groups for pods be used?
Answer: Use Security Groups for Pods when you need AWS-native, per-pod network isolation or least‑privilege access that node-level security groups and Kubernetes NetworkPolicies cannot express — for example multi-tenant workloads, database frontends, strict egress controls, or when a pod must present a specific SG to access AWS resources. This is provided by the amazon-vpc-cni-k8s plugin (ENI trunking / pod ENI modes) and requires the CNI and IAM permissions (EC2 Create/Attach/Describe/DeleteNetworkInterface, etc.). Verify operation by assigning the pod SG via the CNI workflow and then checking pod IP/ENI mapping with kubectl get pods -o wide and aws ec2 describe-network-interfaces --filters Name=attachment.instance-owner-id,Values=amazon-eks-node to confirm the SG is attached.

7698. [EKS Security and Networking] How do you encrypt Kubernetes secrets in EKS?
Answer: Create a symmetric AWS KMS Customer Master Key (CMK) and grant EKS control plane decrypt/encrypt permissions, then enable envelope encryption for Kubernetes secrets in the control plane. Example: create enc.json:
{"resources":["secrets"],"provider":{"keyArn":"arn:aws:kms:us-west-2:123456789012:key/abcd-1234","providerName":"aws:kms"}}
Then run:
aws eks update-cluster-config --name my-cluster --encryption-config file://enc.json
Verify with:
aws eks describe-cluster --name my-cluster --query "cluster.encryptionConfig"
and confirm secrets still mount via kubectl get secret <name> -o yaml; EKS will encrypt data at rest in etcd using KMS envelope encryption.

7699. [EKS Security and Networking] How do you integrate EKS with AWS KMS?
Answer: Create or choose a KMS CMK and add a key policy allowing the EKS control plane (Service principal eks.amazonaws.com) and your account IAM to use kms:Encrypt,Decrypt,GenerateDataKey*. Provide an encryption config JSON (example below) and pass it to the EKS CreateCluster API or eksctl at cluster creation:

enc.json
{"resources":["secrets"],"provider":{"keyArn":"arn:aws:kms:region:acct-id:key/<key-id>"}}

Example:
eksctl create cluster --name my-cluster --region us-west-2 --version 1.26 --encryption-config file://enc.json

You cannot enable control-plane envelope encryption for existing clusters via the console; it must be set at creation. Verify by creating a Kubernetes Secret (kubectl create secret generic s --from-literal=x=1) and confirming KMS Encrypt/Decrypt events in CloudTrail for the CMK.

7700. [EKS Security and Networking] How do you integrate Secrets Manager with EKS?
Answer: Use IRSA for pod-level AWS permissions and one of two common patterns:

1) CSI driver: install Secrets Store CSI Driver and AWS provider (Secrets Store CSI Driver Provider for AWS). Create a SecretProviderClass referencing the Secrets Manager ARN and mount it; verify with kubectl describe pod and check files under the mount path (e.g., /mnt/secrets-store). Ensure the pod’s serviceAccount has iam.amazonaws.com/role annotation and the IAM role grants secretsmanager:GetSecretValue.

2) Kubernetes external secrets: deploy External Secrets Operator (external-secrets.io) configured for AWS and create an ExternalSecret that syncs a Secrets Manager secret into a Kubernetes Secret; verify with kubectl get secret. Validate IRSA via aws sts get-caller-identity from the pod.

7701. [EKS Security and Networking] What is the Secrets Store CSI driver?
Answer: The Secrets Store CSI Driver is a Kubernetes Container Storage Interface (CSI) driver that mounts secrets, keys, and certificates from external secret stores (for example Azure Key Vault, AWS Secrets Manager/Parameter Store, HashiCorp Vault) into pods as files. You declare a SecretProviderClass CRD which references the provider and which objects to fetch; mount it as a CSI volume using driver name secrets-store.csi.k8s.io in your Pod spec. It can optionally create Kubernetes Secrets via the secretObjects field. Installable via Helm or manifests; verify with kubectl get secretproviderclass, kubectl describe pod to see the CSI volume, and kubectl get secret to confirm secret sync.

7702. [EKS Security and Networking] How do you scan EKS images?
Answer: Use image-scanning at registry and CI time plus periodic cluster checks. For ECR-native scans: enable ECR image scanning (ECR uses Amazon Inspector), then trigger and view findings with real AWS CLI commands, e.g.
aws ecr start-image-scan --repository-name my-repo --image-id imageTag=latest
aws ecr describe-image-scan-findings --repository-name my-repo --image-id imageTag=latest --query 'imageScanFindings.findings'
For pipeline or local checks use open-source scanners (example commands):
trivy image --severity HIGH,CRITICAL myrepo/myimage:tag
anchore-cli image add myrepo/myimage:tag && anchore-cli image vuln myrepo/myimage:tag all
Also periodically pull cluster images and scan nodes (kubectl get pods -o jsonpath='{..image}' | xargs -n1 trivy image) to verify deployed images.

7703. [EKS Security and Networking] How do you restrict privileged containers?
Answer: Enforce admission controls and pod security settings: set the Pod Security Admission policy to "restricted" for a namespace (kubectl label namespace default pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted --overwrite) and require non-privileged pods by using securityContext in pod specs (securityContext.privileged: false is only valid for containers under the (containers[].securityContext.privileged) field in CRI runtimes; prefer omitting true). Drop capabilities (securityContext.capabilities.drop: ["ALL"]), set runAsNonRoot/runAsUser, seccompProfile.type: RuntimeDefault and AppArmor profile. For clusters without PSA, deploy an OPA Gatekeeper constraint to forbid privileged: true. Verify rejection by creating a privileged pod and observing kubectl apply failure or Audit/AdmissionReview logs returning a denied response.

7704. [EKS Security and Networking] How do you implement Pod Security Standards?
Answer: Enable and configure the built-in PodSecurity admission and apply namespace labels to enforce levels. For control-plane-managed clusters, ensure the PodSecurity admission plugin is enabled (kube-apiserver --enable-admission-plugins=PodSecurity if required). Label namespaces to set enforcement, audit, and warn levels, e.g.:

kubectl label ns my-namespace pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/audit=baseline \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn=baseline --overwrite

Verify labels with kubectl get ns my-namespace -L pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce,pod-security.kubernetes.io/audit,pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn and attempt kubectl apply -f pod.yaml; non-compliant pods will be rejected with a Forbidden admission error. You can tune per-namespace or cluster-wide policies this way.

7705. [EKS Security and Networking] How do you audit EKS API activity?
Answer: Enable and collect both AWS control-plane audit logs and CloudTrail. For EKS control-plane audit logging run:
aws eks update-cluster-config --name my-cluster --logging '{"clusterLogging":[{"types":["audit"],"enabled":true}]}' --region us-west-2
which streams JSON audit records to CloudWatch Logs (or S3 if configured in the console). Verify by querying CloudWatch:
aws logs filter-log-events --log-group-name "/aws/eks/my-cluster/audit" --limit 5
Also ensure CloudTrail is enabled for AWS API activity (creates, IAM changes). Query CloudTrail for EKS API calls:
aws cloudtrail lookup-events --lookup-attributes AttributeKey=EventSource,AttributeValue=eks.amazonaws.com --max-results 10
Correlate timestamps and requestIDs between CloudTrail and audit logs for full forensic context.

7706. [EKS Security and Networking] What is CloudTrail?
Answer: AWS CloudTrail is a regional and multi‑region AWS service that records account API activity (management events), resource data events (S3, Lambda), and optional Insights events as JSON audit records. You create a trail (aws cloudtrail create-trail --name NAME --s3-bucket-name BUCKET), enable logging (aws cloudtrail start-logging --name NAME), and optionally forward logs to CloudWatch Logs or SNS. Validate delivery with aws cloudtrail get-trail-status --name NAME and by listing S3 objects (aws s3 ls s3://BUCKET/AWSLogs/ACCOUNTID/CloudTrail/), or query recent activity with aws cloudtrail lookup-events --lookup-attributes AttributeKey=Username,AttributeValue=alice. Trail records include eventTime, eventSource, eventName, and userIdentity for forensic and compliance use.

7707. [EKS Security and Networking] What is the EKS control-plane logging feature?
Answer: EKS control-plane logging is a managed option that streams logs from the Amazon EKS managed control plane components (api, audit, authenticator, controllerManager, scheduler) to Amazon CloudWatch Logs. You enable/disable specific types via the EKS API (UpdateClusterConfig logging field), the AWS Console, or eksctl (eksctl utils update-cluster-logging --enable-types=<api,audit,...>). Logs are retained and viewed in CloudWatch log groups named /aws/eks/<cluster-name>/<component>. Verify with aws eks describe-cluster --name <cluster> --query 'cluster.logging.clusterLogging' to see enabled types and confirm delivery by checking CloudWatch Logs for the corresponding log group and streams.

7708. [EKS Security and Networking] Which EKS control-plane logs can be enabled?
Answer: EKS supports enabling five control-plane log types: api, audit, authenticator, controllerManager, and scheduler. You can enable them via the API/CLI (aws eks update-cluster-config --name <cluster> --logging '{"clusterLogging":[{"types":["api","audit","authenticator","controllerManager","scheduler"],"enabled":true}]}' ), via eksctl (cluster.logging.clusterLogging in the cluster config), or in the AWS console. Verify with aws eks describe-cluster --name <cluster> --query "cluster.logging.clusterLogging" and by viewing the resulting CloudWatch Logs streams for the cluster. These logs are emitted by the managed control plane and billed as CloudWatch Logs usage.

7709. [EKS Security and Networking] How do you monitor EKS using CloudWatch?
Answer: Deploy CloudWatch Container Insights and log forwarding using the official DaemonSets and IRSA. Enable OIDC for the cluster, create an IAM service account, then install agents:

1) eksctl OIDC and service account:
   eksctl utils associate-iam-oidc-provider --cluster CLUSTER --approve
   eksctl create iamserviceaccount --cluster CLUSTER --namespace amazon-cloudwatch --name cwagent-sa --attach-policy-arn arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/CloudWatchAgentServerPolicy --approve

2) Install agents:
   kubectl apply -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/aws/amazon-cloudwatch-agent/master/kubernetes/amazon-cloudwatch-agent.yaml
   kubectl apply -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/aws/aws-for-fluent-bit/mainline/deployment/aws-for-fluent-bit.yaml

Verify pods: kubectl get pods -n amazon-cloudwatch; verify metrics in CloudWatch under Namespace "ContainerInsights" (aws cloudwatch list-metrics --namespace "ContainerInsights") and logs with aws logs describe-log-groups.

7710. [EKS Security and Networking] How do you collect application logs from EKS?
Answer: Run a log collector as a DaemonSet (Fluent Bit/Fluentd) to tail /var/log/containers and forward to your sink, or use FireLens for Fargate/ECS tasks. Common pattern: deploy aws-for-fluent-bit as a DaemonSet with a ConfigMap defining input (tail on /var/log/containers), parsers, and output (CloudWatch Logs, Kinesis, S3, OpenSearch). Use IRSA for permissions (eksctl create iamserviceaccount or aws iam OIDC + eksctl). Example images: amazon/aws-for-fluent-bit:latest. Verify: kubectl get ds -n kube-system fluent-bit and kubectl logs -n kube-system <fluent-bit-pod> -c fluent-bit; confirm log groups in CloudWatch Logs console (e.g., /aws/containerinsights/<cluster>/application) or documents in OpenSearch. You can also use kubectl logs <pod> for ad-hoc retrieval.

7711. [EKS Security and Networking] How do you troubleshoot pod-IP exhaustion?
Answer: Check whether cluster- or cloud-level IP pools are exhausted: kubectl get nodes -o jsonpath='{.items[*].spec.podCIDR}' and kubectl get pods --all-namespaces -o wide to see unassigned IPs. Inspect CNI/agent logs (e.g. kubectl logs -n kube-system ds/aws-node for AWS VPC CNI; kubectl logs -n kube-system ds/calico-node or calicoctl ipam show --ipv4 for Calico). On cloud providers, verify ENI/secondary-IP and subnet capacity (aws ec2 describe-subnets and describe-instances to view ENIs/secondary IPs and AWS account quotas). Check kube-controller-manager and kubelet events (kubectl get events --all-namespaces | grep -i ip) and node ip addr (ssh node && ip addr) to confirm allocation failures, then expand pod CIDR, subnets, or CNI IP pools accordingly.

7712. [EKS Security and Networking] What is VPC CNI prefix delegation?
Answer: VPC CNI prefix delegation is a mode of the amazon-vpc-cni-k8s plugin where the CNI requests IPv4 CIDR prefixes from EC2 for an ENI (using the EC2 APIs AssignIpv4Prefixes/UnassignIpv4Prefixes) and then assigns pod IPs from those delegated prefixes as secondary addresses. This lets a single ENI host many more pod IPs (reducing ENI churn and increasing pods/node) because the CNI no longer needs one-to-one ENI provisioning per small IP allotment. Verify by checking aws-node logs, kubectl get pods -o wide for pod IPs in the subnet range, ip -4 addr show dev <device> on the node, and aws ec2 describe-network-interfaces --network-interface-ids <eni-id> to see Ipv4Prefixes.

7713. [EKS Security and Networking] How does prefix delegation increase pod density?
Answer: Prefix delegation lets the cloud CNI delegate an IPv4/IPv6 CIDR prefix to a node’s ENI instead of only assigning individual IPs, so a single ENI can host many more pod IPs. The CNI (for example AWS VPC CNI with prefix-delegation) allocates a /28, /26, etc., to the node and the node’s IPAM hands out addresses from that prefix to pods, bypassing strict ENI-count limits and increasing pods-per-node by the prefix-size (e.g., a /28 yields ~16 addresses). Verify by inspecting aws-node/ipamd logs (kubectl logs -n kube-system daemonset/aws-node) and by calling AWS APIs: aws ec2 describe-network-interfaces --network-interface-ids <eni-id> shows Ipv4Prefixes/SecondaryPrivateIpAddresses, and kubectl describe node shows podCIDR assignments.

7714. [EKS Security and Networking] What is custom networking in the VPC CNI?
Answer: Custom networking in the Amazon VPC CNI (amazon-vpc-cni-k8s) lets pods receive IPs from customer-managed subnets rather than the node’s primary subnet by associating per-node ENIConfig CRs that specify subnet IDs and security groups. You create an ENIConfig YAML, apply it (kubectl apply -f), then annotate a node with k8s.amazonaws.com/eniConfig=<ENIConfigName>. The CNI then attaches ENIs from the configured subnets to that node and assigns pod IPs from those subnets. Verify with kubectl get eniconfig -n kube-system; kubectl describe eniconfig <name>; kubectl describe node <node> to see the annotation; kubectl get pods -o wide to confirm pod IPs belong to the expected subnet, and check aws-node logs for ENI allocation details.

7715. [EKS Security and Networking] How do you upgrade EKS securely?
Answer: Review EKS/Kubernetes release notes and test in a staging cluster. Upgrade the control plane via AWS CLI or eksctl: aws eks update-cluster-version --name my-cluster --kubernetes-version 1.26; or eksctl upgrade cluster --name my-cluster --version 1.26. Upgrade add-ons and CNI (aws-node) before nodes: aws eks update-addon --cluster-name my-cluster --addon-name vpc-cni --resolve-conflicts OVERWRITE. Upgrade node groups (managed): aws eks update-nodegroup-version --cluster-name my-cluster --nodegroup-name ng-1 --kubernetes-version 1.26, or recreate/self-managed nodes with a new launch template and cordon/drain (kubectl cordon/ drain). Verify with kubectl get nodes -o wide, kubectl get pods --all-namespaces, aws eks describe-cluster, and check daemonset rollout status (kubectl rollout status ds/aws-node -n kube-system). Monitor logs and rollback if issues occur.


Git Fundamentals
----------------
7716. [Git Fundamentals] What is Git?
Answer: Git is a distributed version control system that tracks project history as snapshots of the working tree stored as objects (commits, trees, blobs) identified by SHA-1 hashes (with optional SHA-256 support). Users create repositories with git init or clone remote repos with git clone; changes are staged with git add and recorded with git commit. Branches are lightweight pointers (git branch, git checkout, git switch) and can be combined with git merge or git rebase. Remote synchronization uses git push and git pull (or fetch + merge). Inspect history and verify state with git log --oneline, git status, git diff, and by examining the .git directory for refs and object storage. Git supports hooks, config, and signed commits.

7717. [Git Fundamentals] What is distributed version control?
Answer: Distributed version control stores the full project history on every developer’s machine instead of relying on a single central server. Examples: Git and Mercurial. Typical local operations—git commit, git branch, git merge, git rebase—run without network access; synchronization happens with git push and git pull (or git fetch + git merge/rebase) to a remote. Cloning (git clone) creates a complete .git database; git log shows the local history and git fsck can verify object integrity. This model improves offline work, branching/merging speed, and resiliency (a lost server can be rebuilt from any clone), while conflicts are resolved during pull or merge operations.

7718. [Git Fundamentals] What is a Git repository?
Answer: A Git repository is a data store that tracks a project’s history as a directed acyclic graph of commits plus the working tree and the staging area (index). Locally it is represented by a .git directory containing objects (blobs, trees, commits), refs (branches, tags), and configuration. Typical operations include creating one with git init or copying with git clone, staging changes with git add, committing with git commit, and inspecting history with git log or git show <commit>. Verify a repo by listing .git (ls -a .git or git rev-parse --git-dir) and checking working-state with git status; view objects with git cat-file -p <sha1> or git ls-files.

7719. [Git Fundamentals] What is a working tree?
Answer: The working tree (working directory) is the checked‑out copy of repository files on disk that you can edit — the contents Git compares against the index (staging area) and the HEAD commit. The .git directory holds repository metadata; the working tree is everything outside it. Use git rev-parse --show-toplevel to locate the working tree root, git status to see modified/untracked files, git diff to view unstaged changes, git diff --staged to view staged changes, and git ls-files --others --exclude-standard to list untracked files. Operations like checkout, merge, and reset update the working tree; commands like git add and git rm move changes between the working tree and the index.

7720. [Git Fundamentals] What is the staging area?
Answer: The staging area (the index) is Git’s intermediate snapshot that records what will go into the next commit. You populate it with git add (including git add -p for hunks or git add --intent-to-add for marking new files). git commit takes the index and writes a tree/commit into .git; git commit -a skips staging for tracked files by auto-adding modifications. Inspect it with git status (shows “Changes to be committed”), git diff --staged (or --cached) to view staged vs HEAD, and git ls-files -s or by examining .git/index. Use git reset <file> to unstage without changing the working tree.

7721. [Git Fundamentals] What is a commit?
Answer: A commit in Git is an immutable object that records a snapshot of the repository: it points to a tree object (the state of tracked files), references zero or more parent commit(s) (one for normal commits, two+ for merges), and stores metadata (author, committer, timestamps) plus the commit message. Commits are identified by a cryptographic object ID (SHA-1 historically). You create one with git add ...; git commit -m "msg". Verify contents with git show <commit> or git cat-file -p <commit> to inspect tree, parent(s), author, committer, and message. Branches and tags are simply refs that name specific commit IDs, and history is built by chaining commits.

7722. [Git Fundamentals] What is a branch?
Answer: A branch in Git is a lightweight movable pointer (a ref) stored under refs/heads/<name> that references a commit object; HEAD points to the current branch name or directly to a commit. You create branches with git branch <name> or git checkout -b <name> / git switch -c <name>, and delete with git branch -d. Branches can track remote refs under refs/remotes/<remote>/<name>. Branch operations change which commit is checked out and how new commits advance the branch pointer; merges or rebases incorporate history between branches. Verify a branch’s tip with git rev-parse <branch> or git show-ref refs/heads/<name>, and inspect history with git log --oneline --graph <branch>.

7723. [Git Fundamentals] What is the default branch?
Answer: The default branch is the repository branch that Git and hosting services use as the initial/current branch (the commit that HEAD points to) for new clones, web views, and pull-request targets. Historically named "master", modern Git and hosts often use "main"; Git 2.28+ respects git config --global init.defaultBranch for git init. After cloning, remote HEAD determines your local checked-out branch; verify with git symbolic-ref HEAD (local) or git remote show origin which reports "HEAD branch: <name>" and git ls-remote --symref origin HEAD. To change it, use git branch -m old new locally, update refs/heads on the server or the host UI, and update symbolic refs so subsequent clones use the new default branch.

7724. [Git Fundamentals] What is the difference between Git and GitHub?
Answer: Git is a distributed version control system: a local toolset (git init, git add, git commit, git branch, git merge, git rebase, git log) that tracks snapshots and history. GitHub is a cloud hosting and collaboration platform that stores Git repositories and adds HTTP/SSH remote access (clone, push, pull), a web UI, pull requests, Issues, GitHub Actions CI, webhooks, and REST/GraphQL APIs. Operationally you use git push origin main to upload commits to GitHub and git remote -v to verify the remote URL; on GitHub you can inspect commits, open a PR, or call the REST API (GET /repos/:owner/:repo) to verify repository state and permissions.

7725. [Git Fundamentals] What is the difference between GitHub, GitLab and Bitbucket?
Answer: GitHub, GitLab and Bitbucket are hosted Git platforms with overlapping goals but different emphases. GitHub focuses on social coding, GitHub Actions for CI/CD, GitHub Packages, and strong ecosystem/integration marketplace; verify by viewing Actions logs on a repo. GitLab provides an integrated DevOps platform—built-in GitLab CI/CD, Container Registry, issue boards, and self-hosted GitLab CE/EE; verify with gitlab-runner and pipeline traces. Bitbucket (Cloud and Server/Data Center) targets teams with tight Atlassian integration (Jira, Confluence) and Bitbucket Pipelines; note Bitbucket dropped Mercurial in 2020. All support PR/MR code review, granular permissions, and enterprise on-premises products (GitHub Enterprise, GitLab EE, Bitbucket Data Center).

7726. [Git Fundamentals] What does git clone do?
Answer: git clone <repository> [<dir>] initializes a new local repository, copies objects and refs from the remote, configures origin as a remote, and checks out the repository’s default branch into a working tree. Under the hood it runs an init, adds the origin remote, fetches refs/objects, and creates local branches that track remote branches (e.g., master or main). For alternatives use --bare (no working tree), --mirror (mirror all refs and remotes), or --depth N (shallow clone). Verify by inspecting .git, running git remote -v, git branch -r, and git status to confirm the checkout and tracking branch are set.

7727. [Git Fundamentals] What does git fetch do?
Answer: git fetch contacts a configured remote (e.g., git fetch origin), negotiates refs and transfers objects in packfiles, and updates remote-tracking branches (refs/remotes/<remote>/<branch>) and tags without modifying your current branch or working tree. It does not merge or rebase; to integrate changes you must run git merge, git rebase, or git pull. Useful options include --prune to remove stale remote-tracking refs, --all to fetch all remotes, and --tags to fetch tags. Verify results with git branch -r to see updated remote-tracking branches, git log HEAD..origin/main to inspect incoming commits, and git status to confirm no working-tree changes.

7728. [Git Fundamentals] What does git push do?
Answer: git push transfers commits and other refs from your local repository to a remote repository and updates the remote refs accordingly. By default (push.default=simple) git push <remote> sends the current branch to its configured upstream; you can also specify refspecs like git push origin main. Git negotiates objects, sends packfiles, and the remote updates refs only on a fast-forward; non-fast-forward updates are rejected unless you use git push --force (or update remote history via pull/rebase first). You can push all branches (git push --all) or tags (git push --tags). Verify with git remote -v, git fetch origin, git log origin/main..main, or git ls-remote origin to confirm what changed.

7729. [Git Fundamentals] What does git status show?
Answer: git status reports the working tree and index state relative to the current branch and its upstream. It shows the current branch name (or detached HEAD), upstream tracking and ahead/behind counts, staged changes ("Changes to be committed"), unstaged modifications ("Changes not staged for commit"), untracked files, and unmerged paths during conflicts or an in-progress merge/rebase. It also prints actionable hints (how to stage, discard, or continue merges/rebases). For scriptable output use git status --porcelain or git status -sb; verify staged content with git diff --staged and unstaged edits with git diff. During a rebase or merge it additionally reports the operation in progress and suggested git commands to resolve it.

7730. [Git Fundamentals] What does git log show?
Answer: git log displays the commit history reachable from the current HEAD (by default the current branch) in reverse chronological order. Each entry shows the commit object identifier (SHA-1, or SHA-256 for repos using that), author, author date, and the commit message; it also encodes parent linkage in the commit graph. You can verify content and layout with commands like git log --oneline, git log --graph --decorate --oneline, git log --stat to see changed files and insertion/deletion counts, or git log -p to show diffs. git log reflects committed history only (it does not show working-tree or index changes).

7731. [Git Fundamentals] What does git diff show?
Answer: git diff displays the textual differences (a unified diff) between two Git tree-ish objects: by default it compares the working tree against the index (unstaged changes). Common variants: git diff --staged (or --cached) shows the index versus HEAD (what will be committed); git diff HEAD shows working tree versus the last commit; git diff <commit1> <commit2> compares two commits. Output includes context lines, file headers, and +/- hunks; use git diff --stat for a file-change summary, git diff --name-only for changed filenames, or git diff --name-status for added/modified/deleted flags to verify what changed.

7732. [Git Fundamentals] What is a remote repository?
Answer: A remote repository is a Git repository hosted separately from your local clone (often on GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, or a self-hosted server) that serves as a shared canonical source of truth. Remotes are referenced by URL and short names (default "origin") and managed with commands like git remote add <name> <url>, git clone <url>, git fetch, git pull, and git push <remote> <branch>. Verify configured remotes and URLs with git remote -v, inspect remote refs with git ls-remote <url>, and view remote branches with git branch -r. Remotes enable collaboration, CI integrations, and centralized backup of commits and refs.

7733. [Git Fundamentals] What is origin?
Answer: In Git, "origin" is the conventional local name (alias) for a remote repository, typically created automatically by git clone. It lives in .git/config as remote "origin" with fetch and push URLs; you can view them with git remote -v or git config --get remote.origin.url. Commands operate against that alias (git fetch origin, git pull origin main, git push origin feature), but it is not a special server—just a pointer to a URL you can rename (git remote rename origin upstream), remove (git remote remove origin), or add (git remote add origin <url>). Use git remote show origin to inspect branches, fetch/push refs, and tracking configuration.

7734. [Git Fundamentals] What is an upstream branch?
Answer: An upstream branch is the remote branch (or local branch explicitly configured as the tracking branch) that your current branch uses as its default target for pull/push and for comparing commits. You set it with git push -u origin main or git branch --set-upstream-to=origin/main, and Git records it in config as branch.<name>.remote and branch.<name>.merge. Verify the upstream with git branch -vv, git status (shows ahead/behind), or git rev-parse --abbrev-ref --symbolic-full-name @{u} to print the upstream ref; git pull without arguments will fetch/merge from that upstream by default.

7735. [Git Fundamentals] How do you create and switch to a branch?
Answer: Create and switch to a new branch locally with either modern or traditional commands. Modern: git switch -c <branch-name> creates and checks out the branch. Traditional: git checkout -b <branch-name> does the same. To create locally and push to set upstream: git push -u origin <branch-name>. Verify you are on the branch with git branch --show-current or git status, or list branches with git branch (current branch is indicated by *). To start from a specific commit or remote branch: git switch -c <branch-name> <start-point> or git checkout -b <branch-name> origin/<remote-branch>. These commands create and switch branches and can be verified with git status.

7736. [Git Fundamentals] What is a merge?
Answer: A merge in Git integrates the changes from one commit history (usually a branch) into another by creating a new commit that records the combined state or by fast‑forwarding the target branch pointer. You invoke it with git merge <branch> from the target branch; a fast‑forward occurs if the target has no divergent commits, otherwise Git makes a merge commit. Conflicts surface when the same lines were edited; resolve them in files, then run git add <file> and git commit, or run git merge --abort to stop. Verify with git status, git log --graph --oneline, and git diff --name-only --diff-filter=U to list unresolved files.

7737. [Git Fundamentals] What is a rebase?
Answer: A rebase in Git moves a series of commits to a new base commit by replaying them onto another commit, rewriting their parent relationships and producing new commit hashes. Typical usage: git checkout feature; git rebase main (or git rebase --onto newbase oldbase feature). Interactive rebase (git rebase -i <base>) lets you reorder, squash, or edit commits. Resolve conflicts with git rebase --continue, abort with git rebase --abort, or skip with git rebase --skip. Verify results with git log --oneline --graph or git reflog and ensure working tree clean with git status; avoid rebasing commits already pushed/shared because history rewriting requires force-push (git push --force-with-lease).

7738. [Git Fundamentals] When should rebase be avoided?
Answer: Avoid rebasing any commits that have been published and may be referenced by others, because rebasing rewrites commit hashes and will require force-pushing (e.g., git push --force-with-lease) and can break collaborators’ checkouts and CI history. Also avoid rebasing when you need to preserve explicit merge commits or topology (use git merge --no-ff instead) or when commit signatures must remain verifiable—rebasing creates new commits that invalidate GPG signatures; verify with git log --show-signature. Don’t rebase commits that are tagged or referenced by external systems (build IDs, bug trackers). If you must rewrite public history, coordinate with consumers and prefer non-destructive alternatives.

7739. [Git Fundamentals] What is a merge conflict?
Answer: A merge conflict occurs when Git cannot automatically reconcile divergent changes to the same lines or file structure during a merge, rebase, or cherry-pick. Typical causes are concurrent edits to the same lines, one commit deleting a file while another modifies it, or conflicting file mode changes. Git halts the operation, marks conflicted files with conflict markers (<<<<<<<, =======, >>>>>>>) in the working tree, and reports them via git status. To resolve, edit the files to produce the desired content, then git add <file> and git commit (or git rebase --continue). You can inspect choices with git checkout --ours/--theirs or use git mergetool; after committing, git status shows no merge in progress.

7740. [Git Fundamentals] How do you resolve a merge conflict?
Answer: Run the merge, inspect conflicts with git status and git diff to see hunks. Open conflicted files, resolve markers <<<<<<</=======/>>>>>>> manually or launch git mergetool (configured tool) to pick/merge changes. If you prefer a side, you can use git checkout --ours <path> or git checkout --theirs <path> to take one side, then edit as needed. After resolving, mark resolved with git add <path> for each file; git status should show no unmerged paths. Finish with git commit (Git will create a merge commit) or git merge --continue if using sequencer. You can verify with git log --merges or git show HEAD to confirm the merge commit.

7741. [Git Fundamentals] What is a fast-forward merge?
Answer: A fast-forward merge occurs when the branch you’re merging into (e.g., main) has no commits ahead of the branch being merged (feature), so Git can simply move the target branch reference forward to the feature commit instead of creating a merge commit. Practically: git checkout main; git merge feature will perform a fast‑forward if git merge-base main feature equals main’s tip; the branch pointer is updated to feature’s commit and history stays linear. Use git merge --ff-only to refuse a non‑FF merge, or git merge --no-ff to force a merge commit even when FF is possible. Verify with git log --oneline --graph or git rev-parse main and git rev-parse feature.

7742. [Git Fundamentals] What is a three-way merge?
Answer: A three-way merge combines two tip commits (typically HEAD and a branch) using their nearest common ancestor as the base to produce a merged result. In Git this happens when you run git merge <branch>: Git computes changes from ancestor→HEAD and ancestor→branch and applies both sets. If changes do not overlap, Git creates a fast-forward or a merge commit; if they conflict, Git writes conflict markers (<<<<<<<, =======, >>>>>>>) into files and sets index stages 1/2/3. Resolve by editing files, then git add <file> and git commit (or run git mergetool). To inspect sources use git show :1:path, :2:path, :3:path; verify with git status and git log --graph --oneline --decorate.


Advanced Git
------------
7743. [Advanced Git] When would you use cherry-pick?
Answer: Use `git cherry-pick` when you need to copy one or a few specific commits from another branch without merging the entire branch. A common example is applying an urgent production hotfix from `main` to a supported release branch: `git switch release/2.x && git cherry-pick <commit-sha>`. Git creates a new commit with the same change but a different SHA. Resolve any conflicts, run tests, and push through review. Avoid cherry-picking a long sequence of related commits because it duplicates history and makes future merges harder; in that situation, merge or rebase the complete branch instead.

7744. [Advanced Git] What is git revert?
Answer: `git revert <commit-sha>` safely undoes a commit by creating a new commit containing the inverse change. It preserves the existing history, so it is the preferred way to undo a commit that has already been pushed to a shared branch. For example, `git revert a1b2c3d` opens a commit message and records the rollback; use `git revert -m 1 <merge-sha>` carefully for a merge commit. Resolve conflicts if necessary, run tests, and push the new revert commit. Unlike `git reset`, revert does not move the branch pointer or discard later commits.

7745. [Advanced Git] What is git reset?
Answer: `git reset` moves the current branch pointer to another commit and optionally changes the staging area and working tree. `git reset --soft HEAD~1` moves HEAD but keeps changes staged; the default `git reset --mixed HEAD~1` keeps changes only in the working tree; `git reset --hard HEAD~1` discards tracked changes. Reset is useful for cleaning up local, unpublished history. Avoid resetting commits already pushed to a shared branch because pushing afterward usually requires a force push and can overwrite teammates' work. Use `git revert` for shared history.

7746. [Advanced Git] What is the difference between reset and revert?
Answer: `git reset` rewrites local branch history by moving the branch pointer; depending on `--soft`, `--mixed`, or `--hard`, it also changes the index and working tree. `git revert` preserves history and creates a new commit that reverses an earlier commit. Use reset for unpublished local mistakes, such as correcting the last commit before pushing: `git reset --soft HEAD~1`. Use revert for commits already shared on `main`: `git revert <sha>`. Reset may require a dangerous force push, while revert is auditable, collaborative, and normally safe to push.

7747. [Advanced Git] What is a soft reset?
Answer: `git reset --soft <target>` moves HEAD and the current branch to the target commit but leaves both the staging area and working tree unchanged. The commits after the target disappear from the branch history, while all their changes remain staged for recommitting. For example, `git reset --soft HEAD~3` lets you combine the last three local commits into one using a new `git commit`. It is useful for reorganizing unpublished history without losing work. Do not use it casually on commits already pushed to a shared branch, because updating the remote would rewrite history.

7748. [Advanced Git] What is a mixed reset?
Answer: A mixed reset moves HEAD and the branch pointer to the target commit, resets the staging area to match that commit, but preserves the files in the working tree. It is the default mode, so `git reset HEAD~1` equals `git reset --mixed HEAD~1`. The removed commit's changes become unstaged modifications, allowing you to edit them and selectively stage files again with `git add`. Use it to undo a local commit while keeping the code. As with other history-rewriting resets, avoid using it on shared, already-pushed commits.

7749. [Advanced Git] What is a hard reset?
Answer: `git reset --hard <target>` moves HEAD and the branch pointer to the target commit, resets the staging area, and makes tracked working-tree files exactly match that commit. For example, `git reset --hard HEAD~1` removes the latest local commit and its tracked changes. Use it only when you intentionally want to discard local tracked work or restore a disposable branch. Check `git status`, save valuable work with a commit or stash, and confirm the target SHA first. Untracked files are not removed unless you separately run a command such as `git clean`.

7750. [Advanced Git] Why is hard reset dangerous?
Answer: A hard reset is dangerous because it immediately discards tracked changes in both the staging area and working tree while moving the branch pointer. Unsaved edits can become difficult or impossible to recover, and resetting shared commits followed by `git push --force` can erase teammates' history. Before running it, inspect `git status` and `git log --oneline`, create a safety branch such as `git branch backup-before-reset`, or stash changes. If a local commit was removed, `git reflog` may help recover its SHA; uncommitted overwritten content may not be recoverable.

7751. [Advanced Git] How do you apply a stash?
Answer: Use `git stash apply` to reapply the latest stash while keeping the stash entry, or `git stash apply stash@{n}` for a specific one. First run `git stash list`, confirm the target, then apply it from a clean working tree if possible. Resolve conflicts like a normal merge, run tests, and use `git status` to verify the result. Use `git stash pop` only when you want Git to remove the stash after a successful apply.

7752. [Advanced Git] What is git reflog?
Answer: `git reflog` shows where HEAD and branch references have pointed recently, including commits that are no longer visible in normal branch history. It is local to your clone and is useful after mistakes like reset, rebase, checkout, or deleted branch recovery. Example: run `git reflog`, find the lost SHA, then recover with `git branch recovery <sha>` or `git reset --hard <sha>` if you are sure. Reflog is not a backup system forever; entries expire based on Git garbage-collection settings.

7753. [Advanced Git] How can reflog recover a lost commit?
Answer: Run `git reflog` to find the SHA where your branch or HEAD pointed before the mistake, then create a safety branch from it: `git branch recovered-work <sha>`. After that, inspect with `git log recovered-work --oneline` and either merge, cherry-pick, or reset depending on the situation. For example, after an accidental `git reset --hard HEAD~1`, reflog normally still contains the removed commit. The safe pattern is branch first, inspect second, then change the main branch only after confirming the commit is correct.

7754. [Advanced Git] What is an annotated tag?
Answer: An annotated tag is a full Git object that stores the tag name, target commit, tagger, date, message, and optionally a GPG signature. It is preferred for releases because it is auditable and can carry release notes. Create one with `git tag -a v1.2.0 -m "Release v1.2.0"` and push it using `git push origin v1.2.0`. In production workflows, annotated and signed tags help prove which commit was released. Avoid moving release tags after publishing unless your team has an explicit incident process.

7755. [Advanced Git] What is a lightweight tag?
Answer: A lightweight tag is just a named pointer to a commit, similar to a branch that does not move. It has no tag message, tagger metadata, or signature. Create one with `git tag v1.2.0 <sha>`. It is fine for temporary local bookmarks, but I would avoid it for production releases because it carries less audit information. For release management, annotated tags are safer because they include metadata and can be signed. Verify tags with `git show v1.2.0` or `git rev-parse v1.2.0`.

7756. [Advanced Git] How do you create a release tag?
Answer: First ensure the release commit is tested and merged, then create an annotated tag: `git switch main`, `git pull`, `git tag -a v1.2.0 -m "Release v1.2.0"`, and `git push origin v1.2.0`. Many pipelines trigger deployment from pushed tags, so tag only immutable release commits. If signing is required, use `git tag -s v1.2.0`. Validate with `git show v1.2.0` and confirm the CI/CD release job picked the same SHA. Avoid retagging published versions; create a patch version instead.

7757. [Advanced Git] What is a detached HEAD state?
Answer: Detached HEAD means Git has checked out a commit directly instead of a branch, so new commits are not attached to a named branch. It often happens with `git checkout <sha>` or checking out a tag. It is safe for inspection or testing, but if you commit in this state, the work can become hard to find once you switch away. To keep it, create a branch: `git switch -c experiment-from-detached`. Use `git status` to confirm whether you are detached before making changes.

7758. [Advanced Git] How do you recover from detached HEAD?
Answer: If you made commits in detached HEAD and want to keep them, create a branch before leaving: `git switch -c recovered-work`. If you already switched away, use `git reflog` to find the detached commit SHA and then run `git branch recovered-work <sha>`. After that, merge or cherry-pick the work into the correct branch. Do not panic and run random resets; first preserve the commit with a branch, then inspect it with `git log --oneline --decorate` and run tests.

7759. [Advanced Git] What is squashing?
Answer: Squashing combines multiple commits into one commit, usually to make a feature branch easier to review and keep main history clean. A common command is `git rebase -i origin/main`, then mark follow-up commits as `squash` or `fixup`. Squashing is best for local or feature-branch cleanup before merge, not for rewriting shared main history. After squashing, run tests because conflict resolution or commit ordering can introduce mistakes. The trade-off is cleaner history versus losing some granular commit-by-commit debugging context.

7760. [Advanced Git] Why should commits be squashed?
Answer: Squashing is useful when a branch has many noisy commits like `fix typo`, `try again`, or `address review`, and the final logical change is easier to understand as one commit. It improves review, release notes, revertability, and `git bisect` quality. For example, squash five work-in-progress commits into one clear commit before merging a small feature. Do not squash unrelated changes together, because rollback becomes harder. Also avoid rewriting a shared branch unless everyone agrees and force-push rules are understood.

7761. [Advanced Git] What is interactive rebase?
Answer: Interactive rebase lets you edit a sequence of commits before they are shared or merged. Run `git rebase -i HEAD~5` to reorder, squash, fixup, edit messages, or drop commits. It is useful for cleaning feature-branch history before opening or merging a pull request. Because it rewrites commit SHAs, avoid using it on public/shared branches unless your team explicitly coordinates it. After resolving conflicts, continue with `git rebase --continue`, verify with `git log --oneline`, run tests, and push with `--force-with-lease` if needed.

7762. [Advanced Git] How do you edit commit history?
Answer: For unpublished local history, use interactive rebase: `git rebase -i HEAD~n`. You can reword commit messages, squash commits, reorder them, edit a commit, or drop one. For the latest commit only, use `git commit --amend`. Because these operations rewrite SHAs, never casually rewrite shared history; use `git revert` for already-pushed commits on main. Before editing, check `git status`, create a backup branch, and after the rebase run tests and inspect `git log --oneline --graph`.

7763. [Advanced Git] What is .gitignore?
Answer: `.gitignore` tells Git which untracked files or patterns should not be added to the repository. Typical entries include build output, logs, local environment files, dependency folders, and editor metadata, for example `node_modules/`, `.env`, `*.log`, or `dist/`. It does not remove files already tracked; for those, use `git rm --cached <file>` and commit the change. In production projects, `.gitignore` helps prevent secrets, generated artifacts, and machine-specific files from polluting the repository.

7764. [Advanced Git] What should never be committed to Git?
Answer: Never commit secrets, private keys, cloud credentials, production `.env` files, tokens, certificates, customer data, large generated binaries, dependency directories, or machine-specific files. Examples include `service-account.json`, `.npmrc` with tokens, SSH keys, kubeconfigs, Terraform state files, and database dumps. Use secret managers, CI/CD credentials, `.gitignore`, pre-commit secret scanning, and protected branch checks. If a secret is committed, rotate it immediately; deleting the file in a later commit does not remove it from Git history.

7765. [Advanced Git] What is Git LFS?
Answer: Git LFS stores large files outside normal Git object storage and keeps lightweight pointer files in the repository. It is useful for binaries such as datasets, models, videos, design assets, or archives that would make clone and fetch operations slow. Configure it with `git lfs install`, then track patterns like `git lfs track "*.psd"` or `git lfs track "*.bin"`. Commit the `.gitattributes` file so everyone uses the same rules. The trade-off is simpler large-file handling but dependence on LFS storage quotas and availability.

7766. [Advanced Git] When is Git LFS required?
Answer: Use Git LFS when files are too large or change too often for normal Git history, such as ML model artifacts, datasets, media files, or packaged binaries. Normal Git stores every version forever, so large binary churn makes clones slow and repositories expensive. LFS keeps the repository lightweight by replacing content with pointer files and downloading real content on demand. Before adopting it, check platform quotas, CI support, backup policy, and whether an artifact registry, object storage bucket, or model registry is a better fit.

7767. [Advanced Git] What are Git hooks?
Answer: Git hooks are scripts that run at specific Git lifecycle events such as before commit, before push, after merge, or on the server before accepting a push. Client hooks live under `.git/hooks`, while teams usually share managed hooks through tools like pre-commit because `.git/hooks` itself is not versioned. Common uses include formatting, linting, unit tests, commit-message checks, and secret scanning. Hooks improve feedback speed, but server-side CI and branch protection should still enforce critical controls because local hooks can be bypassed.

7768. [Advanced Git] What is a pre-commit hook?
Answer: A pre-commit hook runs before Git creates a commit. It can block the commit if formatting, linting, tests, or secret scans fail. For example, using the `pre-commit` framework, teams define hooks in `.pre-commit-config.yaml` and developers run `pre-commit install`. This catches issues before code reaches CI. Keep hooks fast and deterministic; long integration tests belong in CI. Also remember pre-commit hooks are local controls, so important security and quality gates should be repeated in protected pipelines.

7769. [Advanced Git] How can hooks enforce code quality?
Answer: Hooks enforce code quality by running automated checks at commit or push time, such as formatters, linters, type checks, unit tests, dependency checks, and secret scanning. A practical setup uses a versioned `.pre-commit-config.yaml`, installs hooks with `pre-commit install`, and mirrors the same checks in CI so bypassed local hooks are caught. Keep the local hook fast enough that developers do not disable it. For production teams, hooks are a first feedback layer; branch protection and CI remain the final enforcement layer.

7770. [Advanced Git] How do you remove an accidentally committed secret?
Answer: First rotate or revoke the secret immediately; assume it is compromised. Then remove it from the current code and history using a tool like `git filter-repo` or BFG, coordinate with the team, force-push the cleaned history, and ask everyone to reclone or carefully clean local copies. Also purge CI caches, artifacts, container images, and package registries that may contain the secret. Add prevention afterward: `.gitignore`, secret scanning, pre-commit hooks, protected CI checks, and moving credentials to a secret manager.


Git Branching Strategies
------------------------
7771. [Git Branching Strategies] What is GitFlow?
Answer: GitFlow is a branching model that uses long-lived main and develop branches plus feature, release, and hotfix branches. It works for controlled release cycles but can become heavy for fast-moving CI/CD teams.

Detailed interview explanation:
Gitflow belongs to the software delivery lifecycle. In interviews, explain how it helps teams move from source code to production safely. The key themes are automation, repeatability, traceability, testing, security validation, deployment control, and rollback.

Production example:
A production pipeline may start when a pull request is opened. CI runs unit tests, integration tests, static analysis, dependency scanning, and image scanning. After approval, the pipeline builds an immutable artifact, pushes it to an artifact registry, and deploys it using Kubernetes, Helm, Argo CD, Flux, or another deployment system. For production releases, teams add approval gates, canary or blue-green rollout, SLO checks, and rollback automation.

Best practices to mention:
- Keep pipeline definitions in Git and review them like application code.
- Promote the same immutable artifact across environments.
- Use secret managers and short-lived credentials instead of hardcoded secrets.
- Add automated checks for tests, security, policy, and deployment health.
- Measure delivery using DORA metrics: deployment frequency, lead time, change failure rate, and MTTR.

Common interview follow-ups:
You may be asked how to handle flaky tests, slow pipelines, failed deployments, manual approvals, artifact promotion, branch strategy, GitOps drift, or rollback. A strong answer connects the concept to faster feedback, safer releases, and better auditability.

7772. [Git Branching Strategies] What branches are used in GitFlow?
Answer: GitFlow uses two long-lived branches: master (production-ready) and develop (integration branch). Supporting branches are: feature/* (branch off develop; e.g., git checkout -b feature/foo develop; merged back into develop with git merge --no-ff feature/foo), release/* (branch off develop; e.g., git checkout -b release/1.2 develop; finish by merging into master and develop, tagging with git tag -a v1.2), and hotfix/* (branch off master; e.g., git checkout -b hotfix/1.2.1 master; finish by merging into master and develop and tagging). Optionally a support/* branch exists for long-term maintenance. Verify topology with git log --decorate --graph --oneline and git branch -a or git tag -l.

7773. [Git Branching Strategies] What is trunk-based development?
Answer: Trunk-based development is a branching model where all developers integrate small, frequent changes directly into a single shared branch (commonly named main or trunk), keeping it always releasable. Teams create very short-lived feature branches (hours to a few days) or work on feature flags, then merge via fast, frequent merges or pull requests. Operationally you enforce it with CI: require green builds and passing tests before git merge or git push origin main; use git pull --ff-only to avoid accidental history divergence; delete short-lived branches (git branch -d feature). Verify health via CI status, git log and git bisect for regressions, and by ensuring deploys from main succeed.

7774. [Git Branching Strategies] How is trunk-based development different from GitFlow?
Answer: Trunk-based development centers work on a single main branch (trunk/main) with short-lived feature branches (typically hours–days) or feature flags; changes are continuously integrated, CI/CD gates commits, and releases are made by tagging main (git tag -a v1.2.3) after a green pipeline. GitFlow uses long-lived develop and master branches plus explicit feature, release, and hotfix branches; features merge into develop, releases branch from develop and get merged to master and develop (common commands: git checkout -b feature/x; git merge --no-ff release/1.2.0; git tag -a 1.2.0), and hotfixes branch from master. You can verify patterns via git branch, git log --graph, and CI history showing frequent trunk merges versus staged release merges.

7775. [Git Branching Strategies] What is a feature branch?
Answer: A feature branch is a short-lived Git branch created off a stable integration branch (e.g., main or master) to implement a single feature or story without affecting others. Typical workflow: git checkout -b feature/NAME from main, commit locally, then git push -u origin feature/NAME. Verify with git branch --all and git log --oneline origin/feature/NAME. Keep it current by git fetch origin and git rebase origin/main (or merge origin/main) to resolve conflicts before review. Open a pull request to merge into main; projects often require CI passing and code review. Merge strategies include git merge --no-ff, fast-forward, or squash merging via the hosting UI.

7776. [Git Branching Strategies] What is a release branch?
Answer: A release branch is a short-lived branch created from the main integration line to stabilize, test, and prepare a specific software release without blocking ongoing feature work. Typical workflow: create it (git checkout -b release/1.2.0), apply bugfix commits and CI/regression validation, then finalize by merging into main (git checkout main; git merge --no-ff release/1.2.0) and back into develop if used (git checkout develop; git merge --no-ff release/1.2.0). Tag the release (git tag -a v1.2.0 -m "Release 1.2.0"; git push origin main release/1.2.0 --tags). Verify with git branch --list, git log --oneline main, and git show v1.2.0 to confirm contents and metadata.

7777. [Git Branching Strategies] What is a hotfix branch?
Answer: A hotfix branch is a short-lived branch created from the release/production branch (often main) to implement an urgent bug fix that must be released immediately without waiting for ongoing feature work. Typical workflow: git checkout -b hotfix/issue-123 main, apply the fix, git add/commit, git push origin hotfix/issue-123, open a PR against main with CI and smoke tests passing. After merging to main create a release tag (git tag -a v1.2.3 -m "hotfix" && git push origin --tags) and then merge the fix back into develop (git checkout develop && git merge --no-ff main) to avoid regressions. Verify by CI, automated tests, and a production smoke check.

7778. [Git Branching Strategies] What is a pull request?
Answer: A pull request is a repository-hosted proposal to merge changes from one branch into another (commonly feature -> main) that bundles commits, discussion, automated checks, and review approvals. You create one after pushing a branch (git push origin feature-branch) via the hosting UI or API (GitHub: POST /repos/{owner}/{repo}/pulls with title, head, base). Reviewers comment, CI status checks run, and maintainers merge using strategies like "merge commit", "squash and merge", or "rebase and merge". To inspect a GitHub PR locally: git fetch origin pull/123/head:pr-123 && git checkout pr-123. Merge is finalized when the host completes the targeted branch update.

7779. [Git Branching Strategies] What is a merge request?
Answer: A merge request (MR) is a repository-hosted review-and-merge workflow (GitLab terminology; GitHub calls it a pull request) that proposes merging a source branch into a target branch, shows the diff and commits, and drives code review, CI/CD pipelines, discussions, and approvals. Operations: create an MR from a feature branch to target, run CI, address comments, then merge via the UI or API (e.g., POST /projects/:id/merge_requests/:iid/merge in GitLab) using merge-commit, fast-forward, or rebase-and-merge semantics configured by the project. Verify locally by git fetch origin; git checkout target; git merge --no-ff origin/source or inspect the MR via GET /projects/:id/merge_requests/:iid in the API to confirm pipeline and approval state.

7780. [Git Branching Strategies] What checks should run on a pull request?
Answer: Mandatory automated checks: CI build (e.g., ./ci/build, exit code 0), unit tests (pytest -q or go test ./... --race), integration/e2e tests in an isolated environment, and lint/format checks (eslint --ext .js,.ts src --max-warnings 0, prettier --check ., or gofmt -l). Enforce static analysis and security scans (mypy . --ignore-missing-imports, CodeQL or sonarqube scan, Trivy/Snyk or npm audit) and dependency/license checks. Verify DB migration compatibility and contract tests where applicable. Operationally require branch protection to block merges until all status checks pass and code-owner approvals are present; confirm artifacts exist (CI artifact list or docker image tag) and final mergeability via git merge-base --is-ancestor origin/main HEAD returning 0.

7781. [Git Branching Strategies] What is branch protection?
Answer: Branch protection is a repository-level policy that prevents direct or unsafe changes to specified branches by enforcing rules such as required pull request review(s), required status checks (CI), required approving reviews from CODEOWNERS, restricting who can push or merge, requiring signed commits, enforcing linear history (no merge commits), and optionally locking a branch. It blocks git pushes or merges that don’t satisfy those rules; a push will be rejected by the remote. You can verify settings via provider APIs, e.g. GitHub: curl -H "Authorization: token $GITHUB_TOKEN" https://api.github.com/repos/owner/repo/branches/main/protection, or GitLab: GET /projects/:id/protected_branches, and confirm enforcement by attempting a disallowed git push.

7782. [Git Branching Strategies] How do you enforce mandatory reviews?
Answer: Use repository branch-protection and merge-request/approval features in your Git hosting product and verify via its API. On GitHub, enable branch protection (Settings → Branches) with "Require pull request reviews before merging" and optionally "Require review from Code Owners" and "Require status checks to pass". You can set/verify via the REST API: PUT /repos/{owner}/{repo}/branches/{branch}/protection with JSON including required_pull_request_reviews (required_approving_review_count, require_code_owner_reviews) and enforce_admins; verify with GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/branches/{branch}/protection. On GitLab, use Protected Branches plus Project → Settings → Merge request approvals or the API (POST /projects/:id/approvals, /protected_branches). Confirm by attempting a direct push (should be denied) or inspecting API protection fields.

7783. [Git Branching Strategies] How do you prevent direct pushes to production branches?
Answer: Enable server-side controls and refuse pushes. On a bare server set git config receive.denyNonFastforwards true and install a pre-receive hook that exits non-zero for refs/heads/production or main, for example:

#!/bin/sh
while read old new ref; do
  case "$ref" in
    refs/heads/production|refs/heads/main) echo "Direct pushes forbidden"; exit 1;;
  esac
done
exit 0

In hosted services use branch protection: GitHub via PATCH /repos/:owner/:repo/branches/:branch/protection (require pull_request reviews, require_status_checks) and GitLab via PUT /projects/:id/protected_branches (protect and set allowed_to_push). Verify by attempting git push and observing the rejection message and by confirming protection in the GitHub/GitLab UI or API.

7784. [Git Branching Strategies] How do you enforce signed commits?
Answer: Configure developers to sign locally and verify on the server. Locally: set a signing key and enable signing, e.g.
git config --global user.signingkey <GPG-key-id>
git config --global commit.gpgSign true
git commit -S -m "message"
Verify locally with git log --show-signature or git verify-commit <sha1>. Enforce on push with a pre-receive hook that checks every new commit: for each oldrev newrev ref read from stdin, run git rev-list "$oldrev..$newrev" | while read c; do git verify-commit "$c" || { echo "Unsigned commit $c"; exit 1; } done. Alternatively enable "Require signed commits" in GitHub/GitLab branch-protection settings to reject unsigned pushes.

7785. [Git Branching Strategies] What is semantic versioning?
Answer: Semantic versioning is a version format like MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH. Major changes indicate breaking changes, minor changes add backward-compatible features, and patch changes fix bugs without changing compatibility.

Detailed interview explanation:
Semantic Versioning belongs to the software delivery lifecycle. In interviews, explain how it helps teams move from source code to production safely. The key themes are automation, repeatability, traceability, testing, security validation, deployment control, and rollback.

Production example:
A production pipeline may start when a pull request is opened. CI runs unit tests, integration tests, static analysis, dependency scanning, and image scanning. After approval, the pipeline builds an immutable artifact, pushes it to an artifact registry, and deploys it using Kubernetes, Helm, Argo CD, Flux, or another deployment system. For production releases, teams add approval gates, canary or blue-green rollout, SLO checks, and rollback automation.

Best practices to mention:
- Keep pipeline definitions in Git and review them like application code.
- Promote the same immutable artifact across environments.
- Use secret managers and short-lived credentials instead of hardcoded secrets.
- Add automated checks for tests, security, policy, and deployment health.
- Measure delivery using DORA metrics: deployment frequency, lead time, change failure rate, and MTTR.

Common interview follow-ups:
You may be asked how to handle flaky tests, slow pipelines, failed deployments, manual approvals, artifact promotion, branch strategy, GitOps drift, or rollback. A strong answer connects the concept to faster feedback, safer releases, and better auditability.

7786. [Git Branching Strategies] What do major, minor and patch versions represent?
Answer: Under Semantic Versioning (MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH): MAJOR increments (e.g., 2.0.0 → 3.0.0) signal incompatible API changes/breaking changes; MINOR increments (e.g., 2.1.0) add backward‑compatible functionality; PATCH increments (e.g., 2.1.3) are backward‑compatible bug fixes. Practically, tag releases as vMAJOR.MINOR.PATCH (git tag -a v2.1.3 -m "…"; git push --tags) and record changes in a CHANGELOG. Use package manager semantics to enforce compatibility: npm install pkg@^2.1.0 allows upgrades <3.0.0, npm install pkg@~2.1.0 allows 2.1.x only. Verify available versions with npm view pkg versions and check consumers with npm outdated or cargo search for Rust crates.

7787. [Git Branching Strategies] What is conventional commits?
Answer: Conventional Commits is a lightweight commit message convention (v1.0.0) that enforces a structured format: <type>[optional scope]: <description>, with optional body and footer. Common types include feat, fix, docs, style, refactor, perf, test, chore. Use a "!" after type/scope or a "BREAKING CHANGE: <description>" footer to signal breaking changes and trigger a major semver bump. Example: git commit -m "feat(parser): add array parsing" or git commit -m "fix(ui)!: remove deprecated API\n\nBREAKING CHANGE: removed api.x()". Tooling verifies and automates releases: npx @commitlint/cli (with a config) enforces messages and npx conventional-changelog or semantic-release generates changelogs and determines next semver based on commit types.

7788. [Git Branching Strategies] How can conventional commits automate releases?
Answer: Conventional Commits enable automated releases by encoding intent in commit messages (e.g., "feat:" → minor, "fix:" → patch, "BREAKING CHANGE" → major). Tools like semantic-release or standard-version parse commits to determine the semver bump, update package metadata, generate CHANGELOG.md, create a Git tag, and publish packages. Typical setup: npm install --save-dev semantic-release @semantic-release/git @semantic-release/npm and add a .releaserc or package.json config; in CI run npx semantic-release (or use semantic-release GitHub Action). Verify results by inspecting generated CHANGELOG.md, listing tags with git tag -l, and confirming published version with npm view <pkg>@latest version. Automated releases require consistent commit messages and CI credentials for git/npm.

7789. [Git Branching Strategies] How do you manage release notes?
Answer: Maintain a single source of truth CHANGELOG.md generated from commit history (Conventional Commits) and automated in CI (e.g., npx semantic-release or conventional-changelog-cli). Create an annotated git tag for each release: git tag -a v1.2.3 -m "Release v1.2.3"; git push --tags. Publish releases to GitHub with the gh CLI: gh release create v1.2.3 CHANGELOG.md -t "v1.2.3" -n "$(sed -n '1,200p' CHANGELOG.md)". Verify artifacts and notes: gh release view v1.2.3 --repo owner/repo and git tag -l v1.2.3; inspect commits with git log v1.2.2..v1.2.3 --pretty=format:"%h %s". Automate and gate changelog generation in CI for reproducibility.

7790. [Git Branching Strategies] Which branching strategy is best for continuous delivery?
Answer: Trunk-based development is best for continuous delivery: teams commit small, short-lived changes directly to main (or integrate via short-lived feature branches merged within a day) and deploy continuously from main when CI passes. Use feature flags to keep incomplete work dormant. Operational controls: protect main (branch protection rules requiring successful status checks and required reviews), CI configured to run on push to main (GitHub Actions example: on: push: branches: [main]), and automated deployment only after green pipelines. Example commands: git checkout -b feature/x; git commit -m "..."; git push origin feature/x; merge quickly into main and git push origin main; tag releases with git tag v1.2.3 && git push origin --tags.
