9287. [SRE, Behavioural & Scenario Questions (861–1000)] Describe a failed architecture decision.
Answer: We picked synchronous multi-AZ PostgreSQL (synchronous_commit=on with synchronous_standby_names) to avoid data loss; writes blocked waiting for remote apply, causing p99 write latency spikes and periodic application timeouts. Detection: Grafana showed histogram_quantile(0.99, rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) rising, and psql "SELECT pid, state, write_lag, flush_lag, replay_lag FROM pg_stat_replication;" showed high write_lag. Remediation: switched to synchronous_commit=local to avoid cross-AZ round-trip on every transaction, deployed Patroni for automated leader election, added Prometheus alerts on pg_stat_replication lag and pg_is_in_recovery(), and verified reduced latency via the same Prometheus query and successful failover tests using patronictl.

9288. [SRE, Behavioural & Scenario Questions (861–1000)] Explain a successful automation project.
Answer: I automated blue/green Kubernetes deploys and infra provisioning using Terraform, GitLab CI, Helm, and Prometheus-based verification. Pipeline ran terraform plan && terraform apply -auto-approve for VPC/EKS, then helm upgrade --install myapp ./chart --namespace prod and kubectl rollout status deployment/myapp -n prod. A pre-cutover smoke test used curl -f http://myapp.prod.svc.cluster.local/health and a Prometheus API query curl -s 'http://prometheus:9090/api/v1/query?query=rate(http_requests_total[5m])' to confirm error rate <0.1% and p95 latency under 200ms. If checks failed, CI executed kubectl rollout undo deployment/myapp -n prod and opened an incident in PagerDuty via its API. Post-deploy, alerts and Grafana dashboards verified steady state.

9289. [SRE, Behavioural & Scenario Questions (861–1000)] Describe a GitOps implementation.
Answer: Store declarative cluster state (YAML/Helm/Kustomize) in Git with branch protection and signed commits; use Flux v2 or Argo CD as the reconciler to continuously apply Git to cluster. Flux: install controllers, use helmrepository/helmrelease or Kustomization CRs and image-reflector/image-automation controllers to update image tags; run flux reconcile kustomization <name> --with-source to force sync. Argo CD: argocd app diff <app> and argocd app sync <app> to apply. Verify by kubectl get pods, kubectl rollout status deployment/myapp, argocd app get <app>, or flux get kustomizations to confirm healthy/synced state, and alert via Prometheus/Grafana on reconciliation failures. Audit via git history and reconcile logs.

9290. [SRE, Behavioural & Scenario Questions (861–1000)] Explain your Kubernetes troubleshooting process.
Answer: Start by scoping: identify affected namespace, pods, and time window with kubectl get pods -n NAMESPACE --show-labels and kubectl get events -n NAMESPACE --sort-by=.metadata.creationTimestamp. Check pod state and logs: kubectl describe pod POD -n NAMESPACE and kubectl logs POD [-c CONTAINER] --previous. If live debugging needed, kubectl exec -it POD -n NAMESPACE -- sh or kubectl debug. Verify resource pressure with kubectl top pod/node and node conditions via kubectl describe node NODE and journalctl -u kubelet on the node. Validate control plane and API with kubectl get --raw /healthz and inspect kube-apiserver, controller-manager, scheduler logs. For network/storage, test connectivity with curl/ping/tcpdump inside pods and check PVC/PV with kubectl describe pvc PVC. Fix iteratively and confirm with kubectl rollout status deployment/DEPLOY -n NAMESPACE.

9291. [SRE, Behavioural & Scenario Questions (861–1000)] Describe a DNS outage scenario.
Answer: Authoritative nameservers for example.com were misconfigured after a zone transfer failed: secondary BIND servers had stale zone files and stopped answering due to an expired SOA serial and DNSSEC signatures timestamped beyond validity. Symptoms: clients time out resolving hostnames, web traffic fails despite healthy application backends. Operations: verify with dig NS example.com; dig @ns1.example.com example.com SOA; dig +trace www.example.com; check ttl and SOA serial. Inspect server health with sudo systemctl status named and journalctl -u named, and capture queries with sudo tcpdump -n -i eth0 port 53. Remediation: reload correct zone file, increment SOA serial, run rndc reload, ensure zone transfers (IXFR/AXFR) permitted, and verify resolution with dig from remote resolvers.

9292. [SRE, Behavioural & Scenario Questions (861–1000)] Explain pod crash debugging.
Answer: Start by kubectl describe pod <pod> --namespace <ns> and kubectl get events to see status, ExitCode, and reasons (ImagePullBackOff, OOMKilled, CrashLoopBackOff). Inspect logs with kubectl logs <pod> [-c <container>] and kubectl logs -p <pod> for previous attempts to get stack traces or startup errors. Check probes in kubectl get pod <pod> -o yaml and resource usage with kubectl top pod <pod> to detect CPU/memory throttling. On the node, use journalctl -u kubelet and dmesg for OOM/kubelet errors and crictl inspect/logs for CRI-level failures. Fix code, image, probe, or resource limits, then verify with kubectl rollout status deployment/<name> and confirm pod becomes Ready.

9293. [SRE, Behavioural & Scenario Questions (861–1000)] Describe a memory leak investigation.
Answer: I reproduced the leak under load, captured process memory and heap profiles, and compared snapshots to identify retained allocations. Commands used: ps aux --sort=-rss, top -H -p <PID>, pmap -x <PID>, smem -k, and for native builds valgrind --leak-check=full --show-leak-kinds=all ./app. For Java I collected GC stats and heap dumps: jstat -gcutil <PID> 1000, jmap -dump:live,format=b,file=heap.hprof <PID>, and jstack <PID> to correlate threads. For Go I used runtime/pprof and go tool pprof -http=:8080 ./binary heap.pprof. I fixed the root cause (e.g., unbounded cache/retained listeners), deployed a rolling release, and verified via repeated heap dumps and Prometheus metrics that RSS and heap usage stabilized.

9294. [SRE, Behavioural & Scenario Questions (861–1000)] Explain a CPU spike incident.
Answer: Symptoms: sustained host or container CPU at >80–100% with user/kernel time high, increased load average, slow responses. Triage commands: top or htop; ps aux --sort=-%cpu; mpstat 1; pidstat -p <PID> 1; perf top; strace -p <PID> to inspect syscalls; pmap -x <PID> and lsof -p <PID>. In Kubernetes: kubectl top pod/node, kubectl logs/describe pod, kubectl exec -- top. Mitigations: restart or roll Pods (kubectl rollout restart), scale replicas (kubectl scale or HPA), apply cgroup limits (cgroup v1: echo <quota_us> > cpu.cfs_quota_us; v2: echo "<max> <period>" > cpu.max), or restart service (systemctl restart). Verify by observing CPU fall with top/mpstat and alert resolution in monitoring (Prometheus CPU usage graph returning to baseline).

9295. [SRE, Behavioural & Scenario Questions (861–1000)] Describe node pressure handling.
Answer: Node pressure handling is when the kubelet detects resource shortages (MemoryPressure, DiskPressure, PIDPressure) and evicts or throttles pods to protect node/system processes. Kubelet uses Node Allocatable, qos classes, pod Priority/Preemption, and eviction settings (--eviction-hard, --eviction-soft, --eviction-minimum-reclaim or equivalent fields in KubeletConfiguration e.g., evictionHard: {"memory.available":"100Mi","nodefs.available":"10%","pid.available":"100"}). Verify with kubectl describe node (shows Conditions and Allocatable), kubectl get events (eviction events), and kubelet logs (journalctl -u kubelet) which include “eviction manager” messages and OOM kill info from dmesg. Resolutions include raising eviction thresholds, adding node resources, moving pods by taints/tolerations or PodPriority, and restarting kubelet after config changes.

9296. [SRE, Behavioural & Scenario Questions (861–1000)] Explain cluster autoscaler issues.
Answer: Common cluster-autoscaler issues: pods remain Pending because requests/limits, node selectors, affinities, taints/tolerations, or topology constraints prevent scheduling; cloud provider limits or max node group size block new node creation; scale-up latency from VM provisioning or API rate limits; scale-down blocked by PodDisruptionBudgets, DaemonSets, local-storage pods, or misdetected node utilization; node readiness/kubelet registration failures or mismatched instance types cause churn. Verify with kubectl get nodes, kubectl describe pod <pod>, kubectl -n kube-system logs deploy/cluster-autoscaler, kubectl top nodes, and cloud APIs (e.g., aws autoscaling describe-auto-scaling-groups or gcloud container clusters describe) to see scaling events and resource/ASG limits.

9297. [SRE, Behavioural & Scenario Questions (861–1000)] Describe API latency troubleshooting.
Answer: Start by defining baseline/SLAs and collect metrics: p50/p95/p99 and error rates. Query Prometheus with PromQL, e.g. histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le)). Capture distributed traces (OpenTelemetry/Jaeger) to find slow spans and dependency hotspots. Reproduce load with hey or ab (hey -z 30s -q 10 -c 100 https://svc/endpoint) and curl -v to inspect headers. Inspect network with tcpdump -i eth0 port 443 -w capture.pcap and ss -tnp to view connections. Check host/resource signals (top, pidstat, iostat), JVM (jstack/jmap) or container CPU/IO throttling, and proxy/load‑balancer config. Verify fixes by observing reduced p99 and trace span durations and rerunning synthetic checks.

9298. [SRE, Behavioural & Scenario Questions (861–1000)] Explain a database bottleneck issue.
Answer: A common database bottleneck is connection-pool exhaustion combined with long-running, unindexed queries causing high CPU and I/O wait. Symptoms: rising connection counts, queueing in the app, and high load averages. Verify with: psql -> SELECT count(*) FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE state = 'active'; check pg_stat_statements and run EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) for slow queries; use iostat -x 1 and sar to confirm high %iowait, and top or pidstat to see CPU hotspots. Remediation: add missing indexes, rewrite queries, limit concurrency at the app (HikariCP maxPoolSize), introduce read replicas for offloading, or scale vertically; validate by observing reduced active queries and lower iowait and response latency in application metrics.

9299. [SRE, Behavioural & Scenario Questions (861–1000)] Describe an observability improvement project.
Answer: [CONTEXT] Legacy microservices had poor coverage: sparse metrics, no distributed traces, high alert noise, and no SLOs; incidents required heavy log spelunking.
[ACTION] I instrumented services with OpenTelemetry SDKs, configured Prometheus scraping (service discovery via Kubernetes annotations), created cardinality-limited metrics, deployed Grafana dashboards and Loki for logs, enabled Jaeger for traces, and defined SLOs in Prometheus recording rules with Alertmanager routes and silences. I added synthetic HTTP checks with k6 and CI-run smoke tests. Verification included validating traces across forks in Jaeger, PromQL queries for latency p95/p99, Grafana panel drilldowns, and Alertmanager alerts firing only for SLO breaches.
[RESULT] Operationally faster root-cause discovery and targeted, actionable alerts.

9300. [SRE, Behavioural & Scenario Questions (861–1000)] Explain a service mesh issue.
Answer: Observed a spike in 503s from Envoy sidecars caused by mismatched TLS settings: a DestinationRule enabled mutual TLS but the ServiceEntry/Service still received plain HTTP, causing Envoy to fail handshakes and mark upstream clusters unhealthy. Verify with: kubectl get pods -n appns; kubectl logs <pod> -c istio-proxy -n appns; istioctl proxy-config clusters <pod> -n appns; istioctl proxy-status; and check Prometheus metrics istio_requests_total{response_code="503"} and envoy_cluster_upstream_cx_connect_fail. Remediate by correcting DestinationRule/mTLS mode or adding proper PeerAuthentication, rolling Pilot control plane (kubectl rollout restart deployment istiod -n istio-system), and confirm recovery via reduced 503s and healthy cluster endpoints in istioctl proxy-config clusters.

9301. [SRE, Behavioural & Scenario Questions (861–1000)] Describe a deployment rollback scenario.
Answer: After a canary caused increased error-rate alerts from Prometheus, I triggered a rollback: for Kubernetes Deployments I ran kubectl rollout undo deployment/my-app --to-revision=2 and then kubectl rollout status deployment/my-app --timeout=120s to ensure the old ReplicaSet scaled up. For a Helm release I ran helm rollback my-app 2 and verified with helm list --namespace prod and kubectl get pods -l app=my-app -n prod. I validated recovery by checking pod logs (kubectl logs), successful health-checks via curl to /health, Prometheus alert status and Grafana panels for error-rate and latency, and confirmed SLOs began to recover before closing the incident.

9302. [SRE, Behavioural & Scenario Questions (861–1000)] Explain blue-green deployment implementation.
Answer: Create two identical environments (blue=live, green=new). Deploy green, e.g., kubectl apply -f green-deployment.yaml and verify pods with kubectl rollout status deploy/green-deployment and kubectl get pods -l app=green. Run automated smoke tests against green’s health endpoint (curl -f http://green.example.internal/health) and validate telemetry (Prometheus error rate, latency). When green passes, switch traffic by repointing the Service/Ingress selector or swapping ALB target groups (aws elbv2 modify-listener --listener-arn <arn> --default-actions Type=forward,TargetGroupArn=<green-tg-arn>) or update Route53 records. Monitor error budget and logs (kubectl logs -l app=green). For DB changes, make migrations backward-compatible or use feature flags; rollback by switching traffic back to blue if issues are detected.

9303. [SRE, Behavioural & Scenario Questions (861–1000)] Describe canary deployment monitoring.
Answer: Canary deployment monitoring continuously compares baseline and canary slices on key SLIs (latency p95/p99, error rate, throughput, CPU/memory) during incremental traffic shifts. Instrumentation: Prometheus metrics, OpenTelemetry traces, and logs; Grafana dashboards and Alertmanager alerts. Typical checks: PromQL for latency (e.g., histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le, service))) and error rate (rate(http_requests_total{code=~"5.."}[5m])) compared between labels. Automate analysis with tools like Flagger (Canary CRDs + Prometheus) to promote or rollback using Kubernetes API (kubectl get canary -n, kubectl rollout undo deployment/<name>) and verify rollout via kubectl rollout status deployment/<name>. Use statistical tests or configured thresholds and abort/rollback on breach.

9304. [SRE, Behavioural & Scenario Questions (861–1000)] Explain infrastructure drift remediation.
Answer: Infrastructure drift remediation is detecting divergence between declared infra and live state, then reconciling them back to the desired configuration. Detect using tools: run terraform plan (compares config → state → provider) or CloudFormation’s aws cloudformation detect-stack-drift and describe-stack-resource-drifts, or continuous checks from AWS Config. Remediate by updating IaC or live resources and applying changes: terraform apply (or terraform apply -replace=module.foo.aws_instance.bar to force recreate), terraform import to bring an out-of-IaC resource into state, or update CloudFormation template and aws cloudformation deploy. Verify by re-running terraform plan (expect no changes) or aws cloudformation describe-stack-resource-drifts showing IN_SYNC, and by checking metrics/logs in Prometheus/CloudWatch to ensure behavior is stable.

9305. [SRE, Behavioural & Scenario Questions (861–1000)] Describe an IaC governance project.
Answer: Implemented organizational IaC governance using Terraform modules in a private registry, mandatory fmt/validate/tflint/conftest checks in CI, and centralized remote state with S3 backend plus DynamoDB locking. Pipeline runs: terraform init && terraform fmt -check && terraform validate && tflint && conftest test policy.rego && terraform plan -out=plan.tfplan; CI rejects non-zero exit codes. Policies (rego) block public AMIs, open security groups, and disallowed instance types; verified by conftest and by terraform show -json plan.tfplan to programmatically assert violations. Enforced merge controls via GitHub branch protections and required passing GitHub Actions. Drift detection configured with scheduled terraform plan runs and alerting to PagerDuty when drift or policy violations are detected.

9306. [SRE, Behavioural & Scenario Questions (861–1000)] Explain secret management implementation.
Answer: Implement secrets with a centralized secrets engine (e.g., HashiCorp Vault) backed by a durable store and auto-unseal via KMS, plus cloud native stores for apps. Configure auth methods (vault auth enable approle; vault write auth/approle/role/my-role secret_id_ttl=10m policies="app-policy"), policies, and dynamic secrets (vault secrets enable database; vault write database/config/...). Use AWS Secrets Manager/KMS for long‑lived secrets (aws secretsmanager create-secret; aws secretsmanager rotate-secret) and Kubernetes Secrets for cluster-local needs (kubectl create secret generic my-secret --from-literal=key=val; kubectl get secret my-secret -o yaml). Verify by fetching: vault kv get secret/my-app, aws secretsmanager get-secret-value --secret-id MySecret, and kubectl describe secret my-secret; enable audit logging and enforce IAM/policy least privilege.

9307. [SRE, Behavioural & Scenario Questions (861–1000)] Describe cloud migration planning.
Answer: Cloud migration planning defines scope, inventory, and phased runbooks: perform discovery (asset inventory via gcloud compute instances list and gcloud sql instances list), classify apps by TCO/complexity (rehost, replatform, refactor), map dependencies, and choose tooling (Migrate for Compute Engine for VMs, Database Migration Service for RDBMS, Storage Transfer Service or gsutil rsync for blobs). Design networking (VPC, subnets, Cloud NAT), identity and access (IAM roles, service accounts), security (Security Command Center, KMS for keys), cost estimates (GCP Pricing Calculator), and a rollback/DR plan. Validate with staging canaries, smoke tests, and metrics (Cloud Monitoring, Trace) plus pre/post checks (connectivity, latencies, data consistency) before cutover.

9308. [SRE, Behavioural & Scenario Questions (861–1000)] Explain a compliance audit experience.
Answer: [CONTEXT] I led the response for a quarterly SOC 2/ISO 27001 audit for a cloud-native service. [ACTION] I produced evidence: exported CloudTrail and AWS Config snapshots, ran Nessus and CIS Docker benchmarks, captured Kubernetes manifests with kubectl get --namespace prod pods, and uploaded signed artifacts to the auditor S3 bucket via aws s3 cp. I documented control mapping and remediation in Jira and applied fixes tracked to tickets. I verified remediation by re-running scans and using aws config get-resource-config-history to show configuration drift resolved, and provided sha256sum checksums for each artifact to prove integrity. [RESULT] The auditor accepted the evidence and closed all non-conformities.

9309. [SRE, Behavioural & Scenario Questions (861–1000)] Describe Kubernetes RBAC troubleshooting.
Answer: Check effective permissions first: use kubectl auth can-i <verb> <resource> [--namespace <ns>] and kubectl auth can-i --list [--as <user> | --as=system:serviceaccount:<ns>:<sa>] to emulate identities. Inspect bindings and rules: kubectl get rolebindings,clusterrolebindings -A -o yaml and kubectl describe role/<name> -n <ns>, kubectl describe clusterrole/<name>. Verify subjects match kind/name/namespace (ServiceAccount namespace matters). Remember scope: Role/RoleBinding are namespace-scoped; ClusterRole/ClusterRoleBinding are cluster-scoped. Check aggregated ClusterRoles and label selectors on aggregationRule. Review API server audit logs and kube-apiserver logs for denied requests and use kubectl --as to reproduce failures (e.g., kubectl get pods --as=system:serviceaccount:<ns>:<sa> -n <ns>). Fix by updating Role/Binding resources and re-testing.

9310. [SRE, Behavioural & Scenario Questions (861–1000)] Explain image vulnerability remediation.
Answer: Run automated image scans (Trivy, Clair, Anchore, or Docker scan) and triage results by CVSS, exploitability, and runtime exposure. Fix by updating the base image or specific packages in the Dockerfile, rebuild and retag (docker build -t myrepo/myimage:fix1 . && docker push myrepo/myimage:fix1). If urgent, apply package-level hotfixes or rebuild with a minimal base (distroless) and republish. Deploy via CI/CD or kubectl set image deployment/my-deploy my-container=myrepo/myimage:fix1 --record and monitor rollout (kubectl rollout status deployment/my-deploy). Verify remediation by re-scanning the pushed image (trivy image myrepo/myimage:fix1) and confirming the CVEs are no longer reported, and optionally validate runtime via cosign verify and runtime policy checks.

9311. [SRE, Behavioural & Scenario Questions (861–1000)] Describe reducing deployment time.
Answer: I reduced deployment time by parallelizing CI, optimizing image builds, and minimizing cluster work during rollout. Practically: enable BuildKit and layer caching (DOCKER_BUILDKIT=1 docker build --cache-from registry/myapp:cache -t registry/myapp:sha .), split pipeline stages and run test shards in parallel (pytest -n auto or GitLab CI parallel: 4), and push immutable images to a registry. Use Kubernetes rolling updates with tuned strategy (spec.strategy.rollingUpdate: {maxSurge: 1, maxUnavailable: 0}) and imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent to avoid re-pulls. Verify with pipeline timestamps and commands: kubectl set image deployment/myapp myapp=registry/myapp:sha -n prod; kubectl rollout status deployment/myapp -n prod --watch and monitor kube_deployment_status_replicas_updated in Prometheus.

9312. [SRE, Behavioural & Scenario Questions (861–1000)] Explain optimizing CI/CD pipelines.
Answer: Optimize CI/CD by reducing work, increasing parallelism, and improving reuse. Cache dependencies (GitHub Actions: actions/cache@v3 with key: ${{ runner.os }}-maven-${{ hashFiles('**/pom.xml') }}; GitLab CI: cache: paths: - .m2/repository). Enable Docker layer caching with BuildKit: DOCKER_BUILDKIT=1 docker build --cache-from myorg/app:latest -t myorg/app:sha. Parallelize tests (pytest -n auto) and jobs, use incremental/test‑selection (pytest --last-failed) and build artifacts to Nexus/Artifactory for reuse. Shift deploys to GitOps (Argo CD/Flux) and use canary/blue-green + feature flags and argo-rollouts for progressive traffic. Measure improvements with workflow run duration (gh run list/view, GitLab CI pipeline minutes) and cache hit rate, and validate deployments via kubectl rollout status deployment/myapp.

9313. [SRE, Behavioural & Scenario Questions (861–1000)] Describe a failed release.
Answer: A release introduced a DB migration that added a NOT NULL column without a default; new pods’ readinessProbe failed (schema mismatch), causing 500s and rapid pod restarts. I confirmed with kubectl get pods -n prod, kubectl logs -f deployment/myapp -n prod, and kubectl rollout status deployment/myapp -n prod; Prometheus showed a spike in http_server_errors (5xx) and Grafana dashboards matched elevated latency. I executed kubectl rollout undo deployment/myapp -n prod to restore the previous ReplicaSet, ran psql -c "SELECT count(*) FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE query LIKE '%ALTER TABLE%';" to verify no ongoing migrations, and monitored Prometheus/Grafana until 5xx rate returned to baseline and PagerDuty incidents cleared.

9314. [SRE, Behavioural & Scenario Questions (861–1000)] Explain disaster recovery testing.
Answer: Disaster recovery testing verifies that backups, failover procedures, and runbooks restore services to meet RTO/RPO objectives. Typical tests: tabletop reviews, partial functional failovers (restore DBs, reattach storage), and full failover into a DR site. Operational steps: define scope and success criteria, run automated playbooks, restore data (e.g., aws rds restore-db-instance-to-point-in-time --source-db-instance-identifier X), bring up infra (kubectl apply && kubectl rollout status deployment/name), switch DNS and verify resolution (dig + curl), validate data integrity (pg_dump/psql queries, compare sha256sum of restored files), measure recovery time, then failback and run a post-mortem capturing gaps and remediation. Verification and metrics must be recorded for compliance.

9315. [SRE, Behavioural & Scenario Questions (861–1000)] Describe backup restoration testing.
Answer: Schedule regular full and incremental restoration drills to a non-production environment, restoring from the same backup type your runbooks would use. Verify backup integrity with checksum (sha256sum) before restore, then perform restores like: for MySQL dumps use mysql < backup.sql, for PostgreSQL custom dumps use pg_restore -C -d postgres backup.dump, for EBS snapshots create-volume from snapshot and attach, or for RDS use aws rds restore-db-instance-from-db-snapshot. Validate data consistency (application smoke tests, counts, critical queries), confirm WAL/transaction replay for DBs, verify credentials and KMS access, and measure RTO/RPO against SLA. Record results, runbook gaps, and automate tests in CI for repeatability.

9316. [SRE, Behavioural & Scenario Questions (861–1000)] Explain a load balancer issue.
Answer: I diagnosed a load balancer outage caused by misconfigured health checks: targets were marked Unhealthy because the LB probed /healthz over HTTP while the app exposed only HTTPS and returned 301s. Verification steps: curl -v http://10.0.1.12:8080/healthz showed 301 → curl -v -k https://10.0.1.12:8443/healthz returned 200, tcpdump -nni eth0 port 80 confirmed probes hitting HTTP, and aws elbv2 describe-target-health --target-group-arn <arn> reported Unhealthy with reason "HTTP_4XX". Fix: updated ALB target group to use HTTPS port 8443 and health check path /healthz, then verified with aws CLI and observed targets become Healthy within the next two probe intervals.

9317. [SRE, Behavioural & Scenario Questions (861–1000)] Describe SSL certificate outage handling.
Answer: Detect via monitoring (expired cert alerts, TLS handshake errors, synthetic curl checks). Verify with openssl s_client -connect host:443 -servername host -showcerts and extract expiry: openssl x509 -noout -dates -in cert.pem. Check chain and OCSP (openssl ocsp or curl --cert-status). If expired, renew/import: certbot renew --dry-run for ACME, or aws acm import-certificate --certificate fileb://cert.pem --private-key fileb://privkey.pem --certificate-chain fileb://chain.pem then aws elbv2 set-listener-certificates --listener-arn <arn> --certificates CertificateArn=<arn>. Reload frontends (systemctl reload nginx or haproxy reload) and validate with curl -vI --tlsv1.2 --resolve host:IP:443 host. Confirm monitoring clears and document root cause.

9318. [SRE, Behavioural & Scenario Questions (861–1000)] Explain how you secure Kubernetes.
Answer: Enable RBAC (--authorization-mode=RBAC) and least-privilege roles (kubectl auth can-i...), disable anonymous access, and rotate certificates (kubelet --rotate-certificates). Enforce Pod Security Admission or OPA Gatekeeper policies to prevent privileged containers; set securityContext (runAsNonRoot, readOnlyRootFilesystem, allowedCapabilities drop) and use seccomp/AppArmor profiles. Apply NetworkPolicies to restrict pod-to-pod traffic and verify with kubectl get networkpolicies. Encrypt Secrets at rest via kube-apiserver --encryption-provider-config and enable audit logging (--audit-log-path) with a reasonable policy, then review with kubectl logs or external storage. Scan images (trivy), run kube-bench/CIS checks, set ServiceAccount automountServiceAccountToken: false, and verify posture with kubectl describe pod and audit log review.

9319. [SRE, Behavioural & Scenario Questions (861–1000)] Describe a platform engineering initiative.
Answer: Built a self-service Kubernetes platform using Terraform (terraform apply -auto-approve) to provision VPCs and EKS clusters, Argo CD for GitOps (argocd app create --repo https://git.example/repo --path apps --dest-server https://kubernetes.default.svc), and Helm for packaging (helm upgrade --install). Enforced policies with OPA Gatekeeper, RBAC roles and namespaces, and automated canaries via Flagger. Observability used Prometheus/Grafana (PromQL: sum(rate(http_requests_total[5m]))), alerting via Alertmanager (kubectl get pods -n monitoring; kubectl port-forward svc/alertmanager -n monitoring 9093:9093) and SLOs stored in Prometheus. Verification included terraform show, argocd app list, kubectl get nodes,pods -A, end-to-end deploy from Git push to Argo CD sync and canary promotion logged in Flagger events.

9320. [SRE, Behavioural & Scenario Questions (861–1000)] Explain how you define SLOs.
Answer: I define SLOs as a measurable target (e.g., 99.9% availability or 95th‑percentile latency ≤200ms) tied to customer‑facing SLIs, an error budget (1 − SLO) and explicit evaluation windows (e.g., rolling 30d and 7d). Implementation uses concrete telemetry: Prometheus recording rules and Grafana dashboards; SLIs like availability = 1 - sum(rate(http_requests_total{code=~"5.."}[30d])) / sum(rate(http_requests_total[30d])). Latency uses histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le)). Error budget burn is computed from those rates and triggers Alertmanager alerts when burn rate exceeds thresholds (e.g., 14× over 1h) to enforce mitigation.

9321. [SRE, Behavioural & Scenario Questions (861–1000)] Describe error budget enforcement.
Answer: Error budget enforcement ties SLO/SLI math to operational controls: when the measured error budget burn rate exceeds thresholds, teams activate graded responses. Verification uses real metrics and tooling (example Prometheus query: sum(rate(http_requests_total{code=~"5.."}[5m])) / sum(rate(http_requests_total[5m])) ). Alertmanager routes and Prometheus alert rules trigger on those queries; runbooks specify actions such as throttling, circuit-breaking, feature-flag rollback (e.g., via LaunchDarkly API), pausing releases in CI/CD, and automated rollbacks with kubectl rollout undo deployment/myapp. Track progress by querying SLO dashboards and replaying queries to confirm burn rate reduction and restored error budget.

9322. [SRE, Behavioural & Scenario Questions (861–1000)] Explain reducing infrastructure costs.
Answer: Use telemetry to find waste (CloudWatch, Prometheus: avg(rate(http_requests_total[5m])); kubectl top nodes/pods). Rightsize via instance-family changes and scaling: aws ec2 describe-instances to list, aws ec2 modify-instance-attribute --instance-id i-123 --instance-type t3.medium for downsizing (stop required), and use AWS Compute Savings Plans or Reserved Instances where steady. Enable autoscaling: create/adjust ASGs (aws autoscaling update-auto-scaling-group --auto-scaling-group-name my-asg --min-size 1 --max-size 10) and Kubernetes HPA (kubectl apply -f hpa.yaml). Use Spot for batch/worker fleets (aws ec2 request-spot-instances) and delete unattached EBS (aws ec2 describe-volumes --filters Name=status,Values=available; aws ec2 delete-volume). Verify savings with AWS Cost Explorer API (aws ce get-cost-and-usage).

9323. [SRE, Behavioural & Scenario Questions (861–1000)] Describe a monitoring dashboard you built.
Answer: [CONTEXT] Built a Grafana dashboard for a Kubernetes-hosted HTTP service using Prometheus and Loki for metrics and logs.
[ACTION] Created Grafana panels with PromQL expressions (e.g., rate(http_requests_total{job="svc"}[5m]), histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le))) and a logs panel querying Loki (query= {app="svc"} |= "error"). Provisioned via Grafana API: curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $API_KEY" -X POST -d @dashboard.json https://grafana.example/api/dashboards/db and added alerting rules in Prometheus using ALERTS and groups.yml, routed via Alertmanager to PagerDuty. Verified panels by curling Prometheus: curl 'http://prometheus.example/api/v1/query?query=rate(http_requests_total[5m])' and reproducing incidents to confirm alert firing.
[RESULT] Dashboard reduced MTTD and provided actionable drilldowns into traces and logs.

9324. [SRE, Behavioural & Scenario Questions (861–1000)] Explain a production debugging strategy.
Answer: Start by triage: confirm impact via alerts/Prometheus (query via /api/v1/query?query=error_rate) and Grafana panels, then isolate offending service or node. Collect logs and state: kubectl describe pod -n app; kubectl logs pod -c web --since=1h; journalctl -u kubelet -f; crictl ps / crictl logs. Reproduce safely using kubectl port-forward pod 8080:8080 and curl -v localhost:8080/health. Capture network and system state: tcpdump -i eth0 -w /tmp/cap.pcap and sudo gcore <pid> to produce a core. For CPU/memory profiling use go tool pprof -http=:9090 ./binary profile.pb.gz. Fix via config/rollback/rolling restart (kubectl rollout undo deployment/frontend) and verify by re-running Prometheus queries and sanity curl checks.

9325. [SRE, Behavioural & Scenario Questions (861–1000)] Describe improving deployment reliability.
Answer: Use proven practices: push all changes through CI with unit/integration/e2e and smoke tests; deploy via blue-green or canary releases (Kubernetes rolling updates or Istio traffic-splitting). Example commands: kubectl set image deployment/myapp myapp=registry:tag && kubectl rollout status deployment/myapp && kubectl rollout undo deployment/myapp. Use feature flags (LaunchDarkly or Unleash) to limit exposure. Validate post-deploy with automated health checks (curl -f http://svc/healthz) and observability: Prometheus queries (sum(rate(http_requests_total[5m])) by (code)), Grafana dashboards, and alerting tied to SLOs/error budgets. Automate rollback on health failures, runbook-triggered incident playbooks, and run chaos tests in staging to verify resilience.

9326. [SRE, Behavioural & Scenario Questions (861–1000)] Explain handling conflicting priorities.
Answer: I prioritize by impact to customer-facing SLOs, time sensitivity, and single-threaded owner availability: I consult the on-call runbook and PagerDuty priority, confirm impact via Prometheus (e.g., rate(error_count[5m]) or grafana dashboard) and alert groupings, and then classify work as P0/P1/P2. For conflicting P0s I escalate to the service owner or engineering manager and apply RACI to assign execution; for lower-priority work I reassign or queue in Jira with SLA and acceptance criteria. I verify resolution by repro steps (curl -I healthcheck), kube checks (kubectl get pods -n NAMESPACE; kubectl logs) and by confirming alerts clear and SLO error budget usage returns to normal.

9327. [SRE, Behavioural & Scenario Questions (861–1000)] Describe a difficult team conflict.

[ACTION] I facilitated a rapid RFC: gathered error logs and metrics (Prometheus queries, 5xx rates, latency percentiles), ran a fail-safe rollback plan using kubectl rollout undo for the deployment, opened an incident channel, and coordinated a follow-up hotfix with CI/CD gated by automated tests. I enforced a decision timeline (10 minutes) and documented agreed criteria for rollback vs. patch.
[RESULT] The rollback restored service within 8 minutes, hotfix deployed later with zero regressions, and the team adopted the documented decision criteria for future incidents.

9328. [SRE, Behavioural & Scenario Questions (861–1000)] Explain how you handle criticism.
Answer: I treat criticism as data: I listen without interrupting, restate the concern to confirm (e.g., “You’re seeing X, Y, Z?”), and reproduce or validate it—using curl -v or kubectl describe pod, checking Prometheus metrics and Grafana panels for the same timeframe. I prioritize fixes by impact, propose a short remediation plan, implement in a canary (kubectl apply, then kubectl rollout status), and verify with automated tests and monitoring before full rollout. I document decisions and actions in the incident ticket (Jira) and a postmortem with measurable outcomes and follow-up owners. I acknowledge mistakes, thank the critic, and close the feedback loop with results.

9329. [SRE, Behavioural & Scenario Questions (861–1000)] Explain a leadership experience.

9330. [SRE, Behavioural & Scenario Questions (861–1000)] Describe your communication style.
Answer: I communicate succinctly, data-driven, and role-aware: during incidents I post a short situation summary, current impact, owner, and next action in the incident Slack channel and PagerDuty incident with timestamps, e.g., "Impact: 10% traffic loss; Owner: svc-team; Next: rollback v2 -> v1 in 10m." I follow RACI and use read-backs and explicit ACKs (Slack reaction or "ack" message) to confirm alignment. I document commands run and outputs in the incident timeline (kubectl get pods -n svc, curl checks) and update Confluence/postmortem with timeline, root cause, and corrective actions. For stakeholders I provide regular ETA-driven updates and a final resolution summary on Statuspage.io.

9331. [SRE, Behavioural & Scenario Questions (861–1000)] Explain a project delay and recovery.

9332. [SRE, Behavioural & Scenario Questions (861–1000)] Describe your biggest technical achievement.

9333. [SRE, Behavioural & Scenario Questions (861–1000)] Explain your biggest failure.
Answer: [CONTEXT] I deployed a schema migration during peak traffic that I hadn’t tested end-to-end against the production dataset; the migration added a NOT NULL column with a default that caused a long table rewrite and caused 30% increased p99 latency and several timeouts.
[ACTION] I executed an emergency rollback by restoring a consistent backup snapshot, scaled read replicas, and applied PostgreSQL pg_cancel_backend to stop the long-running ALTER; I ran the migration in a blue-green fashion on a staging copy and validated with pgbench and synthetic traffic, added a slow_migration Grafana dashboard and Prometheus alert for ALTER/long-running queries.
[RESULT] Postmortem documented the change: require non-blocking migrations, rollback runbooks, and CI tests that run migrations against production-sized data before deploy.

9334. [SRE, Behavioural & Scenario Questions (861–1000)] Describe a time you learned quickly.

9335. [SRE, Behavioural & Scenario Questions (861–1000)] Explain how you handle ambiguity.
Answer: I break ambiguity into measurable questions, state assumptions, and run small experiments with clear success criteria. I timebox investigation, prioritize hypotheses by user impact and error budget/SLO risk, and implement safe mitigations (rollback or canary via kubectl set image / incremental traffic shift). 9336. [SRE, Behavioural & Scenario Questions (861–1000)] Describe working with cross-functional teams.
